assignments.description:
A01 — Unofficial transcript

Due: Wednesday of Semester Kick Off Week, by end of day.

Your unofficial transcript is the "receipt" of your college journey so far:

  • Transcript = what you've done
  • Progress report (A02) = what you still need
  • Degree plan (A03) = how you're going to finish strong

What students will submit

Submit two files in Canvas:

  1. Transcript PDF — export/download your unofficial transcript as a PDF. File name: {COURSE}_A01_UnofficialTranscript_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf
  2. Quick reflection (short write-up) — a short reflection as PDF or Markdown. File name: {COURSE}_A01_TranscriptReflection_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf (or .md)

Requirements

Part 1 — Get your unofficial transcript (PDF)

  • Log in to your institution's student portal / single sign-on.
  • Open the self-service system.
  • Find "Unofficial Transcript."
  • Download/export as PDF.
  • Confirm the PDF opens and looks readable (not blank, not sideways, not one pixel tall).
  • Look at your GPA and make sure you can live with it, or have a plan to fix it.
  • Check for any transfer credit that should be there but is missing.
  • Give it a vibe check for anything that feels off from your lived experience.

Part 2 — Reflection (answer all prompts)

In 5–10 sentences total, answer:

  • What surprised you when you looked at your transcript?
  • What's one thing you're proud of so far?
  • What's one thing you want to improve this semester (study habits, attendance, time management, asking for help, etc.)?
  • Any issues to flag (missing credit, repeated course, transfer credit weirdness, hold, incorrect grade posting)?

If you spot something that looks wrong, that's not "bad news" — that's useful intel. Bring it up early so it can get fixed.

Privacy / safety rules (important)

  • Do not post your transcript anywhere public (GitHub, Discord, etc.).
  • Submit only through Canvas.
  • If your transcript contains sensitive information (it often does), keep it private and don't share it with classmates.

Common problems + fixes

  • "I can't find the transcript option." Search your self-service system for "transcript" and look for "unofficial transcript."
  • "My transcript looks wrong." Submit what you can and mention the issue in your reflection — it'll get handled together.
  • "I have a hold and can't access it." Submit a screenshot of the hold message (if allowed) and write what happened in the reflection.

Notes (instructor)

This pairs with A02 (Progress Report) and A03 (Degree Plan). Goal: know what it takes to graduate — identify issues early, and start planning with accurate data. See rubrics/A01_rubric.md for grading.

assignments.description:
A02 — Progress report

Due: Wednesday of Semester Kick Off Week, by end of day.

Why we're doing this

Your progress report (from the registrar) is the closest thing to "the truth in writing" about your degree requirements. It shows what you've completed, what still remains, and where your gaps are. This assignment makes sure you know how to find it and how to read it — the same software that runs your graduation check produces this report.

What you will submit

Submit two items:

  1. Progress Report PDF — export your progress report from your institution's self-service system as a PDF.
  2. Short summary — either a Canvas text entry, or a second page in the same PDF.

File naming (PDF): {COURSE}_A02_ProgressReport_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf — e.g. CS1_A02_ProgressReport_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fall.pdf.

Step-by-step instructions (how to get the report)

  1. Log in to your institution's single sign-on.
  2. Open self-service (the same system where you access other student tools).
  3. Search for "Progress Report."
  4. Open your report and export/download as PDF.
  5. Save it somewhere you can find it again — you'll use it again for A01.

Summary requirements (your written part)

Write 6–10 sentences that answer these prompts:

  1. What degree/major does the progress report show?
  2. What areas/categories are listed (Gen Ed, major core, electives, etc.)?
  3. List 3 specific requirements you still need (courses or requirement blocks).
  4. Identify one thing that surprised you, or one part you don't understand yet.
  5. What's your next step? (E.g. "I need to ask an advisor about ," or "I need to plan when I'll take .")

If something looks wrong

If anything seems incorrect or missing, say so in your summary and include the exact section name you're referencing. Don't panic — just document it.

Need help?

If you can't find the report or something looks unexpected, message the instructor.

See rubrics/A02_rubric.md for grading.

assignments.description:
A03 — Personal semester-by-semester degree plan

Due: Wednesday of Semester Kick Off Week, by end of day.

Why we're doing this

This assignment helps you build a realistic plan for graduation. You'll use your unofficial transcript (A01), progress report (A02), and your institution's catalog/schedule to map out your remaining semesters and confirm prerequisites and course availability. Connect the dots and land on the semester you actually expect to graduate.

This is a planning tool you should keep and update all semester — bring it to advising appointments. (Tape it to your wall for the days you want to give up.)

What you will submit

Upload one PDF, exported from a spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets).

File naming: {COURSE}_A03_DegreePlan_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf — e.g. CS1_A03_DegreePlan_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fall.pdf.

Requirements (what must be in your spreadsheet)

1) Title + basics (top of page) — your name; major (and minor if applicable); option (if applicable); your expected graduation semester (e.g. "Spring 2028").

2) Semester-by-semester plan (the main table) — list every semester from now until graduation. For each planned course: course prefix/number, course name, credits, and optional notes ("needs prereq," "only offered fall," etc.). For each semester: total credits.

3) Prerequisites + reality check — show evidence you checked your institution's course catalog/schedule offerings, your progress report (what remains), and your unofficial transcript (what's completed). This can be a short "checked list," notes in a dedicated column, or a small "Verification" box.

4) Two scenarios (minimum) — e.g. Scenario A (~12 credits/semester) and Scenario B (~18 credits/semester with summer classes). For each, show the expected graduation term and what changes between the two plans.

5) Advising notes / questions — a short list (minimum 2 items) of questions or notes for an advisor, e.g. "Is Course X offered every spring?" or "Do I need an elective in category Y?"

Step-by-step instructions (how to build it)

  1. Open Excel or Google Sheets.
  2. Create a sheet named "Degree Plan."
  3. Add your title + graduation target at the top.
  4. Build your main table (suggested columns: Semester | Course # | Course Name | Credits | Notes).
  5. Add semester totals (a SUM at the bottom of each semester block works).
  6. Duplicate the sheet (or add a second section) for Scenario B.
  7. Export as PDF (Excel: File → Export → Create PDF; Google Sheets: File → Download → PDF).

Late / revision notes

If something doesn't make sense (missing prereqs, unsure offering), mark it clearly as a question — don't guess silently. Planning is allowed to be imperfect; hiding uncertainty is not.

Need help?

If anything looks unexpected in your progress report or transcript, message the instructor.

See rubrics/A03_rubric.md for grading.

Credits, prerequisites considered, offerings checked
Included and clearly explained (e.g. 12 cr/semester vs. 18 cr/semester + summer)
Readable, labeled, totals included
Correct format + filename

assignments.description:
A08 — Degree Reflection

Due: Wednesday of Semester Kick Off Week, alongside A01–A03, by end of day.

Why this is a separate assignment

A01–A03 prove you can find the data (transcript, progress report, degree plan) and read it correctly. This assignment is graded on whether you actually thought about what that data means for you. It is deliberately not a paragraph folded into the end of A01 or A03 — it is its own assignment, with its own points, and every question below is its own graded line. Reflection is the part of Semester Kick Off Week that's easiest to skip when it's buried as an afterthought in another assignment's write-up. Making it separate, numbered, and individually pointed is this course's way of saying: this isn't filler, it's the point of the week.

Where this structure comes from

The questions below borrow their shape from two goal-setting/productivity frameworks — Michael Hyatt's Your Best Year Ever (naming what excites you and what you're afraid of, then converting both into a real plan) and Free to Focus (sorting what's ahead of you instead of just reacting to it). You don't need to have read either book. The questions stand on their own; the framework just explains why they're shaped the way they are, in case you're curious.

Using an LLM here (encouraged, with one boundary)

Use an LLM to think wider, not to think for you:

  • Stuck on Q5 (three mitigating ideas)? Ask an LLM to brainstorm eight or ten, then pick your own three and say why.
  • Not sure what a class or requirement actually involves? Ask an LLM to summarize a syllabus or department page you paste in, then react to that summary in your own words.

The choice, the reasoning, and the plan have to be yours. An LLM that writes your answer for you defeats the purpose — this assignment exists to find out what you think about your own degree, not what a model guesses a good student would say. Grading can tell the difference (see rubrics/A08_rubric.md): a generic, could-be-anyone answer scores lower than a specific one, regardless of how polished the writing is.

What you will submit

A Canvas text entry (no file upload) with nine numbered answers, answered individually — don't merge them into one essay. Numbering them separately is what makes each one gradable, and visible, on its own.

Part 1 — What excites you

Q1. Which class or requirement still ahead of you excites you the most? Name it specifically — a course number and title if it's a single course, or the exact requirement category (e.g. "the lab science requirement," not "gen eds" or "a science class") if it isn't tied to one course yet — and say why. (2 pts)

Q2. What's the best use of your time between now and when you take it, so you actually get the most out of it — not just survive it? (2 pts)

Q3. How does that class connect to the career you're aiming for? Name the specific job-market skill or requirement it builds toward — be concrete, not "it'll help in general." (2 pts)

Part 2 — What worries you

Q4. What are you afraid of for your degree — a specific class, requirement, or milestone? Name it. ("Math" is not an answer; "Calculus II, because I barely passed Calculus I" is.) (2 pts)

Q5. List three mitigating ideas for that situation — three genuinely different approaches, not three phrasings of the same one idea. (3 pts — 1 per distinct, real idea)

Q6. Which of the three is your favorite — the one you'll actually act on? Why that one, and not the other two? (2 pts)

Q7. Given that choice, what's the best use of your time between now and when you face it? (2 pts)

Q8. How will closing this gap help your career — what specific job-market skill or requirement does it protect? (2 pts)

Part 3 — Why it matters

Q9. Look back at your A03 degree plan. Name one place it truly reflects what you value, and one place it doesn't yet — and what would have to change (in the plan, or in you) to close that gap. (3 pts)

Total: 20 points

Need help?

If a question doesn't apply cleanly to your situation (undeclared major, transferring soon, etc.), answer it for the closest real version of your situation and say so — don't skip it silently.

See rubrics/A08_rubric.md for grading.
assignments.name: A08 — Degree Reflection

rubric.long_description: Q1 (2 pts) — names a specific exciting course/requirement with a real personal reason, not a generic "I like this subject." Q2 (2 pts) — a concrete action before that class, not "study hard." Q3 (2 pts) — a specific job-market skill/requirement it connects to, not "it'll help in general."

Q4 (2 pts) — names a specific feared class/requirement/milestone, not a vague subject area. Q5 (3 pts total, 1 pt per genuinely distinct mitigating idea, up to 3 — three restatements of one idea score 1, not 3) — three mitigating ideas. Q6 (2 pts) — a real reason for the favorite idea: fit, feasibility, or past experience, not "I don't know, this one."
Q7 (2 pts) — a concrete action tied to the specific idea chosen in Q6. Q8 (2 pts) — names a specific job-market skill/requirement that closing the gap protects.
Names one specific point of fit and one specific point of tension with A03, plus what would change to close it (one holistic 0–3 judgment, not sub-divided further).

assignments.description:
A04 — Resume

Due: Friday of Semester Kick Off Week, by 4:00 PM.

Why we're doing this

Your resume is a living document, not a one-time chore before you need a job. This assignment kicks off the habit: get a real, current resume on file now, then keep building it all semester with the 3-2-1 CV/resume habit taught earlier today (3 daily notes, 2 weekly CV paragraphs, 1 monthly resume bullet).

This is a first draft. There's a check-in later in the semester where you revisit and strengthen it — this version just needs to be real and current, not perfect.

Remember: CV = your full story. Resume = your best highlights for one job. If you kept the 3-2-1 habit going since Week 1, this is curation, not a panic-write.

What you will submit

Upload one document (PDF preferred; Word is acceptable).

File naming: {COURSE}_A04_Resume_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf — e.g. CS1_A04_Resume_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fall.pdf.

Requirements

1) Create or update your resume. Include sections for contact information, work experience, education, skills, and accomplishments.

  • Recent high school graduate? Include relevant high school achievements (leadership, activities, awards, work).
  • Been out of school a while? Focus on your more recent accomplishments.

2) Use achievement framing, not duty framing. Apply the STAR bullet formula from Friday of Semester Kick Off Week: [Power verb] + [what you did / context] + [result or benefit]. "Resolved 15+ customer issues per shift, improving satisfaction" beats "Responsible for customer service."

3) Save it as a document you'll keep updating. This isn't a one-time submission — you'll be adding to it and refining it throughout the semester.

Getting feedback

  • Visit Career Services or the Writing Center.
  • Ask your advisor, an instructor, or a mentor to review it.
  • Watch a LinkedIn Learning video on resume writing for extra tips.

Need help?

If you don't have much work experience yet, ask the instructor — projects, coursework, and volunteer work all count.

See rubrics/A04_rubric.md for grading.

rubric.long_description: Contact info, work experience, education, skills, accomplishments all present

assignments.description:
A05 — Dream Job Paper

Due: Friday of Semester Kick Off Week, by 4:00 PM.

Why we're doing this

This isn't a hypothetical exercise. Naming a real job you could actually apply for — now or in a few years — turns "career" from a vague worry into a specific target you can plan toward. It also feeds directly into A06 — Professional Gap Analysis, due the following week: you can't measure the gap between where you are and where you're going until you've named where you're going.

What you will submit

A short paper (roughly 1–2 pages, or as your instructor specifies).

File naming: {COURSE}_A05_DreamJobPaper_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf — e.g. CS1_A05_DreamJobPaper_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fall.pdf.

Requirements

1) Choose a specific, real dream job. Not "something in tech" or "something creative" — an actual job title/role you could realistically apply for, whether now or after you finish your degree.

2) Research the job. Look into:

  • Education, skills, and experience it requires
  • Day-to-day responsibilities and typical work environment
  • Career advancement opportunities from that role

3) Write an essay covering:

  • Why this is your dream job — what excites you about it, what you find most appealing.
  • How it aligns with your skills and interests — how your current skills, education, and experience make you a fit (or what's missing — that's fair game to name here, you'll dig into it in A06).
  • What it would take to get there — a realistic first step or two.

Need help?

If you're not sure what you want yet, that's normal — pick the closest real target you can find and treat this as a first draft of a direction, not a lifetime contract.

See rubrics/A05_rubric.md for grading.

assignments.description:
A06 — Professional Gap Analysis

Due: Friday of Semester Kick Off Week, by 4:00 PM.

Why we're doing this

Knowing your dream job (A05) is only half the picture. This assignment compares who you are right now against what that job actually requires — so your remaining semesters (and your degree plan from Semester Kick Off Week's A03) can target real gaps instead of guessing.

What you will submit

A short written analysis (roughly 1–2 pages, or as your instructor specifies).

File naming: {COURSE}_A06_GapAnalysis_Last_First_Year_Semester.pdf — e.g. CS1_A06_GapAnalysis_Evert_Jeremy_2003_Fall.pdf.

Requirements

1) Name your target job. Use the dream job from A05 (or refine it if your thinking has changed since then).

2) Assess your current skillset. List what you currently have — both hard skills (technical abilities) and soft skills (communication, teamwork, leadership, etc.).

3) Conduct the gap analysis. Compare your current skillset against what the job actually requires. Name the specific skills and qualifications you're missing.

4) Build an action plan. For each gap, name a concrete action (a course, a certification, a project, an internship, relevant experience) and a realistic timeline for closing it.

5) Reflect. A few sentences on what you learned from doing this analysis — anything that surprised you, or changed how you're thinking about your remaining semesters.

Need help?

If you're not sure what a job actually requires, look at real job postings for that role, not just a job title's general reputation.

See rubrics/A06_rubric.md for grading.
assignments.name: A06 — Professional Gap Analysis

rubric.long_description: Real hard + soft skills listed, not generic filler
Specific, named gaps between current skillset and target job requirements
Concrete actions (courses, certifications, projects, experience) with realistic timelines
Genuine sentence-level reflection on what the analysis revealed

assignments.description:
A09 — Career Reflection

Due: Friday of Semester Kick Off Week, alongside A04–A06, by 4:00 PM.

Why this is a separate assignment

A04–A06 prove you can build a resume, name a real target job, and compare your skills against it. This assignment is graded on whether you actually thought about what that target job means for you — what you're looking forward to, and what genuinely worries you about it. Like A08, it's separate from A04–A06 on purpose, with its own points on its own numbered lines, so there's no ambiguity about whether reflection is optional. It isn't.

Where this structure comes from

Part 1 borrows from the idea of a "Desire Zone" (from Michael Hyatt's Free to Focus) — the parts of a job where you're both good at the work and genuinely want to do it, as opposed to work you can do but dread. Part 2 borrows from the same book's sorting habit — name the hard thing honestly, then find a real way to handle it, rather than hoping it resolves itself. Part 3 borrows from Your Best Year Ever's "find your why." You don't need to have read either book.

Using an LLM here (encouraged, with one boundary)

Use an LLM to research and widen your options — summarize a real job posting, generate more mitigating strategies than you'd think of alone, or role-play what a day in that job might actually look like. Then decide for yourself and write the decision in your own words. An LLM writing the final answer for you defeats the point — grading rewards specific, personal reasoning over generic polish (see rubrics/A09_rubric.md).

What you will submit

A Canvas text entry (no file upload) with nine numbered answers, answered individually — don't merge them into one essay.

Part 1 — What you're eager for (the Desire Zone)

Q1. From your A05 dream job, what specific part of the work are you most eager for? Name the actual task or responsibility (not just "the job" or "the money"), and say why. (2 pts)

Q2. Which class, project, or experience — name it specifically — best prepares you for that part? (2 pts)

Q3. What's the best use of your time this semester to build toward it? (2 pts)

Part 2 — What will be hardest

Q4. What part of this career do you expect to be the most difficult? Name a specific skill, task type, or environment — not "it'll be hard." (2 pts)

Q5. List three mitigating strategies for that difficulty — a course, a habit, a person to ask, a project to attempt. Three genuinely different approaches, not one idea said three ways. (3 pts — 1 per distinct, real idea)

Q6. Which is your favorite — the one you'll actually act on? Why that one, and not the others? (2 pts)

Q7. Which class, skill, or experience between now and graduation most directly addresses this difficulty? (2 pts)

Q8. What's your concrete next step, and by when? (2 pts)

Part 3 — Why it matters

Q9. How does this career direction align with your values? Name one place of real fit, and one place of real tension — and how you'd resolve the tension. (3 pts)

Total: 20 points

Need help?

If you're between two target jobs, pick the one you named in A05 and answer for that one — you can revisit the other later.

See rubrics/A09_rubric.md for grading.

A07 — Advisor name and meeting time

Due: When registration/enrollment opens for next semester. (Exact date is set by the registrar's calendar each term — confirm the real date before publishing this to students.)

Why we're doing this

Your academic advisor is the person who can catch problems your degree plan (A03) and progress report (A02) can't — substitution rules, graduation-application deadlines, sequencing quirks specific to your program. Knowing who your advisor is and having an actual meeting on the calendar is a small task that prevents big problems later.

This is timed to when you can actually act on your advisor's guidance — right as registration for next semester opens, not buried earlier when there's nothing yet to register for.

What you will submit

A short Canvas text submission (no file upload required).

Requirements

  • Set up an appointment with your academic advisor.
  • Submit your advisor's name and the date of your upcoming meeting.
  • If you've had difficulties with your advisor in the past, briefly share what happened — that's useful, not a complaint that gets you in trouble.

If you don't know who your advisor is, or aren't happy with your current one

Reach out to your department chair. They can help you get connected to the right advisor — and it's fine to say plainly why you want a change.

Need help?

If anything about the appointment process is confusing or something unexpected comes up, message the instructor.

See rubrics/A07_rubric.md for grading.

A10 (Optional / Bonus) — Success Foundations Reflection

This assignment is optional bonus work, not required. It has no fixed due date tied to A04–A06/A09 or the rest of Kickoff Week's Friday load — complete it whenever you like during the semester. (Earlier, this was briefly assigned as required, graded work due the same day as A04-A06/A09; Jeremy reversed that call the same day — see semester_kickoff_week/success_foundations_supplemental/README.md for the history.)

Why this is here

Building a resume (A04), naming a real target job (A05), and comparing your skills against it (A06) all raise the same question in the background: how do you actually get from where you are now to that job? This assignment lets you step back and think about that, using the mastery framework from the companion reading, success_foundations_reading.md (drawn from How Learning Works, Ch. 3). Complete the reading first; answer in your own words, not copied sentences from it.

What you will submit

A Canvas text entry (no file upload) with four numbered answers, 2–4 sentences each unless a question says otherwise.

Questions

  1. Recall/comprehension. The reading identifies three things learners need to develop mastery: component skills, integration/fluency of those skills, and knowing when/where to apply them. Pick one of the three and explain, in your own words, what it means and why it's not enough on its own. (3 pts)

  2. Recall/comprehension. What does the reading mean by "cognitive load," and what are the three types it names (intrinsic, extraneous, germane)? (2 pts)

  3. Application (required) — tie to A06. Use the same target job you named in A05/A06. Break the skill gap you identified in A06 into at least three component skills the way the reading describes breaking down "write a grant" or "analyze a case." Which of those component skills is currently your weakest, and how do you know? (3 pts)

  4. Application. The reading describes an "expert blind spot," where experienced people underestimate how much a novice needs explained. Describe one time you experienced this — either as the novice confused by an expert's shortcut, or as someone further along who caught yourself assuming something was obvious. (2 pts)

Total: 10 points (bonus)

These 10 points are real and gradable, but sit in Canvas's default, 0%-weighted assignment group rather than any of docs/grading-model.md's weighted categories — the same "ungrouped" placement A4 (Show and Tell reflection) uses. Whether points earned here can actually push a student's final percentage above 100% is a Canvas-mechanics question that depends on grading-scheme details this repo hasn't decided; treat this as "extra, optional, earns real points on record" rather than a confirmed boost to the final grade.

Source and Limitation Note

This assignment is derived from friday_entering_your_career/success_foundations_reading.md, itself drawn from How Learning Works, 2nd ed. (Ambrose, Bridges, DiPietro, Lovett, Norman), Chapter 3. No claims here go beyond what that reading already states.

See rubrics/A10_rubric.md for grading.

assignments.description:
Student Activity — AI I Week 2: Gather Context

Big Question: What information would make the AI answer dramatically better?

Last week you wrote down what you'd have to ask before a vague request was worth acting on. This week you supply it — and you decide how much of it is actually worth sending.

You don't need any prior AI experience for this activity, and you do not need to be able to write the program yourself. Your job is to specify it. You can work alone or with a partner.

The Scenario

The student who runs the campus coffee cart put a note on the department bulletin board:

"Can someone write me a program that calculates the total?"

That's the whole request. Your instructor will show an instructor-authored illustration: five clean lines that add up three arbitrary numbers and print The total is: 30. No bugs. No coffee. A live AI response can differ, but it still needs the missing information before it can address the coffee-cart task.

Step 1: Write Three Versions of the Same Request

Same task, three levels of context.

Version 1 — no context. This one's done for you. It's the request as posted:

"Write a Python program that calculates the total."

Version 2 — some context. Add what the task actually is. Someone types in a price and a number of drinks; the program prints a total. Write the request out in one or two sentences.

Version 3 — rich context. Add the rest. Work through these — most people skip at least two:

  • Audience. Who runs this program? And who wrote it — what has that person actually learned so far?
  • Background. What does the AI need to know about coffee that it can't get from the word "total"? (Start here: how many drinks can someone buy? Can it be 2.5?)
  • Constraints. How long should it be? Is anything off-limits?
  • Format. What should the output look like? Would you hand a customer a price that reads 14.549999999999999?

Step 2: Say What Each Version Still Has to Guess

Before you run anything, write down — for each of your three versions — what does the AI still have to guess?

This is the actual work of the activity. "Version 3 is better" is not an answer. "Version 2 doesn't say whether the number of drinks is a whole number, so the AI has to pick" is.

Step 3: Compare

If you have access to an AI tool:

  1. Submit Version 1. Save the response.
  2. Submit Version 2. Save it.
  3. Submit Version 3. Save it.
  4. Compare all three: for each one, what did the AI have to guess, and would this actually work for the coffee cart?

If you don't have tool access:

Your instructor will show three prepared programs, one for each version, and the class compares them the same way. (These are examples your instructor wrote to show the contrast, not real AI output — but the comparison works identically, and this is not a lesser version of the activity.)

Privacy reminder: The coffee cart is made up. Keep it that way — never paste real names, real contact information, real business details, or any private, protected, or confidential information into an AI system.

Step 4: The Test That Matters

Add these four sentences to your Version 3:

"The coffee cart has been running since 2019. It's usually busiest between classes. My favorite drink is the lavender latte. The cart is painted teal."

Every one of them is true in this fictional scenario. Every one is about the coffee cart. Which of them changes the program requirements? A live AI may still change wording or code for unrelated reasons; judge whether it changed anything that matters to the task.

If the answer surprises you, that's this week:

More context is not always better. Relevant context is better.

There's one test, and it isn't "is this true?" or "is this related?" It's: does it change the answer?

Step 5: Save Your Portfolio Artifact

Fill out your own Context Comparison Sheet using what you produced in Steps 1–4. If you worked with a partner, discuss together but complete your own sheet. Save it with your Problem Definition Card from last week — together they're one continuous piece of thinking, and you'll want both at the end of the course.

The last line of the Sheet is the one worth slowing down for: one true thing you deliberately left out, and why it wouldn't have helped. Anyone can add information. Knowing what to leave out is the harder half, and it's the difference between a good request and a long one.

Exit Ticket

Before you leave: in one sentence, what's the difference between context that changes the answer and detail that just makes the request longer?

Student Activity — AI I Week 3: Plan the Work

Big Question: Why should we ask AI to plan before we ask it to produce?

Last week you chose context that actually mattered and named what was still unknown. This week, use those facts before anyone drafts. Your job is to make the route visible—not to have AI write your CS1 work.

Start With Your Week 2 Handoff

Open your Context Comparison Sheet. Copy one context-selected task, one useful fact, and one consequential gap or assumption into your Plan-first Workflow. That real task is your default planning input.

If your task has a decision, use it for your own plan. If it does not, plan the whole route: settle needed information, name a real dependency, choose a task-appropriate checkpoint, and state what the eventual draft should do. If Week 2 ended with no open gap, carry forward one important gap you already settled or one assumption the plan still needs to check; do not invent a problem. The shared study-room scenario below is a complete common model for the CS1 branching connection and your fallback if you do not have the Week 2 sheet.

Shared CS1 Scenario

The campus library wants a tiny reminder program for a study room. A user enters an integer number of minutes remaining in a reservation. Expected valid values are 0 or greater. We trace -1 as an invalid test value and route it to “ended” only to keep this Week 3 condition-order example small. Production-quality input handling might reject the value and ask again; that later design is not part of this lesson.

The program should say:

Minutes remaining Message
0 or less Your reservation has ended.
1 through 10 Wrap up soon.
more than 10 Your room is still available.

This scenario is fictional. Do not use real names, reservation records, or private information in an AI tool.

Step 1: Start With What You Know

Write these on your Plan-first Workflow for your own carried-forward task. Use the study-room answers only if you are using the shared scenario:

  • One useful fact from last week's kind of work: the input is an integer number of minutes.
  • One gap that must be settled before drafting: does 0 mean ended or ending soon? For this task, it means ended.

Step 2: Plan Before Any Draft

Complete all six parts of your Workflow:

  1. objective;
  2. ordered stages;
  3. needed information;
  4. decision points or dependencies;
  5. risks; and
  6. quality checkpoints.

For a task with a decision, include: make a decision table, trace boundary values, and only then draft a branching chain. The shared CS1 scenario must use those stages. For a non-branching task, use another concrete pre-draft checkpoint, such as a hand calculation, required-information check, or exact-output check. A plan tells the route. It does not list separate modules, jobs, or interfaces—that is next week's question.

Step 3: Critique and Revise

For the shared case, check your plan with these values: -1, 0, 1, 10, and 11. For your own carried-forward task, choose comparable boundary values, decisions, calculations, requirements, or checkpoints.

Ask: “Will my route send each value to the intended message? Is a broad condition placed before a narrower one?” For a non-branching task, ask whether the route settles the needed facts and checks the exact result before drafting. Record one risk or assumption, then make one visible improvement to the route—an order, checkpoint, needed fact, or explanation. Revision shows what inspection taught you; it does not mean the first plan was a failure.

Step 4: Write Only After Revision

Complete the Write From the Revised Plan field. For a branching task, write one final plain-language decision rule. For the study-room example: “Check whether the reservation has ended before checking whether it is ending soon.” For a non-branching task, write a plain-language instruction or next-draft statement that follows from the route—for example, “Calculate the subtotal and tax, then check the exact two-decimal output before drafting the program.” In the associated CS1 work, you may use your own plan to write your own code. Do not copy code from an AI tool.

Step 5: Compare Two Workflows

If you have a course-approved AI tool, try both workflows:

  1. Use the instructor’s prepared direct-work draft as the immediate-write comparison. It is instructor-authored, not AI output.
  2. Ask a tool for a plan only: stages, needed information, risks, and quality checks. Ask it to critique the plan without writing code.

For the shared case, ask which workflow made the 0-minute decision visible sooner. For your own carried-forward task, name the key decision, dependency, assumption, or checkpoint that planning made visible sooner.

If you do not have a tool, use the instructor’s prepared direct-work draft and plan-first comparison. It gives you the same evidence and is not a lesser activity.

Step 6: Save Your Portfolio Artifact

Complete your own Plan-first Workflow, including its final plain-language write. Save it with your Problem Definition Card and Context Comparison Sheet. Your artifact is the plan, its revision, and the statement produced from that revised route—not a finished program.

Exit Ticket

In one sentence: what did the plan let you notice before a draft could hide it?

Student Activity — AI I Week 4: Decompose the Task

Delivery note: Monday is Labor Day, so this activity begins with a short introduction before Wednesday’s Professional Minds conversation. Complete the pipeline as light homework or carry-forward work.

Big Question: How do we split large AI tasks into smaller, safer, more useful pieces?

The Scenario

A campus team wants a proposal for a campus food pantry app. The app may help people learn pantry hours, understand available services, and plan a visit.

This is a fictional scenario. Do not add real names, student records, health information, food-access information, or other private details.

Step 1: See the Large Request

The large request is:

Create a proposal for a campus food pantry app. Identify users, define goals, gather requirements, list features, identify risks, build a timeline, draft the proposal, critique it, and revise it.

Before splitting it up, answer:

  • What decisions are hidden inside this request?
  • What could go wrong if the proposal were drafted immediately?

Step 2: Build the Pipeline

Use the portfolio artifact to create at least three ordered stages. The complete source example includes these possible stages:

  1. identify stakeholders;
  2. define goals;
  3. gather requirements;
  4. list features;
  5. identify risks;
  6. build a timeline;
  7. draft the proposal;
  8. critique the proposal;
  9. revise the proposal.

You may combine stages when you can explain why one boundary is enough. You may add a stage when it catches an important uncertainty.

For every stage, record:

  • Input: What information does this stage receive?
  • Action: What focused work happens here?
  • Output: What does this stage produce?
  • Quality check: How will you know the output is usable before moving on?

Step 3: Check the Handoffs

Inspect your pipeline:

  1. Does each stage have a usable input?
  2. Does each output become useful input for the next stage?
  3. Is the order justified?
  4. Is there a concrete check before an error spreads downstream?

For example, a feature should be connected to a requirement, and a requirement should be connected to a goal or stakeholder need.

Step 4: Identify the Dangerous Stage

Choose the stage that would be most dangerous to skip.

Explain:

  • what mistake could enter the work there; and
  • what later stage would be affected.

Example: If stakeholder identification is skipped, the requirements may ignore pantry staff or intended users, and the feature list may solve the wrong problem.

Step 5: Critique and Revise

Ask a classmate, instructor, or approved AI tool:

Which stage has the weakest boundary? What input is missing, what output is vague, or what quality check would fail to catch a likely error?

Record the critique. Then make one visible improvement to your pipeline and explain why the revision makes it safer or clearer.

If you use AI, use only fictional course information. AI access is optional; the instructor’s printed example supports the same work.

Step 6: Connect to CS1

CS1 branching uses smaller, testable decisions. A nested decision such as “first test urgency, then test eligibility” follows the same pattern as a pipeline: each stage has a boundary and a result that guides the next step.

Write one sentence explaining how your pipeline uses that same idea.

Save Your Portfolio Artifact

Complete and save the Decomposed Task Pipeline with your name, date, and week. Save it with your earlier AI I portfolio work.

Exit Ticket

Which stage would be most dangerous to skip, and what error could move downstream if you skipped it?

Student Activity — Select the Right Model

Big Question: How do we choose the right AI tool for the job?

The Scenario

You are checking two correct CS1 programs for this task:

Print the numbers from 1 through 5 exactly once.

A for solution is:

for number in range(1, 6):
    print(number)

A while solution is:

number = 1
while number <= 5:
    print(number)
    number += 1

Both print:

1
2
3
4
5

Your job is to choose which AI tool or mode is the better fit for explaining and checking this task.

You may use two free tools, two free modes of one tool, a locally available tool, or the printed responses provided by your instructor. You do not need a paid subscription.

Do not enter personal, confidential, or restricted course information into any tool.

Step 1: Use the Same Prompt

Use this prompt with both tools or modes:

Explain why this task can use either a for loop or a while loop. State which loop you would recommend for printing 1 through 5 and why. Mention one mistake that could cause an off-by-one or non-terminating loop. Do not write a different program.

Record the tool or mode names. If you use the printed fallback, label them Response A and Response B.

Step 2: Compare the Responses

Use these criteria:

  • correctness;
  • clarity;
  • speed;
  • cost or access;
  • usefulness for this exact task.

For each response, record concrete evidence. “It was better” is not evidence. Write what the response correctly explained, omitted, or made easier to use.

Step 3: Verify the CS1 Details

Check each response against the programs:

  • Does range(1, 6) include 1 and exclude 6?
  • Does the while loop update number?
  • Would number < 5 omit 5?
  • Would omitting number += 1 prevent termination?

Write one verification statement.

Step 4: Choose a Fit

Select the tool or mode that best fits this task.

Explain:

  1. Which task requirement mattered most?
  2. What evidence supports your choice?
  3. What trade-off did you accept?

A trade-off might be speed versus detail, brevity versus explanation, or access versus capability. There is not one required winner; your reasoning must fit the task.

Step 5: Save Your Portfolio Artifact

Complete the Model Comparison Table with your name, date, and week. Save it because it records how you made a tool decision and what evidence supported that decision.

Pair Check

With a partner, compare your recommendations. If you chose differently, identify which task requirement or trade-off caused the difference. Each student keeps an individual table.

Exit Ticket

What is one task requirement that could change which AI tool or mode you choose?

Student Activity — AI I Week 7: Research and Retrieve

Big Question: How do we ground AI output in trusted information?

The Scenario

You are checking a CS1 explanation about function return values. You will ask the same question two ways:

  1. without a source;
  2. with a short source excerpt.

Your goal is to notice what the source changes and whether the answer stays within the evidence.

Source Excerpt

A function is a named, reusable piece of a program. Parameters allow a function to receive information. A return value sends a result back to the part of the program that called the function. A returned result can be stored, printed, or used in another calculation. A function may perform an action without returning a value.

What RAG Means

RAG means retrieval-augmented generation.

In plain language, it means giving an AI relevant source material before asking it to answer. The source may be a lesson, syllabus, public article, policy, or dataset.

RAG can make an answer more specific and reduce guessing. It does not guarantee a correct answer: the source may be incomplete, the wrong source may be selected, or the answer may make claims beyond the source.

Complete the Comparison

Write your name, date, and week at the top.

1. Ask without the source

Prompt:

What is one purpose of a return value in a Python function?

Record the response you receive. If you are not using AI, use this prepared response:

A return value sends a result back to the code that called the function. The result can then be stored, printed, or used in another calculation.

2. Ask with the source

Prompt:

Use only the source excerpt below. What is one purpose of a return value in a Python function? Identify the supporting idea. If the excerpt does not establish something, say so.

Paste or attach the source excerpt above. Record the response you receive. If you are not using AI, use this prepared response:

One purpose of a return value is to send a result back to the part of the program that called the function. The result can then be stored, printed, or used in another calculation. The excerpt does not explain how Python represents a missing return value.

3. Compare

Answer each question:

  • What became more specific when the source was provided?
  • Which response identifies an idea supported by the excerpt?
  • Did either response make a claim the excerpt does not establish?
  • Which response would be more useful for a beginning CS1 student? Why?

Give at least two concrete observations. For example, name a claim, phrase, or omission.

CS1 Connection

Consider:

def add_fee(amount, fee):
    return amount + fee

A known test case is:

add_fee(10, 2) should return 12

Explain the analogy in 2–3 sentences:

How is checking this known function behavior like checking an AI answer against a source?

One Limitation or Use Case

Complete both sentences:

  • I would retrieve source material first when ______.
  • A source document does not guarantee a good answer because ______.

Exit Ticket

In one sentence:

When should you provide or retrieve source material before asking AI to answer?

Student Activity — AI I Week 8: Reason

Big Question: When do we need deeper analysis instead of quick generation?

Today you will analyze one decision: how to extract a room from a campus announcement. Your goal is not to produce the longest answer. Your goal is to make the decision inspectable.

Shared Scenario

A CS1 program receives announcements such as:

CS1 Lab | Room: SCI 204 | Bring laptop

The program needs to extract the room.

You are choosing among:

  • indexing a character at a known position;
  • slicing a known range of characters; or
  • searching for "Room: " and then slicing around it.

Step 1: Make a Quick Recommendation

Complete this sentence:

My quick recommendation is to use _ because _.

Step 2: Analyze the Recommendation

Answer all four questions:

  1. Recommendation: What method would you choose?
  2. Assumptions: What must be true for your choice to work?
  3. Tradeoffs: What does your choice make easier, and what does it make harder?
  4. Verification: What test or evidence would show whether your choice works?

Step 3: Challenge the Assumptions

Analyze these announcements:

CS1 Lab | Room: SCI 204 | Bring laptop

CS1 Lab | Bring laptop | Room: SCI 204

CS1 Lab | Bring laptop

For each one, write whether it supports your recommendation, challenges an assumption, or requires a new rule.

Step 4: Revise

Write one specific revision:

After checking the examples, I changed ______ because ________.

Your revision may change the method, add a condition, narrow the input format, or identify evidence you still need.

Step 5: Final Decision

Complete:

I would now ______. This decision depends most on _____. Before trusting it, I would test _______.

Optional AI Tutor

You may ask an approved AI tool:

Recommend whether this string task should use indexing, slicing, or searching. First state your recommendation, then list your assumptions, tradeoffs, uncertainty, and the evidence or tests that would change your recommendation. Do not write code.

AI use is optional. Do not enter personal, confidential, or real student information. Treat any response as a recommendation to inspect. You are responsible for the analysis and revision.

Portfolio Artifact

Save your completed Assumptions and Tradeoffs Analysis with:

  • your name;
  • the date;
  • Week 8;
  • your quick recommendation;
  • your analyzed recommendation;
  • assumptions;
  • tradeoffs;
  • uncertainty or missing information;
  • test cases or evidence;
  • your revision;
  • your final decision.

Exit Ticket

Which assumption mattered most in your decision, and what evidence would test it?

Student Activity — AI I Week 10: Critique

Big Question: How can AI help us find weaknesses in AI-generated work?

Scenario

A campus makerspace wants a checkout helper. Its goal is:

Create a checkout copy without changing the original inventory.

The first draft is:

inventory = {"markers": 12, "tripods": 3, "microphones": 2}

checkout = inventory
item = input("Item to check out: ")
checkout[item] = checkout[item] - 1

print("Original inventory:", inventory)
print("Checkout copy:", checkout)

For the input tripods, the program prints:

Original inventory: {'markers': 12, 'tripods': 2, 'microphones': 2}
Checkout copy: {'markers': 12, 'tripods': 2, 'microphones': 2}

Round 1 — Architect

Record the goal in your own words.

What should remain true after one item is checked out?

Round 2 — Critic

Find one specific weakness.

  • Evidence: What exact line, behavior, or output shows the weakness?
  • Consequence: Why does it matter for the goal?
  • Revision: What should change?
  • Verification: What test or observation would show that the revision works?

Avoid comments such as “the code is bad” or “the AI made a mistake” without evidence.

Optional Critic Tool

If your instructor provides an approved AI tool, you may use it. Do not enter personal, confidential, or real makerspace data.

Use this prompt:

You are the Critic in an AI Debate Club. The goal is: create a checkout copy without changing the original inventory. Examine the draft below. Identify up to three specific weaknesses. For each, name the relevant line, explain the consequence, and propose a verification check. Do not rewrite the whole program.

Copy the tool’s critique only if your instructor asks you to save it. Check every claim against the code and output.

Human Decision

Which critique should guide the revision first? Why?

Revision Plan

Describe the change in plain language. Do not copy a complete program from a tool.

Verification

Complete this prediction for the revised behavior:

  • Original number of tripods after checkout: ______
  • Checkout number of tripods after checkout: ______
  • Why these values show whether the revision worked: ________

Carry-Forward Rounds

The full Debate Club is larger than today’s Monday Moment. For the next lab or homework, complete these two questions:

Customer: What could confuse or concern a person using this checkout helper?

Project Manager: What small test or follow-up task should happen before the helper is trusted?

Portfolio Record

Save this completed record with your other course work. It preserves how you inspected a draft, selected a revision, and planned a check.

Exit Ticket

What is one specific weakness a critic could help you find before you trust a draft?

Student Activity — AI I Week 11: Verify

Big Question: How do we know whether an AI answer is trustworthy?

A polished answer can still contain false claims. Your job is to separate claims from style, identify the evidence needed, and record what the evidence actually shows.

The Scenario

A library is considering a small Room Reservation Records program. Read this confident answer:

The Room Reservation Records program is ready for delivery. It stores each reservation in a dictionary, so every reservation is preserved and can be looked up quickly. The sample data contains two reservations for Ari, and the program will keep both of them. Since the program works on the sample data, it will also work for an empty list of reservations. The library should adopt this approach because dictionaries are the best choice for reservation systems. By next semester, most campus reservation systems will use this pattern.

This is a fictional scenario. Do not use real names, reservation records, or private information in an AI tool.

Claim Types

Use the type that best fits each claim:

  • Factual: describes information that can usually be checked against a reliable source or the given data.
  • Programmatic: describes what code does. Check it by tracing or running relevant inputs.
  • Predictive: describes what may happen in the future. Current evidence can support or weaken it, but cannot confirm the future today.
  • Normative/design: says what should be chosen or done. Evidence can inform the judgment, but does not settle the value choice by itself.

These claim types are not equally easy to verify.

Evidence for the Scenario

scores = {}
for name, score in records:
    scores[name] = score

print(scores)

records = [("Ari", 80), ("Bo", 90), ("Ari", 95)]

The output is:

{'Ari': 95, 'Bo': 90}

For:

records = []

the output is:

{}

A dictionary maps each key to one current value. Assigning a new value to an existing key replaces the previous value for that key.

Your Task

Complete one row in your Claim Verification Table for each important claim in the answer.

For each row:

  1. state the claim clearly;
  2. explain why it matters;
  3. identify the evidence, source, or test needed;
  4. record what source or test you checked;
  5. mark the result verified, corrected, or uncertain; and
  6. explain your result in the notes.

Do not mark a claim verified because it sounds polished. “Uncertain” is a valid result when the available evidence cannot settle the claim.

AI Option

If a course-approved AI tool is available, you may ask it to separate the answer into claims or suggest verification methods. Its response is not evidence. Check its suggestions yourself.

Do not enter real student, reservation, or institutional data into an AI tool.

Non-AI Option

You can complete the activity entirely from the program, inputs, outputs, and dictionary fact printed above.

Save Your Work

Save your completed Claim Verification Table with your name, date, and week. Keep it as evidence of how you checked an answer before relying on it.

Exit Ticket

In one sentence:

What made the original answer sound trustworthy, and what evidence did it actually provide?

Student Activity — AI I Week 12: Revise

Big Question: How do we turn critique and verification into better work?

Weeks 10 and 11 gave you two kinds of information:

  • Critique: what may be unclear, incomplete, or poorly suited to the task.
  • Verification: what the work actually does when you test or inspect it.

Today you use both. Do not begin with a fresh, unreviewed draft.

Shared Scenario

A first-pass StudyRoom class reports how much time remains in a reservation:

class StudyRoom:
    def __init__(self, name, minutes_remaining):
        self.name = name
        self.minutes_remaining = minutes_remaining

    def reminder(self):
        if self.minutes_remaining <= 10:
            return "Wrap up soon."
        else:
            return "Your room is still available."

The goal is:

  • 0 or less: "Your reservation has ended."
  • 1 through 10: "Wrap up soon."
  • more than 10: "Your room is still available."

The review notes are:

  • Critique: The method’s responsibility is not obvious to a CS1 reader.
  • Verification: With minutes_remaining = 0, the result is "Wrap up soon."
  • Audience note: Explain the behavior clearly without adding unnecessary features.

Step 1: Bring Forward Your Notes

Use the critique and verification notes from your previous work. If you do not have them, use the shared StudyRoom notes above.

Write the goal of the work. Then identify what each note is really asking you to consider.

Step 2: Prioritize the Notes

Label each note:

  • Must revise: The problem prevents the work from meeting its goal.
  • Should revise: The problem affects clarity, trust, or audience fit.
  • May defer: The suggestion is reasonable but less important than the current goal.

For the shared scenario, the incorrect result for 0 is a must-revise issue.

Step 3: Plan the Revision

Before changing the work, complete these statements:

  • The highest-priority issue is:
  • The evidence for that priority is:
  • I will change:
  • I will preserve:
  • I will check the revision by:

For the shared scenario, your check should include 0, 1, 10, and 11.

Step 4: Make the Revision

Revise your original work. If you are using the shared scenario, fix the condition order and make the method’s behavior clear.

Your revision should address the highest-priority note before surface polishing. A small, targeted change is acceptable.

Step 5: Verify Again

Check the revised version against the goal and the evidence you named.

For the shared scenario, the expected results are:

Minutes remaining Expected message
0 Your reservation has ended.
1 Wrap up soon.
10 Wrap up soon.
11 Your room is still available.

Record whether the revision passed each check. If it did not, describe the next change needed.

Step 6: Explain the Before and After

Complete the portfolio artifact:

  • What changed?
  • Which critique or verification note caused the change?
  • Why was this change more important than the deferred suggestion?
  • What stayed the same?
  • What evidence shows that the revision improved the work?

Optional AI Comparison

If you have access to a course-approved AI tool, you may ask:

Help me prioritize these critique and verification notes by impact on the stated goal. Do not rewrite the work. For each note, explain what evidence would show whether it matters.

Compare the tool’s recommendation with your own decision. You remain responsible for the priority, the revision, and the verification. Do not enter personal, confidential, or private information.

If you do not use a tool, use the shared notes and scenario. You can complete the same activity.

Save Your Portfolio Artifact

Save your completed Before/After Revision artifact with your earlier critique and verification work. Version history matters: another reader should be able to see how evidence changed the work.

Exit Ticket

What changed between version 1 and your final version, and what evidence showed that the change improved the work?

Student Activity — AI I Week 13: Decide

Big Question: How can AI help us compare options without replacing human judgment?

AI can help you see options, criteria, tradeoffs, risks, and consequences. It does not own your priorities or your final decision.

Shared Scenario

Your CS1 team is building a small campus-world program with Student, Room, and Reservation objects. The program needs to represent room state, make reservations, and allow the team to add another room type later.

Compare these designs:

  • Design A: inheritance for specialized room types;
  • Design B: composition with cooperating objects;
  • Design C: composition with related classes separated into multiple modules.

Your job is not to find the universally best design. Your job is to decide which design best fits your team’s priorities.

Step 1: Choose Criteria

Choose at least three criteria:

  • cost;
  • time;
  • risk;
  • fairness;
  • usefulness;
  • difficulty;
  • stakeholder impact; or
  • another criterion you can explain.

Write what each criterion means in this decision. For example, “time” might mean “can our team build and understand the first version within one week?”

Step 2: Compare the Options

Use the instructor’s comparison, your class materials, or a course-approved AI tool.

If you use AI, ask:

We are designing a small Python campus-world program with Student, Room, and Reservation classes. Compare these three designs: A — inheritance for specialized room types; B — composition with cooperating objects; C — composition with related classes separated into multiple modules. Compare them using time, difficulty, risk, usefulness, and maintainability. Identify assumptions, tradeoffs, and one claim that needs verification. Do not recommend a design and do not decide which criterion matters most.

Do not enter personal, confidential, or identifying information.

Step 3: Make a Decision Matrix

Use 1 for a weak fit, 2 for a moderate fit, and 3 for a strong fit. Add a short reason for every rating.

Criterion Design A Design B Design C

One important tradeoff I see:

One assumption or risk I need to check:

One claim I verified, and how I checked it:

Step 4: Make the Human Recommendation

Complete these sentences:

I recommend Design _ because our highest-priority criterion is _____.

This design gives up or makes harder ________.

Another design is stronger when ____, but I did not choose it because ______.

Step 5: Reflect

Where did comparison help the decision?

Where did human judgment matter most?

Save Your Portfolio Artifact

Save this Decision Matrix with your name, date, and week. It records how you reasoned about a real technical choice before implementation.

Exit Ticket

In one sentence:

Where did comparison help this decision, and where did human judgment matter most?

Student Activity — AI I Week 14: Automate

Big Question: What parts of an AI workflow can become repeatable?

This week, automation means a reusable written checklist or prompt sequence. You do not need to write software or use an API.

Weeks 1–13 built a workflow from defining a task through gathering context, planning, prompting, researching, reasoning, generating, critiquing, verifying, revising, and deciding. Now make the repeatable parts usable again.

Shared Scenario

You are preparing a Coding Odyssey checkpoint. You changed a small part of a program and want to review it before committing and pushing it.

A weak routine is:

  1. Change code.
  2. Ask AI whether it works.
  3. Commit.
  4. Push.
  5. Submit.

A stronger routine makes its checks visible:

  1. Define the change and success condition.
  2. Gather the relevant code, requirements, and test information.
  3. Ask AI for an explanation or critique—not authority.
  4. Inspect the response and test the code yourself.
  5. Revise if needed.
  6. Review the diff and status.
  7. Commit with a meaningful message.
  8. Push and confirm the remote update.
  9. Record what changed and what remains uncertain.

The Git routine is a course connection: checking the change, committing, pushing, and confirming the update are repeatable steps. This activity does not ask you to learn new Git commands.

Your Task

Create a reusable prompt chain for reviewing a coding change before commit and push. If your instructor permits, you may instead choose another recurring course task, such as explaining a CS1 error or preparing a project reflection.

Your workflow must include:

  1. define the task and success condition;
  2. ask for missing information;
  3. draft or explain;
  4. critique;
  5. verify;
  6. revise;
  7. produce the final output.

For each stage, write:

  • what information goes in;
  • what the prompt or action does;
  • what evidence or result comes out.

Then identify:

  • what stays the same each time;
  • what changes each time;
  • where a human must decide;
  • one risk if someone follows the workflow carelessly;
  • one revision that makes the workflow safer or clearer.

Optional Tool Comparison

If you have access to a course-approved AI tool, you may test one or two prompts. Do not paste private information, credentials, API keys, private repository content, or unreleased project material.

Compare an immediate request:

“Does this coding change work? Tell me what to commit.”

with a reusable chain. Use these criteria:

  • Does the chain ask for missing context?
  • Does it separate critique from human verification?
  • Does it produce a repeatable final checkpoint?

If you do not use a tool, use the shared scenario and printed workflow. You can complete the same activity without an account or internet connection.

Save Your Portfolio Artifact

Complete Reusable Prompt Chain and save it with your earlier AI I portfolio artifacts. You are saving it because a clear workflow can be reused, inspected, and improved during future coding and AI-supported work.

Exit Ticket

Which step in your workflow should happen every time, and which step must remain a human decision?

Student Activity — AI I Week 15: Measure

Big Question: How do we know whether one AI output or workflow is better than another?

This week is fully asynchronous. There is no live class meeting. Complete this activity independently. You do not need an AI account, internet access, or a partner.

Goal

You will compare two outputs using the same explicit criteria. Your final artifact will show not only which output you prefer, but why.

The scenario is fictional. Do not submit personal information, private grades, or confidential course material.

Scenario

A student is preparing to submit a Coding Odyssey assignment. The student needs a trustworthy progress update that helps them decide what to fix before submitting.

Output A

I made good progress. The program works, the explanation is clear, and I think it meets the requirements. I would probably submit it after a quick review.

Output B

The program handles the three required cases and includes comments explaining the main steps. However, the explanation does not identify one limitation, and the final test evidence is missing. I would run the required cases again and add the missing limitation before submitting.

Rubric

Score each output from 0 to 2 on every criterion.

Criterion 0 — Not shown 1 — Partly shown 2 — Clearly shown
Accuracy Makes a claim unsupported by the scenario Mostly matches the scenario but is imprecise Claims match the scenario
Completeness Omits most needed information Includes some requirements or next steps Includes status, missing evidence, and next action
Usefulness Does not help someone decide what to do Suggests a general review Gives a specific next action
Evidence Gives no checkable detail Gives one detail but leaves an important claim unsupported Points to concrete cases, requirements, or missing evidence
Audience fit Tone or detail does not suit a student preparing to submit Understandable but unevenly focused Clear, direct, and appropriate for the intended reader

Complete Your Rubric Evaluation

1. Identify the goal

Write the goal in your own words.

The goal of these updates is to:

2. Score both outputs

Criterion Output A score Output B score
Accuracy
Completeness
Usefulness
Evidence
Audience fit
Total

3. Record evidence

For at least three criteria, point to specific words or details in the outputs.

Criterion Evidence from Output A or B

4. Decide

Which output better serves the stated goal? Explain how your scores and evidence support the decision.

The better output is:

It is better because:

5. Identify a trade-off

What does the other output do better, or what might your decision overlook?

One trade-off or limitation is:

6. Revise one criterion

Choose one criterion that could be easier to apply consistently. Rewrite it so that it names observable evidence.

Original criterion Revised criterion

Explain what your revision makes easier to measure.

7. Optional AI use

You may ask an approved AI tool to suggest possible criteria. This is optional. Do not provide personal, private, or confidential information. Review every suggestion yourself.

If you used this option, answer:

What did you keep, change, or reject, and why?

If you did not use it, write:

I used the provided rubric and completed the evaluation without an AI tool.

Save Your Portfolio Artifact

Save your completed Rubric Evaluation with your name, date, and Week 15. Keep it because it shows how you measured quality with explicit criteria.

Exit Ticket

I can tell that an AI output is better for a particular goal when…

Student Activity — AI I Week 16: Reflect and Improve

Big Question: How has my thinking changed because of this course?

This is the capstone. You are not learning a new AI technique today. You are assembling evidence of how the first 15 lenses changed the way you think and work.

A Single Thread: Your Portfolio

Imagine that you will use AI tomorrow in a course you have not taken. Before trusting its first answer, what would you do?

Write one action. It might involve defining the task, checking assumptions, asking for critique, verifying a claim, revising the result, or measuring whether it meets the goal.

Now use your own Weeks 1–15 portfolio to show how you learned that habit.

Step 1: Find the Change

Choose:

  • one early artifact that shows how you started;
  • one later artifact that shows a stronger practice; and
  • one critique, verification, or revision that connects them.

Write:

Earlier, I ____. Now, I ___. The change happened or became visible when _____.

Be specific. “I got better at AI” is not enough.

Step 2: Complete the Evidence Map

Use these artifacts as possible evidence:

  • Problem Definition Card;
  • Context Comparison Sheet;
  • Plan-first Workflow;
  • Decomposed Task Pipeline;
  • Model Comparison Table;
  • Prompt Makeover;
  • RAG On/Off Comparison;
  • Assumptions and Tradeoffs Analysis;
  • Audience Transformation Outputs;
  • Debate Club Critique Record;
  • Claim Verification Table;
  • Before/After Revision;
  • Decision Matrix;
  • Reusable Prompt Chain;
  • Rubric Evaluation.

You do not need to use every artifact. Select the evidence that actually supports your claims.

Step 3: Assemble Eight Sections

Your final portfolio must contain:

  1. My AI thinking philosophy
  2. My best prompt and why it works
  3. My biggest AI mistake and what I learned
  4. My best critique example
  5. My best verification example
  6. My best revision example
  7. My reusable AI workflow
  8. My plan for using AI responsibly in future courses or work

For each section, reference the artifact or artifacts you used. Explain what the evidence shows; do not merely list a filename or week.

Step 4: Write Your Reusable Workflow

Write a short sequence that you could repeat:

  1. define the task and success condition;
  2. provide relevant context and identify what is missing;
  3. plan or ask for an approach before producing;
  4. critique assumptions, reasoning, or output;
  5. verify important claims and behavior;
  6. revise;
  7. evaluate whether the result meets the goal and course rules.

Adapt the sequence to your own practice. A workflow should be repeatable and proportionate, not unnecessarily long.

Step 5: Plan Forward

Complete:

In a future course or workplace, I will use this workflow when ____. I will use AI responsibly by ___. I will still personally check _____.

You do not need to name a personal employer, project, health matter, family situation, or other private detail.

Optional AI Coach

If you have access to a course-approved tool, you may use it only as a reflection coach:

I am assembling a final portfolio from my own course artifacts. Ask me questions that help me identify one specific change in my thinking, the evidence for that change, and how I will use the habit in future work. Do not invent evidence, write my reflection for me, or make claims about artifacts you have not seen.

Do not enter private information or anything your course policy prohibits. Check every suggestion against your own artifacts. You write the final portfolio.

If you do not use a tool, use the questions and template in this activity. That is the complete alternative.

Exit Ticket

Complete this sentence:

Because of this course, I now ______ before I trust or use AI output.

Week 2 Wednesday Reading Assignment: Learning That Lasts

  • Type: reading assignment (checks and extends engagement with the reading; distinct from the Wednesday slides assignment)

  • Scheduling (intended, not yet pushed to Canvas): opens Monday (2 days before the session, giving real pre-class reading time), closes Wednesday 8:00 AM — before the session starts, so it functions as pre-class retrieval practice rather than a post-hoc formality. Per prompt 018 outcome 5's spacing rule, this assignment's close date must not match the Wednesday slides assignment's close date.

Instructions

Complete this after reading readings/week_02_wed_retrieval_practice.md in full. Answer in your own words — do not copy sentences from the reading. Each answer should be 2-4 sentences unless the question says otherwise.

Questions

  1. Recall/comprehension. What is the difference between the illusion of fluency and durable learning? Use the reading's discussion of rereading or familiarity to explain why something can feel learned without being readily available from memory.

  2. Recall/comprehension. How does retrieval practice or testing build learning? Describe one detail from the flight simulator example or the eighth-grade science-class quiz example that shows testing can function as practice rather than simply as a final judgment.

  3. Application (required). Think of something you are currently learning — in this course or elsewhere. Describe one retrieval-practice activity you could do without looking at your notes or instructions, and explain what a weakness in your recall would help you identify.

  4. Application. Choose a new tool, role, or skill you are learning. Describe one piece of prior knowledge or one mental model you could connect to it, using the baseball batter example to explain how that connection could help you make sense of changing information and respond effectively. Also explain why relying only on a supposedly preferred learning style could limit your learning.

Source and Limitation Note

This assignment is derived from readings/week_02_wed_retrieval_practice.md, itself drawn from Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning (Brown, Roediger, and McDaniel), Chapter 1, "Learning Is Misunderstood." No claims here go beyond what that reading already states.

— Question 3 (required) - **4 — Full credit:** Describes a real, currently relevant learning goal, proposes a specific retrieval-practice activity that can be completed without looking at notes or instructions, and explains with concrete evidence what a weakness in recall would reveal or help identify. - **2 — Partial credit:** Names a learning goal and a generally relevant practice activity, but the activity is too vague to show retrieval, or the explanation of what weak recall would identify is asserted without a specific connection to the learner's needs. - **0 — No credit:** Question left blank, or the activity depends on simply rereading or looking at notes and does not meaningfully require retrieval.

— Question 4 and overall - **3 — Full credit:** Question 4 identifies a specific new tool, role, or skill; connects it to genuine prior knowledge or a mental model; accurately explains how that connection could support responding to changing information using the baseball batter example; explains why relying only on a supposedly preferred learning style could limit learning; and all four questions are answered. - **1.5 — Partial credit:** The connection, baseball-batter explanation, or learning-style limitation is generic, underdeveloped, or only partly accurate, or one other question is missing/underdeveloped. - **0 — No credit:** Question 4 is blank, unrelated to the reading's mental-model or learning-style concepts, or multiple questions are missing.

  4. Application. Describe a test, alert, screen, or filter you personally rely on — in your studies, your work, or your daily life. Estimate roughly how common the thing it looks for actually is, and use that estimate to say whether you would expect most of its positive results to be real.

Question 2 correctly attributes the imbalance to the base rate: with a 0.8% cancer rate, only about 8 women in 1,000 can generate a true positive while roughly 992 are available to generate false ones. - **1.5 — Partial credit:** One answer is accurate and in the student's own words; the other is vague, copied near-verbatim from the reading, conflates the two probabilities, or explains the mammogram imbalance by blaming test quality rather than the base rate. - **0 — No credit:** Neither answer accurately reflects the reading, or both are copied verbatim.

Questions

  1. Recall/comprehension. What did Secrist's data show about top- and bottom-performing businesses over time, and how did Hotelling's review show that Secrist's explanation (competitive forces) was wrong even though his data was real?

  2. Recall/comprehension. Explain, using Galton's height data, why regression to the mean happens whenever an outcome combines a stable factor with chance. Why do extreme cases tend to look less extreme the next time they are measured?

  3. Application (required).   4. Application. Choose one example from the reading — Secrist's business data, the home-run "on pace" pattern, or the bran study — and explain in your own words why it is an example of regression to the mean rather than a real causal effect.

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Ellenberg, Jordan. How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking. The Penguin Press, 2014. Chapter "The Triumph of Mediocrity."
  • All primary-source claims and responsible paraphrases are drawn only from the supplied chapter file.

Clearly explains that the randomized-controlled-trial result (increased antisocial behavior) revealed the program's actual effect, and draws the general lesson that a "before and after" claim without a comparison or control group cannot be trusted. - **2 — Partial credit:** Recognizes that Scared Straight's apparent success was misleading, but the explanation of why (the selection-based design versus the randomized trial) is incomplete, vague, or does not clearly connect to regression to the mean. - **0 — No credit:** Question left blank, or the answer does not meaningfully explain the Scared Straight example or the risk of claims without a comparison group.

— Question 4 and overall - **3 — Full credit:** Accurately explains one chosen example (Secrist's business data, home-run "on pace" claims, or the bran study) as regression to the mean rather than a real causal effect, correctly identifying the role of selection on an extreme measure and chance. Questions

Explain why "all six worked" should lower rather than raise your confidence, name the two mechanisms the reading offers that could produce such a record (publication bias and optional stopping), and describe what evidence you would ask for before believing the onboarding process actually works.

  4. Application. Wednesday's reading argued that a single positive result depends on how rare the thing is. Explain in your own words how publication bias is the same kind of problem operating on a whole literature rather than a single test.

This assignment is derived from readings/week_06_fri_understanding_replication.md, itself drawn from Understanding Statistics and Experimental Design by Herzog, Francis, and Clarke, Chapter 10, "Understanding Replication."
