rubric.long_description: — Questions 1–2 - **3 — Full credit:** Question 1 correctly explains that power is the chance a study detects a real effect, that underpowered studies of small effects may fail to replicate even when the effect exists, and that a bare replication rate is therefore consistent with both a real effect and no effect. Question 2 correctly states that TES compares the number of significant outcomes expected from reported effect sizes and study power against the number actually reported, and that an excess of successes signals internal inconsistency because realistic power implies some studies should have failed. - **1.5 — Partial credit:** One answer is accurate and in the student's own words; the other is vague, copied near-verbatim, omits the role of power, or describes TES as evaluating individual studies rather than the coherence of a set. - **0 — No credit:** Neither answer accurately reflects the reading, or both are copied verbatim.

— Question 3 (required) - **4 — Full credit:** Correctly explains that with small samples the honest expectation was roughly two or three significant results, so six-for-six is arithmetically improbable rather than impressive. Names both mechanisms accurately: publication bias (departments where the pilot failed were dropped or unreported) and optional stopping (each pilot ran until the numbers looked good). Identifies concrete evidence that would settle it — the number of pilots actually started, pre-registered stopping rules or fixed sample sizes, and the results from departments not reported. - **2 — Partial credit:** Recognizes that uniform success is suspicious, but the expected-successes reasoning is underdeveloped, only one mechanism is named or described accurately, or the request for further evidence is vague. - **0 — No credit:** Question left blank, or the response treats six-for-six as strong support for the onboarding process.

— Question 4 and overall - **3 — Full credit:** Question 4 draws the parallel correctly and in the student's own words: in both cases what is visible is a filtered sample, and sound judgment requires reasoning about the invisible portion — the large population without the condition on Wednesday, the unpublished null results on Friday. All four questions are answered. - **1.5 — Partial credit:** The parallel is asserted but not explained, connects the two readings only superficially, or misidentifies which part is invisible in one of the two cases; or one other question is missing or underdeveloped. - **0 — No credit:** Question 4 is blank, unrelated to publication bias, or multiple questions are missing.

Wednesday - Verify one machine claim

Today you will create the first AI investigation receipt of the semester.

1. Choose a claim

Use the claim you predicted Monday, an AI-generated claim, or this no-account fallback:

The machine architecture reported by Python and the operating system will always describe the physical processor in exactly the same way.

Keep the claim small enough to test today.

2. Gather machine evidence

Use Python's standard library so the required path stays portable:

python3 - <<'PY'
import os, platform, sys
print('python:', sys.version.split()[0])
print('platform.system:', platform.system())
print('platform.machine:', platform.machine())
print('platform.processor:', platform.processor() or '<not reported>')
print('logical_cpus_visible:', os.cpu_count())
PY

If available on your system, add one independent operating-system observation such as:

uname -a
uname -m

Windows students may use PowerShell/system-information output instead. The point is the evidence, not a specific shell command.

3. Separate observation from interpretation

Record:

  • proposal: what was claimed;
  • observation: the relevant command output;
  • evidence source: machine command, official documentation, or specification;
  • interpretation: what the observation means;
  • limitation: what the evidence does not establish.

A container, VM, compatibility layer, remote shell, or subsystem may report a useful execution view without describing every fact about the physical host. That is not an error. It is context.

4. Submit the investigation receipt

Your receipt should contain:

  1. bounded question/claim;
  2. relevant context;
  3. AI/tool/fallback proposal;
  4. evidence commands and relevant output;
  5. conclusion;
  6. one revision after verification.

Do not submit a raw AI transcript or an unannotated screenshot dump.

  • lab/fallback_data/week05-machine-reference.json

Live path

assignments.description:
Wednesday - Use the operating system as a telescope

A command is not a vocabulary word to memorize. It is an instrument that exposes one view of the machine.

1. Decompose one vague question

Start with:

What is this computer and what is it doing?

Break it into observable questions such as:

  • What operating system/kernel is visible?
  • What ISA/machine label is visible?
  • How many logical processors are visible?
  • How much memory is visible?
  • What processes are running?
  • What kind of file/binary is this?

2. Start with the course Observatory

From the course repository root:

./lab/bin/archprobe --out-dir /tmp/arch-week04
cat /tmp/arch-week04/machine.txt

The Observatory labels evidence scope rather than pretending a container/VM/subsystem view is the entire physical host.

3. Add operating-system instruments where available

On Linux, useful observations include:

uname -a
uname -m
lscpu
free -h
ps -eo pid,comm,%cpu,%mem --sort=-%cpu | head
file /bin/sh

To look at bytes without turning the week into shell trivia:

printf 'ABC\n' > /tmp/arch-week04-bytes.txt
od -An -tx1 -c /tmp/arch-week04-bytes.txt

If a named command is unavailable on your supported environment, use the Observatory/fallback packet and record that limitation. Do not install privileged tools merely to imitate Linux output.

4. Observation receipt

Choose one machine claim and provide:

  1. question;
  2. command/instrument;
  3. relevant raw observation;
  4. interpretation;
  5. evidence scope;
  6. one thing the observation does not prove.

Example distinction:

  • Observation: platform.machine() returned x86_64.
  • Interpretation: the current execution environment presents an x86-64 machine interface.
  • Not proven: every physical-host detail, performance characteristic, or virtualization layer.

rubric_settings.title: Week 04 - Architecture Investigation Rubric

assignments.description:
Wednesday - Investigate / Break / Measure

Question

Can I build a compatible $1,500 machine for one workload, then move about $150 without losing track of what I am trading away?

This is a design investigation, not a shopping contest. You are not buying anything.

Professional Minds - The Art of Thinking Clearly

Use one shared question while you work:

Which attractive number is most likely to trick me into feeling more certain than my evidence allows?

Do not create a second Professional Minds assignment. Carry that question into the Architecture investigation.

1. Predict

Before current market research, record:

  • your workload;
  • the component/resource category you expect should receive the largest budget share;
  • your predicted bottleneck or uncertainty;
  • what kind of evidence would make you move about $150 to a different category.

Do this before asking an AI tool or builder to recommend parts.

2. Perturb

You will create:

  1. one baseline compatible machine under the $1,500 constraint;
  2. one controlled reallocation that moves about $100-$200 while keeping the workload and total budget approximately fixed.

Good reallocations change one design emphasis rather than rebuilding the entire computer from scratch.

Change deliberately: where a bounded part of the budget is spent.

Hold reasonably constant: workload, total budget, new-retail/not-required-used assumption, and basic tower scope.

Why this is useful: the comparison turns “tradeoff” from a vocabulary word into a design action.

3. Run - Part A: Would It Run?

Use PCPartPicker or another builder if it is convenient and accessible. The course does not require a particular commercial builder.

Choose:

  • CPU;
  • motherboard;
  • memory;
  • primary storage;
  • case;
  • power supply;
  • cooling when needed;
  • discrete GPU only when the design requires one.

Then complete this bounded compatibility receipt.

Check Your evidence Result
CPU ↔ motherboard socket/platform exact model + manufacturer/spec URL PASS / concern
motherboard ↔ memory type/capacity exact model + manufacturer/spec URL PASS / concern
storage ↔ board interface/slot exact model + spec evidence PASS / concern
board/GPU/cooler ↔ case fit form factor/clearance evidence PASS / concern
CPU/GPU ↔ PSU power/connectors power/connectors evidence PASS / concern
usable graphics path exists integrated or discrete evidence PASS / concern

A builder showing no warning is helpful. It does not replace your ability to explain the important checks.

4. Measure - Part A: current market evidence

Capture market evidence in a table or CSV with at least these fields:

category,component,observed_price_usd,source_url,observed_date,architecture_property,property_value,official_spec_url,notes

Rules:

  • record the price you actually observed;
  • record the observation date;
  • use the manufacturer page for architecture/spec claims when practical;
  • do not silently replace a missing price with MSRP;
  • do not treat an AI recommendation as market/spec evidence.

Your baseline total should be at or below $1,500 before tax/shipping under the course scope.

5. Measure - Part B: Dollars Per and budget share

Calculate:

Required literal capacity metrics

  • RAM $/GB;
  • primary storage $/TB (or $/GB, but label units clearly).

Required deliberately naive proxy

Choose one that fits your design:

  • CPU $/advertised physical core; or
  • discrete GPU $/GB VRAM.

If your CPU has heterogeneous core types, state exactly what you counted. The awkwardness is part of the lesson.

Required budget-share view

For at least CPU, motherboard, memory, storage, GPU if present, case, PSU, and cooling if separately purchased:

[ \text{budget share} = \frac{\text{component price}}{1500} \times 100\% ]

A table is enough this week. Do not spend time making a decorative chart.

6. Build the first hierarchy ledger

Record what your designed/observable evidence can support.

Layer Capacity Separately purchased? Observed price Price/capacity meaningful? Persistent? Evidence source/date What this number hides
L1 cache no N/A no no latency/organization/locality
L2 cache no N/A no no latency/organization/locality
L3 cache no N/A no no latency/organization/locality
RAM yes yes no latency/bandwidth/timings
primary SSD/NVMe yes yes yes latency/bandwidth/endurance/controller
optional secondary storage yes yes yes workload/access pattern

Do not invent a retail price for cache. Do not paste a universal latency table and call it measurement.

7. Run - Part B: observe one real machine

From the course repository, on a supported Observatory path:

mkdir -p dossier/evidence/week05-archprobe
./lab/bin/archprobe --out-dir dossier/evidence/week05-archprobe

Preserve both:

dossier/evidence/week05-archprobe/machine.json
dossier/evidence/week05-archprobe/machine.txt

Read the scope line.

If it says container-visible or WSL-visible, that is part of the evidence. Do not silently promote what the environment can see into a claim about the physical host.

Fallback

If archprobe is unavailable on your supported path after reasonable troubleshooting, use the course-owned Week 5 reference snapshot from lab/fallback_data/.

Identify it as course-provided fallback evidence. You still complete the same Machine Map and scope interpretation. There is no grading penalty.

8. Perturb the budget

Now move roughly $100-$200.

Keep the workload and total budget approximately fixed.

Record:

Baseline Reallocation
money moved from
money moved to
total price
compatibility changed?
capacity/spec metric improved
capacity/spec metric worsened
workload hypothesis strengthened/weakened
new risk/uncertainty

The goal is not to prove the second build is better. The goal is to expose what a design choice buys and costs.

9. Explain

Answer these before Friday:

  1. Which component/resource got the largest intentional budget share?
  2. What compatibility fact mattered most?
  3. Which metric made one option look especially attractive?
  4. What does that metric fail to measure?
  5. What changed when you moved about $150?
  6. What piece of evidence would you most like to have before claiming your build is actually faster/better for the workload?

10. Revise

Return to Monday's prediction.

Write one sentence for each:

  • Keep: what part of the prediction survived?
  • Change: what did market/compatibility evidence make you revise?
  • Narrow: what claim became more careful?

Machine Dossier v0

Create dossier/machine-map.md containing:

Workload and constraints

  • chosen workload;
  • $1,500 budget;
  • three concrete tasks/priorities;
  • predicted bottleneck/uncertainty.

Designed machine

  • baseline parts table;
  • compatibility receipt;
  • controlled reallocation table;
  • dated market evidence path.

Hierarchy ledger

Use the Week 5 table above. Mark unknown rather than inventing precision.

Observable machine

  • short human-readable summary;
  • path to machine.json;
  • evidence scope;
  • one way the observable machine differs from your proposed design.

Initial metrics

  • RAM $/GB;
  • storage $/TB or $/GB;
  • one deliberately naive proxy;
  • component budget shares.

Claim waiting to be attacked

Finish this sentence:

Right now I believe __ matters most to this workload because _. The later measurement most likely to prove me wrong would be ___.

What this investigation does not prove

A compatible, intelligently budgeted machine is not automatically a measured fast machine.

This week does not prove:

  • real application performance;
  • cache latency;
  • memory bandwidth;
  • multicore scaling;
  • accelerator benefit;
  • energy efficiency;
  • benchmark leadership.

We have built a testable design story. The rest of the course gets to make it earn its confidence.

Re-run / cleanup

No special cleanup is required.

Keep the dated market table and archprobe receipt. Week 14 needs the original evidence, not your memory of it.

Question: What must software and hardware agree on for a program to run?

Professional Minds

Statistics Done Wrong. Use the strand to improve evidence interpretation, not to create a second assignment.

Experimental grammar

Predict -> Perturb -> Run -> Measure -> Visualize -> Explain -> Revise

Supported path

./lab/bin/archlab run riscv --out-dir dossier/evidence/week06-riscv

The interpreter proves bounded architectural instruction/state behavior. It does not prove cycle timing, pipeline depth, cache behavior, or the implementation of a modern CPU.

Understanding by Design. Ask what evidence would demonstrate actual understanding rather than component naming.

Question Evidence / answer
ISA semantic promise
current PC / instruction
source register(s) or immediate
selected ALU/function
memory read/write needed?

next-PC choice
architectural state changed

Software Project Management. Let the strand coexist; do not force a page-table/project-management metaphor.

getconf PAGESIZE

assignments.description:
Wednesday - Investigate / Break / Measure: Make the Machine Pay the Bill

Use the fixed shared workload. Do not rewrite Farkle to make your favorite strategy look good.

The experiment grammar is:

Predict -> Hold the workload still -> Run -> Measure -> Compare -> Explain -> Revise

Controlled variable

Your main software variable is the strategy or effort level.

Choose two from:

  • bank_at_300
  • learner:500
  • learner:2000
  • rollout:10
  • rollout:25

Keep these fixed between the runs you compare:

  • game rules;
  • target score;
  • game count;
  • deterministic seed;
  • host/execution lane.

Step 1 - Verify the execution lane

From the repository root:

cd weeks/week-16
PYTHONPATH=code python3 -m architecture_farkle.cli host

On Windows PowerShell, python may be your launcher instead of python3.

The required path should report:

execution_mode: native-python-cpu
accelerator_used: false

A GPU may physically exist in the machine. This command does not use it.

Step 2 - Run your declared comparison

Example:

PYTHONPATH=code python3 -m architecture_farkle.cli compare \
  --strategy-a learner:2000 \
  --strategy-b bank_at_425 \
  --games 500 \
  --seed 6262 \
  --repeats 3 \
  --lane-label student-cpu \
  --out-dir artifacts/my-comparison

If your first chosen strategy is different, replace only --strategy-a.

If you want to compare two members of the fixed menu directly, use the second one as --strategy-b while preserving the same game count, seed, repeats, and lane.

Step 3 - Inspect the receipt, not just the terminal

The run writes:

artifacts/my-comparison/architecture_farkle_receipt.json
artifacts/my-comparison/architecture_farkle_trials.csv

Find evidence for all four currencies.

Effectiveness

  • win_rate_a
  • wins_a, wins_b, ties
  • starts_a, starts_b

Preparation

  • preparation_seconds_a
  • training_turns_a
  • model_size_bytes_a

Operation

  • evaluation_seconds
  • games_per_second
  • summary median/min/max throughput

Machine / environment

  • hostname;
  • CPU model;
  • logical CPU count;
  • execution mode;
  • lane label;
  • accelerator-used flag.

Step 4 - Ask the Architecture question

Do not report only:

Strategy A won more.

Instead ask:

  • How much more effective was it?
  • Where did it pay its cost: before play or during play?
  • How large was the throughput difference?
  • How noisy were the repeated timings?
  • Under my objective, did that extra work purchase enough improvement?

Optional fixed suite

The instructor may run the complete bounded suite:

PYTHONPATH=code python3 -m architecture_farkle.cli suite \
  --games 100 \
  --seed 6262 \
  --repeats 3 \
  --lane-label local-cpu \
  --out-dir artifacts/fixed-suite

The suite is useful for a class discussion or Stack Showcase. You are not required to optimize every strategy.

What this experiment does not prove

A local CPU timing does not by itself establish:

  • energy consumption;
  • purchase price;
  • GPU performance;
  • cloud cost;
  • compiler speedup;
  • container overhead;
  • performance on another student's machine.

Those would require additional controlled evidence.

Before Friday

Write down one sentence that begins:

The extra computation bought...

Then decide whether what it bought was worth paying for under the objective you named Monday.

Use Wednesday's two-run receipt to make one bounded reproducibility claim.

Answer:

  3. Which facts could still differ on another computer?
  4. What evidence would another person need to decide whether a difference is meaningful?

A strong conclusion does not say "the results are identical, therefore the machines are identical."

A stronger shape is:

The same course source and command produced the same required evidence shape across repeated runs. The receipt records the executing environment, while host hardware and timing may still differ. Another person can reproduce the reasoning task by preserving _ and recording _.

Choose the strongest machine claim from Wednesday and defend it.

  4. Interpretation: what does that observation support?

  6. Revision: how would you ask the question more precisely next time?

Fast-thinking trap

A familiar command can tempt us to skip from output directly to a story. Resist that jump.

A good Architecture investigator can point to the exact observation and say why the explanation follows, while keeping virtualization, containers, permissions, and evidence scope in view.

Week 5 will use these instruments to begin the Machine Dossier. The goal this week is to arrive there knowing how to look before you claim.

Friday - Explain / Defend

This is not a parts-list submission. Your job is to defend one bounded design judgment from Week 5 evidence while naming what you still do not know.

Professional Minds - How Not to Be Wrong

Carry forward the shared question:

How do attractive numbers and familiar stories trick us into feeling more certain than the evidence allows?

Your Architecture receipt is the only required product here. Do not create a separate book-response assignment.

1. Claim / answer

Complete this idea in your own words:

For my $1,500 __ workload, I spent most intentionally on _ because . I deliberately compromised on because ___.

A good claim is specific enough that later evidence could change it.

2. Evidence that matters

Use the smallest evidence set that actually supports your claim.

Include:

  • workload + budget;
  • the relevant component prices and budget shares;
  • the one spec/capacity fact that matters most;
  • the relevant compatibility evidence;
  • the baseline vs controlled-reallocation difference;
  • the exact naive metric you used, with units.

Do not paste your entire market table or terminal session into the explanation.

3. Architecture mechanism / resource story

Explain why the resource you funded should matter to your workload.

At Week 5 depth, this may be a claim about:

  • useful capacity;
  • number/type of processing resources;
  • storage role;
  • graphics/accelerator need;
  • avoiding an obvious compatibility/interface constraint;
  • preserving budget for the resource you believe is closest to the workload.

Do not invent benchmark conclusions you did not measure.

4. Limitation

Name one way your best-looking metric could mislead you.

Examples:

  • $/core does not measure how well my workload uses the cores;
  • $/GB VRAM does not measure GPU throughput or data movement;
  • $/TB storage says nothing by itself about latency, bandwidth, endurance, or controller behavior;
  • cache capacity has no meaningful retail $/GB in this design;
  • a compatibility checker cannot prove workload performance.

Then name one future measurement that would make your design judgment stronger or force you to revise it.

5. Revision

Compare Monday's prediction with Wednesday's evidence.

  • Prediction: what did you initially think deserved the budget?
  • Reallocation: what did you move and why?
  • Revision: what did the controlled change teach you about the tradeoff?

A strong answer may keep the original design. “I kept it” is meaningful only when the evidence explains why.

6. AI / tool use and verification

If AI or another recommendation tool helped:

  • what assumption/metric did it appear to optimize?
  • what compatibility/spec/price claims did you verify independently?
  • where did your final design disagree with the recommendation, if anywhere?

AI said this is the best part is not evidence.

If you used course-provided AI recommendation samples instead of a live tool, identify them as course-provided.

Machine Dossier

Action: ADD.

Your dossier/machine-map.md, dated market evidence, and week05-archprobe receipt become the baseline that later weeks may revise.

Do not rewrite the Week 5 evidence later to make your original design look smarter. Preserve the original snapshot. Week 14 is more interesting if the record remembers what you actually believed.

Friday - Explain / Defend: Was the Extra Compute Worth It?

Write a short architectural judgment for your own learning, discussion, or portfolio evidence. Week 16 is inside the Fall 2026 dead-days window, so this is not a graded Canvas submission and does not create a new Machine Dossier checkpoint.

Use your Wednesday JSON/CSV evidence to answer the six parts below. If you used the course fallback receipt rather than a local run, identify it honestly and make the same bounded judgment from that evidence.

1. Bounded claim

Complete this sentence:

For this Farkle workload, on this execution lane, under the objective _, I would choose _ because ____.

Name the actual strategies you compared.

2. Evidence that matters

Give at least three concrete pieces of evidence from your receipt.

Include:

  • one effectiveness measure;
  • one preparation or operating-cost measure;
  • one machine/execution-context fact.

Good evidence sounds like:

The strategy won X of Y games while the comparison won Z, and its repeated CPU throughput had a median of ___ games/s.

Do not paste the entire JSON file.

3. Architecture connection

Name one prior Architecture idea that helps explain why the cost/result relationship matters.

Possible lenses include:

  • latency;
  • throughput;
  • parallelism;
  • locality;
  • specialization;
  • resource constraints;
  • data movement;
  • amortization of up-front cost.

Use the idea to explain the evidence. Merely naming a vocabulary word is not enough.

4. Limitation

State one thing your run does not establish.

Examples:

  • it did not measure power;
  • it did not execute on the GPU;
  • it did not compare two physical machines;
  • it did not establish purchase-price efficiency;
  • three timing repeats do not capture every source of system noise.

5. Revision after evidence

Return to Monday's prediction.

Choose one:

  • DEFEND: the evidence strengthened my original prediction;
  • REVISE: I changed the architecture I would choose;
  • QUALIFY: my prediction was directionally useful but needed a narrower condition;
  • REFUSE: the evidence is not sufficient to make the broader claim I originally wanted to make.

Explain in two or three sentences.

6. AI/tool use and verification

If an AI/tool helped you interpret the receipt, name what it helped with and identify one field or relationship you independently checked in the raw JSON/CSV.

If you did not use one, say so. There is no paid-AI requirement.

Final one-sentence verdict

End with:

The extra computation was / was not worth paying for because ____.

Different objectives may produce different defensible winners. That is the point.

Keep this judgment if it is useful to you. The learning value is the evidence-backed decision, not a Week 16 point value.

A7 - Final Reflection: What Can You See Now?

Purpose

This reflection closes Computer Architecture in place of adding another technical exam/project sprint.

The Machine Dossier froze in Week 14. Week 17 asks you to read the evidence you already made and explain what you understand now that you could not explain at the beginning of the semester.

Choose five prompts

Answer five prompts total, with at least one from each category. Use concrete evidence from your Machine Dossier, lab receipts, plots, traces, code/binary evidence, Week 16 Farkle receipt, or other course-produced work when it strengthens the answer.

Seeing the machine

  • What can you now explain about what happens underneath a program that you could not explain in August?
  • Which machine observation, trace, or experiment made an abstraction become physical for you?
  • Which Architecture word changed from a definition you memorized into something you can recognize in evidence?

Evidence and judgment

  • Which prediction were you most wrong about, and what evidence changed your mind?
  • Which measurement taught you that a simple performance story was incomplete?
  • Where did you learn to separate observation from interpretation?

Design and tradeoffs

  • Revisit one Week 5 machine/design choice. Why would you keep it or change it now?
  • Which tradeoff in your final Machine Dossier matters most for the workload you chose?
  • When did "more" hardware, more parallelism, more optimization, or more computation stop being automatically better?

Tools, AI, and professional growth

  • Describe one time AI/tool output was useful but needed independent verification.
  • What reproducibility habit will you carry into another technical course or job?
  • What kind of systems thinker/problem-solver are you becoming, and what is your next step?

Closing requirement

Finish with one paragraph beginning:

At the start of the semester I thought a computer was... Now I think a computer is...

Specific and honest reflection matters more than polish. Do not turn Week 17 into a retrospective feature sprint or rebuild the frozen dossier.

A6 - Professional Pathway Artifacts

Purpose

Use the professional evidence you began or recovered during the shared Week 1 success-foundations work. Do not manufacture a fresh artifact merely because the semester is ending. Bring real work forward, improve what the evidence justifies, and make your reasoning visible.

This assignment owns the two graded Architecture professional-pathway moments in Weeks 14 and 15. The governing loop is:

Claim -> Evidence -> Gap -> Decision

A professional claim should be supported by inspectable evidence. A gap should be named honestly as either a skill gap (you cannot yet do something at the needed level) or an evidence gap (you may be able to do it, but cannot yet show convincing evidence). Your next decision should follow from that distinction.

The shared Week 1 baseline remains owned by semester_kickoff_week.

Week 14 - Professional evidence update - graded 5%

By the end of the technical core, revisit a real target role, role family, internship direction, graduate-school direction, or other professional next step that matters to you.

Submit a concise evidence update that does all of the following:

  1. Claim: State one or more professional claims you can now make honestly.
  2. Evidence: Point to concrete evidence that supports each claim. Useful evidence may include a Machine Dossier excerpt, reproducible experiment, Explain / Defend receipt, technical presentation, project decision log, repository, resume entry, portfolio item, or another inspectable artifact.
  3. Gap: Compare your evidence with real expectations for the direction you named. Identify at least one skill gap and/or evidence gap where the comparison justifies it.
  4. Improve: Improve one or more real artifacts so your evidence becomes stronger, clearer, or easier for another person to inspect.
  5. Decision: Record what you changed, what you deliberately kept, and what the evidence says you should do next.

Your update may include changes to a resume, GitHub/portfolio/LinkedIn or equivalent profile, degree/certification plan, target-role research, skill-gap analysis, or another artifact that genuinely matters to your path.

The grade rewards the quality of the reasoning and evidence, not cosmetic polish.

Week 15 - Departure package and decision - graded 5%

Week 15 is asynchronous wind-down, not a new technical project.

Organize the professional evidence you already have into a useful departure package. Include only artifacts that genuinely apply to your path. A normal package may contain:

  • resume or professional profile material;
  • GitHub, portfolio, or project evidence;
  • a Machine Dossier checkpoint or excerpt;
  • transcript/degree-audit or degree-plan evidence;
  • target-role research;
  • skill-gap and/or evidence-gap analysis;
  • certification or training-path evidence;
  • another inspectable artifact that supports a professional claim.

Then answer:

Given the evidence I have now, what is my next professional move, and why?

Your next move may be to apply for something, strengthen a skill, expose evidence you already possess, finish a credential, revise a degree plan, expand a project, or deliberately gather more evidence before choosing.

Reuse rule

Bring an existing artifact when it already satisfies the need. Explain the update, equivalence, or decision rather than manufacturing churn.

Integrity and equity rules

Do not claim a skill, project, benchmark, system, profile update, or career result that the submitted evidence cannot support. AI may help revise wording; the underlying evidence must remain yours and verifiable.

Expensive tools, premium AI, personal hardware, or paid services cannot raise the attainable grading ceiling. A rough artifact with clear evidence and justified reasoning can outperform a polished artifact with no evidence trail.

pages.title: Monday — Survive this semester
pages.body:
Monday — Survive this semester

Today's goal: launch day, not panic day.

Slides — Monday (PDF)

Good habits, not talent

What actually makes people successful in a demanding course isn't raw talent — it's a small set of habits:

  1. Small steps, tested often. Don't write (or plan, or build) a huge amount before checking your work. Check constantly.
  2. A clear debugging story: Expected → Actual → Tried. When something goes wrong — in code, in a proof, in a project, in life — you can name what you expected, what actually happened, and what you already tried. That's the difference between a bad help request and a good one: - Bad: "It doesn't work." - Good: "I expected X, I got Y, here's what I tried."
  3. Evidence over vibes. Screenshots, error messages, specific examples — not just a feeling that something is wrong.

If your own "debugging story" (about anything — tech or not) involved trying more than one thing before it worked, you're already doing this. That instinct is the whole skill; the rest is practice.

What this course actually is

(CS1 reference instance — replace per course, see docs/NAMING.md)

CS1 is problem solving, communication, and habits — not memorizing syntax. The building-block mindset: every program is made of small, testable pieces, assembled in order.

What's due this week

  • A01–A03 (unofficial transcript, progress report, degree plan) — due Wednesday
  • A04–A06 (resume, dream job paper, gap analysis) — due Friday by 4:00 PM

Split across the week on purpose, so it's not all due at once. Open the Week 1 Overview in Canvas and get familiar with what's expected.

Why Friday at 4:00 PM specifically: that's this term's last day to add a class without special permission. This whole week — transcript, degree plan, dream job, gap analysis — exists so you have real information about your major and your direction before that door closes, not after.

The full picture: 7 assignments, spread across the semester

A01–A06 aren't the whole story either — this course has 7 assignments total that build your degree and career readiness:

# Assignment Due
A01 Unofficial transcript This Wednesday
A02 Progress report This Wednesday
A03 Personal semester-by-semester degree plan This Wednesday
A04 Resume This Friday, 4:00 PM
A05 Dream Job Paper This Friday, 4:00 PM
A06 Professional Gap Analysis This Friday, 4:00 PM
A07 Advisor name and meeting time Later — when registration opens for next semester

You'll hear about A04–A07 again on Wednesday and Friday this week — this is just so nothing on that list is a surprise later.

Exit ticket

  1. One habit I'll practice, one reason it matters, and one action I'll take.
  2. Two things I'll do in the first 10 minutes when I get stuck.
  3. One question I have right now.

Go to the Monday Exit Ticket assignment — submit your answers there for real credit (10 points).

pages.title: Monday — Student activity: Debugging Story Drill
pages.body:
Monday — Student activity: Debugging Story Drill

In-class activity — no submission required. Do this live with a partner; nothing here is turned in on its own. The two habits you pick in Part 2 are what you'll write up for real credit on the Monday Exit Ticket right after this activity.

Part 1 — Tell your story (5 minutes)

Think of any time something didn't work — tech or non-tech, doesn't matter. Write 3 sentences:

  1. What I expected:
  2. What actually happened:
  3. What I tried:

Share with a partner, then be ready to share with the class.

Part 2 — Pick 2 habits and make them concrete (10 minutes)

From today's three "good habits" (small steps tested often; a clear debugging story; evidence over vibes), pick two and write:

Habit 1: ____

  • What it looks like when I do it well (give a real example):
  • What I'll do when I get stuck (name 3 steps):

Habit 2: ____

  • What it looks like when I do it well (give a real example):
  • What I'll do when I get stuck (name 3 steps):

Why this matters

A bad help request sounds like "it doesn't work." A good one sounds like "I expected X, I got Y, here's the error, here's the input, here's what I tried." If your Part 1 story already had you trying more than one thing, you already have the instinct — today is about making it deliberate.

pages.title: Wednesday — Thrive in your degree
pages.body:
Wednesday — Thrive in your degree

Today's goal: turn "I hope I graduate" into "I know my next steps."

Your unofficial transcript and progress report are the closest thing to "the truth in writing" about where you stand. They show what you've completed, what still remains, and where your gaps are. The same office that runs your graduation check produces both documents — knowing how to read them is a real, transferable skill, not a one-time chore.

What your transcript and progress report actually show

Your unofficial transcript is what you've done:

  • Courses taken, grades, credit hours
  • Transfer credit
  • Course completion history
  • Your GPA

Your progress report is what you still need — the registrar's own software reorganizes that same history against your specific degree requirements:

  • Areas/categories (Gen Ed, major core, electives, etc.)
  • What's satisfied vs. still outstanding in each area
  • Specific requirement blocks or substitutions still open

Why both matter here: prerequisites, sequencing, and your graduation timeline all depend on them together — the transcript shows where you've been, the progress report shows what's left. It's also a quick "how am I doing at this college thing?" check-in.

Degree plan = a map, not a prophecy

Plans change. The actual skill is updating the plan without panic when they do. Today you'll start a rough semester-by-semester grid: which courses, which semester, how many credits — and you'll get a classmate's eyes on it before you finalize anything.

Rules of thumb for building it:

  • Put required math/core courses early — prerequisites are gates, not suggestions.
  • Pick one hard class per semester, not four.
  • Balance heavy semesters — don't stack every difficult course together.
  • Summer classes are often online; some programs offer interim options too.
  • Leave breathing room. Life happens. Your plan should survive it.

A quick grounding technique, while we're at it

Box breathing: in 4 seconds, hold 4, out 4, repeat 4 times. When you're stressed, your brain lies to you about how much is actually wrong — this is how you take the wheel back before planning something as consequential as your degree path.

What's due today (by end of day)

  • A01 — Unofficial transcript (upload + short reflection)
  • A02 — Progress report (upload + short summary)
  • A03 — Personal semester-by-semester degree plan
  • A08 — Degree Reflection (nine short, individually-graded questions — what excites you, what worries you, and why it matters; see below)

Friday isn't a free pass — A04, A05, and A06 (resume, dream job paper, gap analysis) are due Friday by 4:00 PM. Today is just about getting the degree side finished and off your plate first.

About A08 — this isn't busywork

A01–A03 prove you can find and read your own data. A08 is where you actually think about what it means — separated out, on purpose, with its own points on each question, because a reflection buried at the end of another assignment is the easiest thing in this whole week to skip. It isn't optional. Nine short answers: three about the class you're most excited about, five working through the thing you're most afraid of (name it, brainstorm three ways to handle it, pick one, plan your time, tie it back to your career), and one about whether your degree plan actually reflects what you value. Full prompts in assignments/A08_degree_reflection.md.

Looking ahead: A07 — Advisor name and meeting time

Your advisor can catch things your transcript, progress report, and degree plan can't — substitutions, deadlines, sequencing quirks specific to your program. Nothing due yet — A07 lands later in the semester, timed to when registration for next semester actually opens, so the meeting happens right when you can act on the advice.

Exit ticket (answer in 2–4 sentences)

  1. One thing I learned about my transcript or degree progress, one concern, and one next step.
  2. Two courses I think I should take next (or two questions I have about sequencing).
  3. One thing I can do this week to reduce stress or stay on track.

pages.title: Wednesday — Student activity: Transcript Treasure Hunt + Degree Plan Start
pages.body:
Wednesday — Student activity: Transcript Treasure Hunt + Degree Plan Start

Part 1 — Transcript Treasure Hunt (5 minutes)

If you have transcript access today, use it. If not, answer from memory and mark uncertain items with a "?" — you'll confirm them for real in A01.

Step 1 — Find your total completed credit hours

Write down your total completed credit hours: ______

Step 2 — Self-check: which tier are you in?

This is a pass/fail self-check, not a test — there is exactly one tier below that's a genuine "flag it" answer. Every other tier is on-track or ahead of the curve.

Under 60 credit hours — building your foundation. You're early, and that's exactly where you should be. Worth knowing now: stacking an associate's degree along the way is a real, legitimate strategy — a lot of your core/gen-ed credit already counts toward one. It's not a fallback or a consolation prize; it's a credential-stacking move some students use deliberately, landing a real credential in hand before finishing the bachelor's. Ask your advisor whether your current course mix already lines up with one — if it does, claiming it costs you very little.

60 to 120 credit hours — you've got a lot of runway. You're in the normal middle of a multi-year plan. This is a good place to be. Keep using this week's habits — a real plan, prerequisites checked, one hard class per semester — to stay on track toward graduation.

Over 120 credit hours — flag this one for a real conversation. This is not "behind" or "failing" — there are plenty of good reasons a student lands here (a changed major, transfer credit that didn't map cleanly, a deliberately slower pace, a double major). But past roughly 120 hours you should either already be very close to done or have a specific, known reason why not. Put a real question about this in front of your advisor this semester — not because something is wrong, but because at this point a second set of eyes is worth having confirm your assumptions. A "wrong" answer here means exactly one thing: go have that conversation. It does not mean you're failing.

Which tier are you in? ______

A few more quick recall checks

  1. What math course are you in, or last completed?
  2. What courses in this subject area have you completed, if any?
  3. Any repeats or withdrawals that might matter?
  4. Using your progress report (not just the transcript): name one specific requirement area you still have outstanding.

Part 2 — Start your degree plan grid (10 minutes)

Build a rough grid: Semester → Courses.

Keep these rules of thumb in mind as you place courses:

  • Required math/core courses go early — prerequisites are gates.
  • Pick one hard class per semester, not four.
  • Balance heavy semesters against lighter ones.
  • Summer classes are often online.
  • Leave breathing room — your plan should survive real life happening.

Starting from a blank page? Use a scaffold.

Two generic starter grids are available if you'd rather fill in a structure than start from nothing:

Semester Course Type Course (fill in) Credit Hours Notes
Semester 1 (Fall) Math/Core Requirement Prerequisite gate — place early
Semester 1 (Fall) Major Requirement
Semester 1 (Fall) Gen Ed
Semester 1 (Fall) Elective
Semester 1 (Fall) Semester total Sanity-check against a manageable load
... Repeat this block per semester until graduation

Full 8-semester versions — one shaped generically around a CS-track's usual mix (math/core-heavy early, major requirements building through the middle), one shaped generically around an Engineering Technology track's usual mix (adds a Lab/Applied Requirement row type, reflecting that ET programs typically carry a heavier applied/lab credit load) — are in the course repo at semester_kickoff_week/templates/ (ask your instructor if you'd like the CSV to import into Google Sheets directly).

These are starting scaffolds, not an official degree audit. The category labels ("Major Requirement," "Gen Ed," etc.) are structural placeholders, not real course numbers — this repo does not have an authoritative, up-to-date copy of the actual degree catalog to pull real course numbers from. Fill in real course numbers from your institution's actual catalog/degree audit, and bring the result to your advisor to verify — the same "check with a real advisor" step Part 3 below and A03 both already ask for.

Part 3 — Partner check (5 minutes each way)

Swap grids with a partner and answer:

  1. What looks strong about this plan?
  2. What looks risky or confusing?
  3. One question you'd bring to an advisor about this plan.

This grid is prep for A03 — Personal semester-by-semester degree plan, due Friday — you're not finalizing anything today, just getting a real first draft and a second set of eyes on it.

pages.title: Friday — Entering your career
pages.body:
Friday — Entering your career

Today's goal: run your life like a project, and turn Week 1 into something submitted.

STAR bullets — achievement bullets, not duty bullets

You get to build your story on purpose: skills, projects, evidence. The shift is duties → achievements — not "what I was responsible for" but "what I accomplished, with evidence."

STAR in one breath:

  • Context (Situation/Task): the situation and task, in one short phrase.
  • Action: a strong verb — built, analyzed, designed, led.
  • Result: the "so what?" — ideally with a number.

Bullet formula: [Power verb] + [what you did / context] + [result or benefit].

Two examples:

  • "Resolved 15+ customer issues per shift, improving satisfaction and reducing manager escalations."
  • "Built a Python script to automate file cleanup, saving ~30 minutes per week."

SMART goals — a way to turn a wish into a plan

  • Specific — exactly what you'll do.
  • Measurable — how you'll track it.
  • Achievable — challenging but possible.
  • Relevant — matters to you right now.
  • Time-bound — a deadline.

"If you can't tell when you're done, it's not a goal yet."

Pomodoro — focus sprints

Your brain starts lying when a task feels big. Pomodoro makes the first step small: 15 minutes on, 5 minutes off (build up to 25/5 with experience). One task only. Phone away, notifications off. When distracted, write it down and come back to the work — don't chase it.

The 3-2-1 CV/resume habit — tiny, repeatable

  • 3 daily notes (wins, work, learning) — a running document you keep on your phone.
  • 2 weekly paragraphs in a running CV doc, written as STAR stories.
  • 1 monthly resume bullet — a measurable achievement.

Remember: CV = your full story. Resume = your best highlights for one job. Building the CV all semester means the resume is just curation later, not a panic-write the week before you need one.

What's due today, by 4:00 PM

  • A04 — Resume: a real, current resume, using STAR bullets, not duty bullets — the 3-2-1 habit above is what makes this easy instead of a scramble.
  • A05 — Dream Job Paper: name a specific, real job you could apply for, and why it's the one you want.
  • A06 — Professional Gap Analysis: compare your current skills against that job's real requirements, and build a plan to close the gap.
  • A09 — Career Reflection: nine short, individually-graded questions — what part of that job you're eager for, what part worries you, and why it matters (see below).

A01–A03 (transcript, progress report, degree plan) were due Wednesday — if you're missing one of those, get it in too, but today's focus is these three.

About A09 — this isn't busywork

Same idea as Wednesday's A08, career side: A04–A06 prove you can build a resume and compare yourself against a real job. A09 is where you think about what that job actually means for you — separated out, individually pointed, so it doesn't get skipped. Three questions about the part of the job you're genuinely looking forward to, five working through the hardest part (name it, find three ways to prepare, pick one, name your next step, tie it to a real class or skill), and one about whether this career direction actually fits your values. Full prompts in assignments/A09_career_reflection.md.

Getting started on A05 and A06

Both ask you to get specific, not hypothetical:

  • A05 (Dream Job Paper): don't pick "something in tech" — pick an actual job posting or job title you could apply for, now or later. A real posting (search any job board in your field) gives you real requirements to write about instead of guessing.
  • A06 (Gap Analysis): use the same job you picked for A05. List what you already have (hard and soft skills) next to what the job actually asks for, and be honest about the gap — that's the point of the assignment, not a flaw in it.

Full instructions are in each assignment file — this is just enough to get you started without overthinking the target.

4:00 PM matters: it's this term's last day to add a class without special permission. Everything this week — including today's three — exists so you have real information before that door closes, not after.

Looking ahead: A07 — Advisor name and meeting time

Not due today. A07 lands later in the semester, timed to when registration for next semester opens, so the meeting happens right when you can actually act on your advisor's advice.

Exit ticket

  1. What did you submit today (A01/A02/A03)?
  2. When is your next scheduled focus sprint for this class (day/time)?
  3. What's one thing you want help with next week?

pages.title: Friday — Student activity: STAR Bullets + SMART Goals
pages.body:
Friday — Student activity: STAR Bullets + SMART Goals

Part 1 — Write one STAR bullet (5 minutes)

Pick something real you did (a job, a project, a class, anything) and write it as an achievement bullet:

Example: "Resolved 15+ customer issues per shift, improving satisfaction and reducing manager escalations."

Your turn:

Write one academic SMART goal and one personal/life SMART goal. Under each, add one line: your first next action, doable in 10 minutes or less.

  • Specific — exactly what you'll do
  • Measurable — how you'll track it
  • Achievable — challenging but possible
  • Relevant — matters to you right now
  • Time-bound — a deadline

Academic goal:

First next action:

Personal/life goal:

First next action:

Round 2: Switch roles, repeat.
