pages.title: Week 05 - Week at a Glance
pages.body:
Week 5 - Build the Machine

Central machine question: What should I build for this workload, what does each part buy me, and how should I compare choices?

Week at a Glance

Useful prior belief we are testing: a better computer is mostly the one with the biggest numbers.

Prediction before the investigation: under a fixed $1,500 tower budget, which component category deserves the largest share of your budget for your workload, and what evidence would make you move about $150 somewhere else?

AI Fluency lens: Lens 5 - Select the Right Model.

Professional Minds: Wednesday - The Art of Thinking Clearly; Friday - How Not to Be Wrong.

Day Mode What happens Evidence
Monday Think / Frame Treat a computer as a negotiated set of workload, compatibility, capacity, cost, and uncertainty constraints. prediction + first design model
Wednesday Investigate / Break / Measure Build one compatible $1,500 system, reallocate about $100-$200 while holding workload/budget steady, calculate deliberately naive metrics, and inspect one real machine with archprobe. dated market table + compatibility receipt + tradeoff comparison + machine snapshot
Friday Explain / Defend Defend one intentional spend and one accepted compromise without pretending a shopping metric is a benchmark. bounded evidence-backed design argument

The common constraint

Your hypothetical tower budget is $1,500 USD.

Include the system unit: CPU, compatible motherboard, memory, primary storage, case, power supply, cooling when needed, and a discrete GPU only when your workload/design requires one.

Exclude tax, shipping, display, keyboard/mouse, operating-system license, and other peripherals. Used hardware is not required.

The budget is hypothetical. You are not being asked to buy anything. Owning expensive hardware does not improve your grade.

Choose a workload

Pick one:

  1. Build & Container Developer - IDEs, compilation, containers/VM-shaped multitasking, general development responsiveness.
  2. Play & Stream - modern interactive/gaming work plus communication/light recording or streaming.
  3. Create - photo/video/content creation where CPU, memory, storage, and optional acceleration compete for budget.
  4. Local Data / AI Explorer - data analysis and modest local inference/experimentation, not giant-model training.
  5. Guarded custom workload - name three concrete tasks, your most important capacity/throughput/responsiveness concern, one likely bottleneck or uncertainty, and why the workload still fits the same $1,500 tower constraint.

You do not need benchmark expertise yet. Week 5 predictions are allowed to be wrong. Later weeks exist to make them better.

Continuity

What returns from Weeks 2-4: skeptical AI use, reproducible work habits, and machine observation.

What this week intentionally carries forward: one workload, one designed machine, one observable machine, one set of assumptions, and one Machine Dossier through Week 14.

Week 14 asks you to return to this same design question with much stronger evidence.

Machine Dossier handoff

Action: ADD

Initialize Dossier v0 with:

  • workload + $1,500 constraint;
  • designed baseline machine;
  • one controlled reallocation/tradeoff;
  • compatibility receipt;
  • dated market/spec evidence;
  • first hierarchy ledger;
  • first Dollars-Per/budget-share metrics;
  • observable-machine archprobe receipt or approved fallback;
  • at least one predicted bottleneck/constraint;
  • one claim you expect later evidence might overturn.

Suggested working shape:

dossier/
  machine-map.md
  evidence/
    week05-market.csv
    week05-archprobe/
      machine.json
      machine.txt

This is the beginning of one living technical record, not the first page in a weekly worksheet pile.

Student path

  1. Read/work through monday.md and record your prediction before shopping/research.
  2. Complete the investigation in wednesday.md.
  3. Use only the evidence that matters to complete friday.md.
  4. Use references.md when you need verification or deeper reinforcement.

Required materials and equity

  • ordinary web browser;
  • course repository/laboratory for archprobe where supported;
  • free manufacturer/retailer information;
  • PCPartPicker or another builder may be used as a convenience, but no commercial builder is required;
  • no paid AI, premium CLI agent, commercial textbook, GPU, private host, or actual hardware purchase required.

If your machine cannot run the current Observatory path, use the named course-owned fallback snapshot and do the same reasoning. The grading ceiling is identical.

Scope

This week is about: workload-driven design, compatibility, hierarchy, cost evidence, intentionally naive metrics, and explicit tradeoffs.

This week is not trying to teach: benchmark interpretation, cache timing, pipeline performance, virtual memory, GPU programming, exhaustive electrical engineering, or “the best PC build.”

Those tempting details arrive only when the course has enough evidence to make them useful.

pages.title: Week 05 Monday - Think / Frame
pages.body:
Monday - Think / Frame

Central question

What should I build for this workload, what does each part buy me, and how should I compare choices?

This is the first week where the course stops preparing the laboratory and starts using it to reason about a machine.

The useful prior belief

Most of us begin with some version of this model:

Bigger numbers make a better computer.

That belief is not stupid. More capacity, more cores, a larger GPU, a higher clock, and a larger budget often can buy capability.

The problem is that “better” has no meaning until we name the workload and the constraint.

A machine is a set of negotiated choices. Money spent in one place is money not spent somewhere else. A part can be impressive and still be the wrong answer to the problem.

Model 1 - workload comes before specification

Start with verbs, not components.

A workload says what the computer has to do:

  • compile and run many development tasks;
  • render frames interactively;
  • encode/edit media;
  • hold large working data sets;
  • move data quickly;
  • perform lots of independent arithmetic;
  • stay responsive while several things happen at once.

A specification is evidence about a component. It is not automatically evidence that the component matters to your workload.

When you see a large number, ask:

  1. What resource does this number describe?
  2. What workload behavior would care about that resource?
  3. What did I give up to buy more of it?
  4. What evidence would tell me the resource is actually the constraint?

Week 5 will not answer #4 completely. That is intentional. Weeks 8, 10, 12, and 13 will give us better measurement tools.

Model 2 - first ask “would it run?”

Before performance, the machine must be coherent enough to exist.

Your bounded compatibility checklist is:

  • CPU ↔ motherboard: supported socket/platform and reasonable firmware/chipset support;
  • motherboard ↔ memory: correct memory generation/type and supported capacity/configuration;
  • storage ↔ motherboard: compatible M.2/NVMe/SATA interface and available slot/port;
  • motherboard/GPU/cooler ↔ case: form factor and physical clearance;
  • CPU/GPU ↔ power supply: adequate power budget and required connectors;
  • graphics path: either a usable integrated-graphics path or a discrete GPU when the chosen parts/workload need one.

A builder website can help catch mistakes. It is not the source of truth for why the parts fit. When a compatibility claim matters, prefer the official specification page for the exact component.

Model 3 - capacity, latency, and bandwidth are different questions

Three numbers are going to haunt this course in useful ways:

  • Capacity: how much can be held?
  • Latency: how long until one requested thing becomes available?
  • Bandwidth: how much can move or complete per unit time once work is flowing?

Those are not interchangeable.

A storage device can have enormous capacity and still be a poor answer to a latency-sensitive problem. A component can advertise huge throughput and still make dependent work wait.

For now, treat the hierarchy qualitatively:

Layer Typical role Capacity tendency Separately purchased? Persistent?
L1/L2/L3 cache keep recently/usefully located data close to CPU execution small relative to RAM no no
RAM active program/data working space much larger than cache yes no
SSD/NVMe persistent local storage much larger again yes yes
optional HDD/other storage inexpensive bulk persistence very large yes yes

We are not memorizing a universal nanosecond table this week. Week 10 will make memory behavior hurt enough to measure.

Model 4 - price is evidence; Dollars-Per is a model

Week 5 preserves the useful historical instinct of Dollars Per.

Retail capacity metrics can be literal:

  • RAM price / RAM GB;
  • storage price / storage TB.

But even correct arithmetic can produce a bad decision rule.

Synthetic teaching example

These numbers are invented for the lesson. They are not current product recommendations.

Option Price Advertised physical cores Naive $/core
CPU A $280 8 $35.00
CPU B $390 12 $32.50

CPU B “wins” dollars per core.

Does that prove CPU B is the better use of the budget?

No.

The metric has not told us:

  • whether our workload scales across those cores;
  • whether the cores are architecturally equivalent;
  • single-thread behavior;
  • memory behavior;
  • power/thermal limits;
  • whether spending the extra $110 somewhere else helps more.

The arithmetic can be true while the conclusion is nonsense.

That is why Week 5 metrics are hypotheses with units, not verdicts.

The $1,500 constraint

Everyone gets the same hypothetical tower budget: $1,500 USD.

The equality is important. We are comparing decisions, not purchasing power.

A useful first look is budget share:

[ \text{budget share} = \frac{\text{component price}}{1500} \times 100\% ]

If your design spends 40% of its budget on one component, that is a design statement even before we know whether it is a good one.

The controlled perturbation

After you build one compatible baseline, you will change it once while keeping the workload and total budget approximately fixed.

Move roughly $100-$200 from one category to another.

Examples:

  • CPU → GPU;
  • storage capacity → RAM;
  • discrete GPU → stronger CPU/RAM/storage when integrated graphics is enough;
  • premium motherboard/case → a resource closer to the workload.

This is the first tiny version of what the whole semester will do:

Hold the question mostly still. Make one architectural resource different. See whether the workload story changes.

AI Fluency Lens 5 - Select the Right Model

Hardware recommendations are a great place to watch AI become confidently conditional.

Ask for two recommendations under meaningfully different framing. You may use:

  • two available models;
  • one model with two different roles/prompts;
  • course-provided recommendation samples if AI access is unavailable.

Useful contrast:

  • “maximize interactive/gaming performance under $1,500”;
  • “maximize development/container responsiveness and long-lived utility under $1,500.”

Do not score the recommendations by how authoritative they sound.

Instead ask:

  • What workload did the recommendation assume?
  • What metric did it seem to optimize?
  • Which compatibility/spec claims can I independently verify?
  • Which recommendation changes when I change the workload?

AI output is a candidate design or hypothesis. It is not price, compatibility, or specification evidence.

Scope and limitation

This week can support claims such as:

  • this set of parts is compatible under the evidence I checked;
  • this build spends more of the budget on resource X than resource Y;
  • this storage choice offers a lower observed $/TB on the date I checked;
  • this design reflects my current hypothesis about the workload bottleneck.

This week cannot yet support claims such as:

  • this CPU is 23% faster for my workload because it has more cores;
  • this larger cache guarantees better performance;
  • this GPU will always be the bottleneck;
  • this $/core number measures actual performance value.

Those require evidence we have not earned yet.

Prediction for Wednesday

Before looking at current parts, write:

Under the $1,500 constraint, I think __ deserves the largest share of my budget for my workload because _. I would move about $150 somewhere else if I found evidence that ___.

Keep this prediction. Friday needs it.

The unresolved question

You can make a machine that fits together and calculate several perfectly correct metrics.

Will those metrics actually tell you what the workload cares about?

Today we build the first story. The rest of the course gets to attack it.

pages.title: Professional Minds Wednesday - Week 5 Reading: Never Judge a Decision by Its Outcome
pages.body:
Week 5 Reading: Never Judge a Decision by Its Outcome

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 5 -- How do we avoid common thinking mistakes?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7-9 minutes
  • Primary source: The Art of Thinking Clearly by Rolf Dobelli (Sceptre, 2013), chapter "Never Judge a Decision by Its Outcome"

Why This Matters Professionally

Professionals are routinely judged by results: a launch succeeded, a hire worked out, a bet paid off, a patient recovered. It is tempting to work backward from a good or bad result and conclude that the decision behind it was correspondingly good or bad. Dobelli's chapter names this shortcut the outcome bias and shows why it produces unreliable judgments about our own choices and other people's.

Week 5 opens the "Reasoning" unit by asking how we avoid common thinking mistakes. Outcome bias is a useful place to start because it is easy to notice once named, yet it quietly shapes how we evaluate ourselves, colleagues, and past decisions almost every day.

Primary-Source Ideas: What The Art of Thinking Clearly Argues

Primary-source claim: Dobelli defines outcome bias as evaluating a decision by its result rather than by the quality of the decision process, and notes it is also called the historian error. (Source location: "Never Judge a Decision by Its Outcome," opening definition.)

Responsible paraphrase: A decision and its result are not the same thing. A careful, well-reasoned decision can still turn out badly because of chance or events no one could have predicted, and a careless decision can still turn out well by luck. Judging the decision by the result alone conflates the two.

Primary-source claim: Dobelli's monkey-stock-market hypothesis illustrates the bias directly: if one million monkeys trade stocks at random, after twenty weeks of successive elimination one "success monkey" remains who picked correctly every week, purely by chance, yet observers would search for a "success principle" behind its performance. (Source location: "Never Judge a Decision by Its Outcome," the million-monkeys thought experiment.)

Responsible paraphrase: When a large enough population makes random choices, some individuals will produce an impressive streak of correct results by chance alone. A dramatic outcome does not, by itself, prove that skill or a sound process produced it.

Primary-source claim: Dobelli applies the same idea to the 1941 Pearl Harbor attack (the "historian error"): assessing the decision not to evacuate the base requires using only the contradictory information available at the time, not the clarity that hindsight provides after the attack occurred. (Source location: "Never Judge a Decision by Its Outcome," the Pearl Harbor example.)

Responsible paraphrase: A decision that looks obviously wrong in hindsight may have been reasonable given what was actually known when it was made. Assessing a past decision fairly means reconstructing the information available at the time, not importing everything learned since.

Primary-source claim: In Dobelli's heart-surgeon example, three surgeons each perform a difficult operation five times, with a stable historical mortality rate of 20 percent for the procedure; surgeon A loses no patients, B loses one, and C loses two. Dobelli argues that ranking A best, B second, and C worst is outcome bias, because five operations is too small a sample to distinguish skill from chance, and purely outcome-based ranking would be "not only negligent but also unethical." (Source location: "Never Judge a Decision by Its Outcome," the heart-surgeon example.)

Responsible paraphrase: Small samples of outcomes are unreliable evidence of skill, even in high-stakes professional settings. Judging performance responsibly requires examining the preparation and execution of the work itself -- the process -- not just counting favorable or unfavorable results from too few trials.

Primary-source claim: Dobelli concludes that a bad result does not automatically indicate a bad decision, and a good result does not automatically indicate a good one; a decision should instead be evaluated by whether its reasons were rational and understandable given the information available at the time. (Source location: "Never Judge a Decision by Its Outcome," closing conclusion.)

Responsible paraphrase: The corrective habit is to separate two questions that outcome bias collapses into one: "Did this turn out well?" and "Was this a sound decision?" A sound decision is worth repeating even after an unlucky result, and a lucky result does not make a careless decision worth repeating.

A Concrete Example

Instructor's own invented professional-life example, not an example from the book: A hiring manager makes two offers using the same careful process: a structured interview, a work sample, and two reference checks. One hire thrives; the other leaves within three months for reasons unrelated to the interview (a family relocation). If the manager concludes the first decision was "right" and the second was "wrong," they have fallen for outcome bias -- both decisions used the same sound process, and one outcome was shaped by an unpredictable factor outside the hiring process itself. The more useful question is whether the structured process reliably surfaces good candidates over many hires, not whether any single hire worked out.

Synthesis

Instructor synthesis: Dobelli's chapter reframes what it means to learn from experience. Chasing good outcomes and avoiding bad ones feels like the obvious way to improve, but a single result -- especially from a small sample -- often reflects luck more than judgment. Avoiding this common thinking mistake means asking a different question after any decision: given what was known at the time, was the reasoning behind it sound? That question, not the result alone, tells us whether to repeat the decision the next time similar circumstances arise.

Reflection Questions

  1. Student application: Describe a decision -- your own or one you observed -- that was praised or criticized mainly because of how it turned out. Was the reasoning behind the decision actually good or bad, based on what was known at the time?

  2. Student application: Think of a small sample of outcomes (a few games, a few sales calls, a few grades) that someone used to judge skill. What would a larger sample or a closer look at process reveal that the small sample could not?

  3. Student application: Why might treating "rational and understandable reasons" as the standard for a good decision feel less satisfying than simply looking at whether things worked out? What would it take to apply that standard to your own choices?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Dobelli, Rolf. The Art of Thinking Clearly. Sceptre, first published in Great Britain 2013. Chapter "Never Judge a Decision by Its Outcome." Citations use the chapter's own section landmarks rather than page numbers because the supplied chapter file does not carry reliable page numbers for this excerpt.
  • All primary-source claims and responsible paraphrases are drawn only from the supplied chapter file.
  • The hiring-decision example is invented by the instructor and is not from Dobelli's chapter.
  • This reading is a bounded companion to one chapter, not a summary of the whole book.

pages.title: Professional Minds Friday - Week 5 Reading: The Triumph of Mediocrity -- Regression to the Mean
pages.body:
Week 5 Reading: The Triumph of Mediocrity -- Regression to the Mean

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 5 -- How do we avoid common thinking mistakes?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7-9 minutes
  • Primary source: How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking by Jordan Ellenberg (The Penguin Press, 2014), chapter "The Triumph of Mediocrity"

Why This Matters Professionally

Wednesday's reading showed that a single outcome -- good or bad, especially from a small sample -- is unreliable evidence of skill. Ellenberg's chapter supplies the mathematical mechanism behind one of the most common ways that mistake fools us in practice: regression to the mean. When today's top performers, harshest critics of a new policy, or most dramatic before-and-after results are selected precisely because they were extreme, some of that extremity was luck, and luck does not repeat. Understanding why makes it possible to avoid a whole family of thinking mistakes: crediting a "cure" for an improvement that would have happened anyway, or explaining a decline with a story when chance alone predicts it.

Primary-Source Ideas: What How Not to Be Wrong Argues

Primary-source claim: Statistician Horace Secrist studied hundreds of businesses over time and found that top-performing firms in one period became closer to average in later periods, while the worst-performing firms improved toward average; he published this finding in 1933 as The Triumph of Mediocrity in Business, concluding that competition itself pushed successful firms down and unsuccessful ones up. (Source location: "The Triumph of Mediocrity," Secrist's study and conclusion.)

Responsible paraphrase: Secrist had real data showing extreme performers moving toward the average over time, but he misdiagnosed the cause -- he attributed a mathematical pattern to a mechanism (competitive pressure) that was not actually responsible for it.

Primary-source claim: Francis Galton had earlier discovered the same pattern in heredity: tall parents tend to have children who are taller than average but shorter than the parents themselves, and short parents tend to have children shorter than average but taller than themselves. Galton understood that height reflects a mix of inherited tendency and other factors (environment, chance), so people at an extreme of the population are likely to have benefited from favorable factors on top of genetics -- factors that do not automatically pass to the next generation. (Source location: "The Triumph of Mediocrity," Galton's height data and explanation.)

Responsible paraphrase: Regression to the mean is not a mysterious force pulling things toward average. It is what happens whenever an outcome combines a stable underlying factor with chance, and you select cases based on how extreme the combined outcome was. Some of that extremity was the stable factor; some was luck. Only the stable factor is likely to persist.

Primary-source claim: Mathematician Harold Hotelling reviewed Secrist's book and showed that the regression pattern was "mathematically obvious" for any variable affected by both stable factors and chance, and did not require Secrist's explanation involving competitive forces; Hotelling demonstrated that the same pattern would also run backward in time, which competition could not explain. (Source location: "The Triumph of Mediocrity," Hotelling's review and rebuttal.)

Responsible paraphrase: A statistical pattern can be real and well-documented while the story someone tells to explain it is wrong. Confirming that a pattern exists is not the same as confirming why it exists.

Primary-source claim: Ellenberg extends the pattern to sports: home-run leaders at a baseball season's midpoint typically hit far fewer home runs in the second half (about 60 percent as many, in one 1976-2000 sample), not because of fatigue or a "curse," but because a league leader is likely to be both genuinely skilled and unusually lucky at the moment they take the lead, and luck does not persist. (Source location: "The Triumph of Mediocrity," the "On Pace" section and home-run-leader data.)

Responsible paraphrase: Declaring a leader "on pace" for a record, or a slumping performer "cursed," often just describes ordinary regression to the mean: extreme early performance combines skill with a temporary run of luck, and the luck component is expected to fade.

Primary-source claim: Ellenberg describes a 1976 British Medical Journal bran study that found bran normalized digestive transit times -- slow transit sped up, fast transit slowed down -- and notes this is exactly the pattern expected even if bran had no effect at all, since people's own transit times vary day to day around their normal level. He also describes the Scared Straight program, whose apparent success (lower arrest rates in participants who were selected as the worst-behaved offenders) disappeared, and reversed into increased antisocial behavior, once tested with random assignment rather than selection based on extreme prior behavior. (Source location: "The Triumph of Mediocrity," the bran-treatment study and the Scared Straight program.)

Responsible paraphrase: When a group is selected because its members were extreme on some measure, and then measured again later, improvement toward average is expected regardless of any treatment applied in between. A study that fails to compare against an untreated or randomly assigned control group cannot distinguish real treatment effects from ordinary regression to the mean -- and worse, a genuinely effective-looking before-and-after result can mask a treatment that produced no benefit or even harm.

A Concrete Example

Instructor's own invented professional-life example, not an example from the book: A sales manager identifies the five lowest-performing reps in the quarter and enrolls them in a new coaching program. Three months later, their average performance has improved, and the manager credits the coaching. But because these five reps were selected for being unusually low performers -- a combination of underlying skill and an unlucky quarter -- some improvement toward the team average was expected even without any coaching at all. Without a comparison group of similarly low-performing reps who did not receive coaching, the manager cannot tell how much of the improvement, if any, the coaching actually caused.

Synthesis

Instructor synthesis: Regression to the mean explains why selecting on an extreme outcome and then observing improvement (or decline) afterward is not, by itself, evidence that anything you did caused the change. Whenever a stable factor and chance jointly produce an outcome, and you pick out the most extreme cases, expect the next measurement to look less extreme -- and expect a story (a curse, a cure, a competitive punishment) to fill the gap when the mathematical explanation is available and simpler. Avoiding this mistake requires either a comparison or control group unaffected by your selection, or explicit reasoning about how much of an extreme result reflects a stable, persistent cause rather than a one-time favorable roll.

Reflection Questions

  1. Student application: Describe a case where you or your organization selected "the best" or "the worst" performers based on one period's results and then tracked them afterward. What would regression to the mean predict, separate from any program or intervention applied?

  2. Student application: Ellenberg shows that a real, well-documented pattern (business firms, batting averages, digestive transit times) can still be misexplained. Where have you seen someone offer a compelling causal story for a pattern that might just be regression to the mean?

  3. Student application: What would it take to add a genuine comparison or control group to a "before and after" claim you have encountered recently, at work, in the news, or in your own habits?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Ellenberg, Jordan. How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking. The Penguin Press, 2014. Chapter "The Triumph of Mediocrity."
  • All primary-source claims and responsible paraphrases are drawn only from the supplied chapter file. Historical material about Francis Galton's later, now-discredited eugenicist writings appears in the source chapter; this reading uses only Galton's statistical discovery of regression to the mean and does not repeat or endorse his views on heredity and social policy.
  • Source locations use the chapter's own section landmarks rather than page numbers, matching the convention used by this book's other appetizer-chapter sessions.
  • The sales-coaching example is invented by the instructor and is not from Ellenberg's chapter.
  • This reading is a bounded companion to one chapter, not a summary of the entire book.

The course-owned Monday/Wednesday/Friday material is the coherent teaching surface. Current products and prices are evidence inputs, not the textbook.

Primary / official truth

Use the official page for the exact part you select whenever a compatibility or architecture claim matters.

Representative official lookup surfaces:

  • AMD Processor Specifications: https://www.amd.com/en/products/specifications/processors.html - cores/threads, cache, socket, memory support, PCIe generation, power and other CPU properties.
  • Intel product specifications / comparison: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/products/compare.html - processor cores/threads, cache, frequency/power and product-specific properties.
  • NVIDIA GeForce comparison/specifications: https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/graphics-cards/compare/ - GPU memory configuration, power, architecture and current family specifications.
  • Exact motherboard/memory/storage/GPU/PSU/case manufacturer page - use the product maker's page/manual for socket, memory generation, slot/interface, dimensions, power/connectors, or other compatibility facts.

The manufacturer page is strongest for what the product is. It is not automatically the strongest evidence for independent performance claims.

Current market evidence

For price:

  • use the retailer/aggregator price you actually observed;
  • record exact model, USD price, URL, and date;
  • do not silently substitute MSRP for an unavailable street price;
  • Week 14 will refresh the market snapshot.

PCPartPicker / builder surfaces

A PC builder such as https://pcpartpicker.com/ may be used to assemble a candidate system and surface compatibility concerns.

It is optional convenience rather than required course truth. During the 2026-08-16 authoring validation pass, automated retrieval of PCPartPicker returned HTTP 403, which is one reason the assignment keeps a course-owned compatibility checklist and accepts equivalent workflows.

Optional / link-first reinforcement

  • Revisit the course's accepted open-source canon in ../../planning/open-source-resource-canon.md if you want deeper architecture context.
  • Manufacturer performance/marketing pages may help generate hypotheses, but treat comparative marketing claims as claims to investigate rather than neutral benchmark truth.

No external instructional content was adapted into Week 5.

The week is course-authored. External manufacturer/retailer pages are linked as current evidence/truth sources for selected products.

pages.title: Week 06 - Week at a Glance
pages.body:
Week 6 - Bits Become Instructions

Central machine question: What must software and hardware agree on for a program to run?

Week at a Glance

Prior belief we are testing: source code has one obvious meaning all the way down.

Prediction before evidence: for transform(4), predict the final return value and name one place where width, signedness, encoding, or register convention matters.

AI Fluency: Lens 6 - Engineer the Prompt.
Professional Minds: Wednesday - Statistics Done Wrong; Friday - Understanding Statistics and Experimental Design.
Checkpoint: Machine Dossier Checkpoint 1.

Day Mode What happens Evidence
Monday Think / Frame Meaning becomes fixed-width bits; instructions are encoded agreements. prediction + representation model
Wednesday Investigate Run the bounded RV32I specimen and connect source, disassembly, and register state. riscv-receipt.json + disassembly
Friday Explain / Defend Defend how one operation survives the trip into machine state and state the model's limit. bounded evidence receipt

Continuity

The Week 5 machine remains the workload/design context. Week 6 starts the persistent Weeks 6-9 ISA teaching context using one course-owned specimen:

int transform(int x) {
    int y = x + 2;
    if (y > 5) {
        y = y * 3;
    }
    return y;
}

Do not imply that a student's proposed desktop literally becomes a RISC-V physical machine. RISC-V is the clean lens we use to inspect the ISA contract.

Machine Dossier handoff

Action: ADD

Add a compact representation/ISA trace and Checkpoint 1 evidence. Do not add binary-conversion worksheets to the dossier.

Student path

  1. Work through monday.md and record the prediction before running the lab.
  2. Complete wednesday.md.
  3. Complete friday.md.
  4. Complete checkpoint.md using the same evidence.
  5. Use references.md to verify/deepen claims.

Equity / required path

CPU-only, zero-cost, no paid AI, no premium agent, no GPU, no private infrastructure. The course-owned RV32I path is deliberately bounded so no QEMU/Spike/RARS installation is required.

Scope

Teach binary/hex, fixed width, signedness, overflow, a humane floating-point taste, RV32I basics, bounded instruction encoding, and the ABI details the specimen actually exposes. Do not turn this into Digital Logic or Compiler Construction.

pages.title: Week 06 Monday - Think / Frame
pages.body:
Week 6 Monday - Bits Become Instructions

The machine question

What must software and hardware agree on for a program to run?

Prediction before evidence

For transform(4), predict the final return value and name one place where width, signedness, encoding, or register convention matters.

Record the prediction before Wednesday. Being wrong is useful if the correction is evidence-backed.

Meaning needs a representation

Humans reason about values and operations. Hardware stores fixed-width bit patterns. Interpretation decides whether the same bits represent an unsigned integer, signed integer, instruction, or bytes.

Fixed width is a constraint

Use a few 8-bit examples to make signed/unsigned interpretation and overflow visible, then move to RV32I's 32-bit integer-register world. For example, 0xff can be 255 under an 8-bit unsigned interpretation and -1 under an 8-bit two's-complement interpretation. The bits did not change; the interpretation did.

Hex is a viewing tool

Hex compresses long bit strings and aligns with four-bit groups. Students only need enough binary/hex fluency to read evidence, not a conversion marathon.

The persistent specimen

int transform(int x) {
    int y = x + 2;
    if (y > 5) {
        y = y * 3;
    }
    return y;
}

The laboratory's source-to-CPU case runs this specimen with input 4 and expects x10/a0 = 18, preserving the same result in x11/a1 = 18.

Instructions are encoded agreements

An instruction identifies an operation and operands in a format the processor agrees to decode. Inspect real RV32I disassembly and one or two bounded encodings; do not memorize the entire opcode map.

ABI only where it earns its keep

Introduce a0/x10 as the return-value register because the specimen makes it observable. Save deeper calling-convention detail for Week 9.

Floating point gets a taste, not the week

Many decimal fractions are approximations in binary floating point. The learning goal is that representation is a contract with tradeoffs, not manual IEEE-754 archaeology.

Scope

The course-owned interpreter proves architectural instruction/state behavior for a bounded RV32I subset. It is deliberately not cycle accurate and does not establish pipeline, cache, or modern superscalar behavior.

AI Fluency move

Lens 6 - Engineer the Prompt. Ask for an explanation, identify vague claims, rewrite the prompt around the exact specimen/value, then verify against disassembly and state.

Wednesday handoff

Monday ends when you can name the model you believe, the exact specimen/value being tested, and the evidence that could force revision.

pages.title: Professional Minds Wednesday - Week 6 Reading: The Base Rate Fallacy
pages.body:
Week 6 Reading: The Base Rate Fallacy

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 6 -- How do we know something is true?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7-9 minutes
  • Primary source: Statistics Done Wrong: The Woefully Complete Guide by Alex Reinhart (No Starch Press, 2015), Chapter 5, "The Base Rate Fallacy"

Why This Matters Professionally

Professionals are handed positive results constantly: a test came back positive, a security scan flagged a file, a candidate cleared a screen, an A/B test showed a lift. The natural reading of a positive result is that the thing it tests for is probably present. Reinhart's chapter shows that this reading is often badly wrong -- and that how wrong it is depends on something the result itself never tells you: how common the thing was to begin with.

Week 6 opens the "Evidence" unit by asking how we know something is true. The base rate fallacy is the right place to start because it separates two questions that feel identical and are not: "how surprising is this result if nothing is going on?" and "how likely is it that something is actually going on?"

Primary-Source Ideas: What Statistics Done Wrong Argues

Primary-source claim: Reinhart defines the base rate fallacy as confusing the probability of seeing extreme data when there is no real effect with the probability that an observed result is false. (Source location: Chapter 5, "The Base Rate Fallacy," opening definition.)

Responsible paraphrase: These are two different quantities. The first asks: if nothing were really happening, how often would data this striking show up anyway? The second asks: now that I am holding this striking result, what are the odds it is misleading me? A test can be very unlikely to fire on nothing and still produce mostly false alarms -- and the reason is what the next claims make concrete.

Primary-source claim: In Reinhart's example of testing 100 cancer drugs, 8 true positives and 5 false positives together mean that 38 percent of the drugs that appear successful are in fact ineffective. (Source location: Chapter 5, the 100-drug testing example.)

Responsible paraphrase: Count the two kinds of positive result separately and the problem becomes visible. Real effects produce some positives; nothing-at-all produces others. The share of your positive results that are wrong depends on the ratio between those two groups -- not on the error rate of any single test. Here, more than a third of the apparent successes are illusions.

Primary-source claim: Reinhart's mammogram example: among 1,000 women with a cancer rate of 0.8 percent, screening produces roughly 7 true detections and about 70 false positives, so only about 9 percent of positive results actually indicate cancer. (Source location: Chapter 5, the mammography screening example.)

Responsible paraphrase: This is the same arithmetic with the base rate turned down, and the result is far more dramatic. When the condition is genuinely rare, the small population that has it can only generate a small number of true positives, while the very large population that does not have it generates false positives in quantity. A positive result can be strong evidence in a high-prevalence setting and weak evidence in a low-prevalence one, with no change whatsoever to the test.

Primary-source claim: Reinhart applies the same reasoning to survey research on defensive gun use: when genuine cases are rare, even small rates of false memories or mistaken affirmative answers among non-users can overwhelm the true reports. (Source location: Chapter 5, the defensive-gun-use survey discussion.)

Responsible paraphrase: The pattern is not confined to medicine or drug trials. Any time you are counting a rare thing by asking a large population, the errors made by the majority who do not have the trait can swamp the honest answers of the minority who do. Rarity, plus a large denominator, is the dangerous combination.

Primary-source claim: Reinhart notes that testing many comparisons sharply increases false-positive risk, reaching about 64 percent for 20 jelly-bean colors and about 99 percent for 100. (Source location: Chapter 5, the multiple-comparisons/jelly-bean discussion.)

Responsible paraphrase: Running more tests manufactures more chances to be fooled. If you look for an effect in twenty places, finding it somewhere is close to expected even when nothing is there. This is the base rate problem arriving by a second route: the pool of opportunities-for-a-false-positive grows while the number of real effects does not.

Primary-source claim: Reinhart's recommendations are to take base rates into account, adjust for multiple testing, and emphasize confidence intervals and effect sizes rather than treating p < 0.05 as though it were a 5 percent chance of error. (Source location: Chapter 5, closing recommendations.)

Responsible paraphrase: The corrective is not to distrust statistics but to ask a further question the statistic does not answer on its own: how common is the thing being tested for, and how many chances did this result have to appear? Reporting the size of an effect and the range of plausible values, rather than a bare threshold verdict, keeps that question in view.

A Concrete Example

Instructor's own invented professional-life example, not an example from the book: A security team deploys a scanner that correctly flags 99 percent of genuinely malicious files and falsely flags only 1 percent of safe ones. That sounds close to airtight. But if the team scans 100,000 files of which 50 are actually malicious, the scanner catches roughly 50 real threats and also flags roughly 1,000 harmless files. Fewer than 5 percent of its alerts point at anything real. Nothing is wrong with the scanner; the analysts are simply working in a setting where the thing being hunted is rare. Concluding "the tool is broken" misdiagnoses it, and so does treating every alert as probably genuine.

Synthesis

Instructor synthesis: Reinhart's chapter answers this week's essential question with an uncomfortable precision. Knowing whether something is true is not a matter of whether a test fired. It requires knowing how often the thing is true in general, and how many opportunities the result had to appear by chance. The same positive result means different things in different worlds. Professionals who internalize this stop asking "did it come back positive?" and start asking "positive out of how many, looking for how rare a thing?" -- which is a question about the design of the search, not about the result at all.

Reflection Questions

  1. Student application: Describe a test, alert, screen, or filter you rely on in your own work or studies. Roughly how common is the thing it is looking for? Given that, would you expect most of its positive results to be real?

  2. Student application: Reinhart shows the same test yielding 38 percent false discoveries in one setting and about 91 percent in another. Explain in your own words what changed between the two settings, given that the test itself did not.

  3. Student application: Why might "p < 0.05" feel like it means "a 5 percent chance this is wrong," and what would you need to know in addition before you could say anything about how likely the finding is to be false?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Reinhart, Alex. Statistics Done Wrong: The Woefully Complete Guide. No Starch Press, 2015. Chapter 5, "The Base Rate Fallacy."
  • All primary-source claims and responsible paraphrases are drawn only from this repository's compiled chapter summary for Chapter 5 (books/summaries/book_summary_statistics_done_wrong.md); citations use chapter section landmarks rather than page numbers.
  • The malware-scanner example is invented by the instructor and is not from Reinhart's chapter. Its numbers are illustrative and chosen for arithmetic clarity, not drawn from any real deployment.
  • This reading is a bounded companion to one chapter, not a summary of the whole book. Reinhart's treatments of statistical power, researcher freedom, and data sharing are addressed elsewhere in the book and are not covered here.

pages.title: Professional Minds Friday - Week 6 Reading: Understanding Replication
pages.body:
Week 6 Reading: Understanding Replication

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 6 -- How do we know something is true?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7-9 minutes
  • Primary source: Understanding Statistics and Experimental Design: How to Not Lie with Statistics by Michael H. Herzog, Gregory Francis, and Aaron Clarke (Springer, 2019), Chapter 10, "Understanding Replication"

Why This Matters Professionally

Wednesday's reading showed that a single positive result can be mostly noise when the thing being tested for is rare. The obvious professional response is to stop trusting single results and start trusting repeated ones. If a finding replicates, surely it is real.

This reading complicates that move in a way worth taking seriously. Herzog, Francis, and Clarke argue that replication is neither always sufficient nor always necessary for belief -- and that a body of findings which succeeds too consistently is more suspicious, not less. Applying Wednesday's reasoning to a whole literature turns out to require a different tool than applying it to one study.

Primary-Source Ideas: What Understanding Statistics and Experimental Design Argues

Primary-source claim: The authors argue that replication rates are meaningful only when interpreted alongside statistical power, since studies of small effects or with small samples may not produce significant results consistently even when the effect is real. (Source location: Chapter 10, "Understanding Replication," on interpreting replication rates.)

Responsible paraphrase: A failed replication is not automatically a refutation. If a study was never likely to detect the effect in the first place -- because the effect is small, or the sample was -- then a non-significant result is close to what you should expect whether or not the effect exists. Reading a replication record without knowing the power behind it tells you very little.

Primary-source claim: The authors state that replication is neither always sufficient nor always necessary for belief, and that implausibly frequent success can be more suspicious than limited replication. (Source location: Chapter 10, on the evidential status of replication.)

Responsible paraphrase: This inverts the intuitive scoreboard. A run of studies that all came out significant is not automatically the strongest possible evidence. Given realistic power, some attempts should have failed. A perfect record suggests that something other than the phenomenon is shaping which results exist -- which is the subject of the next claims.

Primary-source claim: The authors describe the Test for Excess Success (TES), which compares the number of significant outcomes that would be expected -- based on estimated effect sizes and study power -- against the number of successful outcomes researchers actually report. (Source location: Chapter 10, on the Test for Excess Success.)

Responsible paraphrase: TES makes the previous point checkable rather than merely rhetorical. From the reported effect sizes and sample sizes you can compute how many of a set of studies should have reached significance. If the published record contains substantially more successes than that computation allows, the set of findings is internally inconsistent, regardless of how convincing any individual study looks.

Primary-source claim: The authors note that publication bias can inflate both observed effect sizes and estimated power by suppressing null findings. (Source location: Chapter 10, on publication bias.)

Responsible paraphrase: This is Wednesday's base-rate problem operating at the level of a literature rather than a single test. If null results are less likely to be published, the studies that reach print are a filtered sample, not a representative one. The effect looks larger and better-supported than it is, because the failures were removed from view before you ever counted.

Primary-source claim: The authors explain that optional stopping increases false-positive risk, because repeatedly testing the data until a result reaches significance creates multiple opportunities for a significant result to appear. (Source location: Chapter 10, on optional stopping.)

Responsible paraphrase: Checking the data as it accumulates and stopping once it looks good is not a neutral act of diligence. Each check is another chance for noise to cross the threshold. The published study reports one test, but the process that produced it ran many -- and only the last one is visible in the write-up.

Primary-source claim: The authors caution that TES should be applied to studies addressing a shared theoretical claim, since unrelated significant experiments do not necessarily test one unified theory. (Source location: Chapter 10, on the proper scope of TES.)

Responsible paraphrase: The tool has a domain of validity. Grouping studies that merely appear together -- in one paper, or one research program -- and demanding statistical coherence from them is a misuse if they were never claims about the same underlying effect. Deciding what counts as "the same claim" is a judgment about the theory, made before the arithmetic starts.

A Concrete Example

Instructor's own invented professional-life example, not an example from the book: A team evaluating a new onboarding process runs six small pilot studies across six departments and reports that all six showed a statistically significant improvement. Reading this as overwhelming support inverts the correct reaction. Given how small each pilot was, the honest expectation might have been two or three significant results even if the process genuinely helps. Six-for-six suggests that the departments where it did not work were quietly dropped, or that each pilot ran until the numbers looked good and then stopped. The uniformity is the warning sign, not the endorsement.

Synthesis

Instructor synthesis: Wednesday asked what a single positive result is worth and answered: that depends on how rare the thing is. Friday asks what a pile of positive results is worth and gives a structurally similar answer: that depends on how many negative results you never saw, and how many chances each positive one had to appear. Both readings refuse the shortcut of treating a result as self-interpreting. Knowing whether something is true means reconstructing the process that produced the evidence -- what was searched, what was published, when the searching stopped -- and that process is usually invisible in the finding itself.

Reflection Questions

  1. Student application: Describe a claim you have seen supported by "study after study." What would you need to know about the studies that were not published before you could judge how strong that support actually is?

  2. Student application: The authors say that implausibly frequent success can be more suspicious than limited replication. Explain in your own words why a perfect record of significant results might be evidence against trusting a set of findings.

  3. Student application: Optional stopping means checking results as data comes in and stopping when they look good. Where in your own work or studies have you been tempted to stop collecting or testing once you got the answer you wanted? What would a pre-committed stopping rule have changed?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Herzog, Michael H., Gregory Francis, and Aaron Clarke. Understanding Statistics and Experimental Design: How to Not Lie with Statistics. Springer, 2019. Chapter 10, "Understanding Replication."
  • All primary-source claims and responsible paraphrases are drawn only from this repository's compiled chapter summary for Chapter 10 (books/summaries/book_summary_understanding_statistics_and_experimental_design.md); citations use chapter section landmarks rather than page numbers.
  • The onboarding-pilot example is invented by the instructor and is not from the authors' chapter. Its numbers are illustrative and are not drawn from any real study.
  • This reading is a bounded companion to one chapter, not a summary of the whole book. The book's treatments of the multiple testing problem, ANOVA, meta-analysis, and experimental design are not covered here.
  • This reading supersedes the replication material in the earlier week-level readings/week_06_knowing_what_is_true.md, which treated replication briefly and did not cover the Test for Excess Success, publication bias, or optional stopping.

pages.title: Week 07 - Week at a Glance
pages.body:
Week 7 - Crack Open the CPU

Central machine question: What has to exist inside the CPU for one instruction to execute correctly?

Week at a Glance

Prior belief: if I know what an instruction means, the inside of the CPU is mostly implementation trivia.

Prediction: for one familiar Week 6 instruction, predict what state must be read, what operation happens, what selections/control choices are needed, and what state changes.

AI Fluency: Lens 7 - Research & Retrieve.
Professional Minds: Wednesday - Understanding by Design; Friday - Rethinking Grading.

Monday builds only the structures the familiar instruction needs. Wednesday traces the instruction through the bounded SWOSU datapath. Friday corrects a deliberate trace error using the model and ISA evidence.

Continuity

Reuse the Week 6 transform() specimen and its disassembly. No new toy program.

Bounded SWOSU datapath

The teaching path is:

PC -> fetch/decode -> register file / immediate -> ALU -> optional data memory -> write-back / next PC

Muxes and control choose which path is active. This is a teaching model, not a transistor-level or modern superscalar diagram.

Machine Dossier handoff

Action: REVISE. Add one CPU/datapath trace or annotation only if it improves the persistent machine model. Do not create a circuit workbook.

Required path

No new simulator is required. Use the Week 6 disassembly plus the course-owned trace table in wednesday.md.

Equity / scope

Zero-cost and CPU-only. Rich real microarchitecture diagrams may appear in the instructor showcase only after the bounded model is understood.

pages.title: Week 07 Monday - Think / Frame
pages.body:
Week 7 Monday - Crack Open the CPU

Question

What has to exist inside the CPU for one instruction to execute correctly?

Start from the ISA promise

Week 6 established what an instruction promises to do to architectural state. Week 7 works backward: what structures must exist to keep that promise?

Build the datapath because the instruction needs it

For a familiar arithmetic/immediate instruction:

  1. the PC identifies the current instruction;
  2. instruction bits are fetched and decoded;
  3. the register file supplies named source state;
  4. an immediate generator supplies encoded constants when needed;
  5. the ALU performs arithmetic/comparison/address work;
  6. muxes select among possible sources/results;
  7. control chooses behavior for this instruction class;
  8. write-back changes architectural state;
  9. the next PC is selected.

State versus plumbing

Registers, memory, and PC behavior are visible in the ISA contract. Muxes, control lines, ports, and the exact teaching datapath are implementation mechanisms.

Load/store and branch taste

Trace one bounded example from another instruction class to show how the path changes. Do not build a complete HDL processor.

Why this is not a modern CPU diagram

A real out-of-order processor can rename registers, issue multiple operations, speculate, and contain many layers absent from our model while still implementing the same ISA-visible behavior.

AI Fluency

Retrieve an authoritative ISA explanation and compare it with an AI-generated datapath explanation. A disagreement may be a scope/model mismatch rather than a simple factual error.

Prediction

Choose one Week 6 instruction and predict its input state, major path, operation, control choices, and changed state before Wednesday.

pages.title: Professional Minds Wednesday - Week 7 Reading: Design Backward from What Learners Should Be Able to Do
pages.body:
Week 7 Reading: Design Backward from What Learners Should Be Able to Do

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 7 — How do we design meaningful learning?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7–9 minutes
  • Primary source: Understanding by Design, expanded 2nd edition, by Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe (ASCD, 2005), Chapter 1, "Backward Design"

Why This Matters Professionally

Learning is often planned in the order that materials occur to us: find a reading, make slides, add an activity, then write a quiz. The result can be busy, polished, and even enjoyable without giving learners a clear destination or a fair way to show that they arrived.

Wiggins and McTighe call this the "twin sins" of design: activities that are hands-on but not minds-on, and coverage that races through content without an intellectual purpose. Neither habit is malicious — both feel like reasonable ways to fill a session. Week 7 asks a harder question first: before choosing what to cover or do, what should the learner be able to do afterward, and how would we know?

Primary-Source Ideas: What Understanding by Design Argues

Primary-source claim: Wiggins and McTighe describe teachers as designers whose product is student learning, and argue that, as with any design, effective results depend on clear purposes rather than on the availability of interesting materials. (Source location: Chapter 1, "Backward Design," opening argument.)

Responsible paraphrase: A designer's job is not just to produce something engaging — a slideshow, a lab, a case study — it is to produce a specific outcome for a specific audience, given real constraints of time, background knowledge, and existing standards. Interesting materials can support that outcome, but they are not the outcome. If the purpose is not stated first, the materials tend to define the class by default.

Primary-source claim: The chapter proposes "backward design" in three stages: identify desired results, determine acceptable evidence, then plan learning experiences and instruction — reversing the common habit of starting from a textbook, a favorite activity, or a topic and hoping learning results. (Source location: Chapter 1, "Backward Design," the three-stage template.)

Responsible paraphrase: Most planning starts in stage three — "what will we do on Monday?" — and works backward into evidence and goals only if there is time left over, which there usually is not. Backward design inverts the order deliberately. A designer first states what students should understand and be able to do, then decides what evidence would actually reveal that result, and only then chooses the readings, explanations, and activities most likely to produce it.

Primary-source claim: Wiggins and McTighe name two recurring design failures: activity-oriented teaching, which is hands-on but not minds-on, and coverage-oriented teaching, which moves through facts without an organizing intellectual purpose — while noting that coverage itself is not inherently wrong when students understand the overarching ideas a survey serves. (Source location: Chapter 1, "Backward Design," the "twin sins" discussion.)

Responsible paraphrase: Both failures can look like a full, well-run class from the outside. The test is not whether students were busy or whether ground was covered — it is whether the content and activities were organized around a meaningful understanding, a transfer goal, and evidence that reveals whether either was reached. A brisk survey lecture can be purposeful if it exists to serve a bigger idea the course keeps returning to; the same lecture is coverage-oriented if it exists only because the syllabus allotted it a week.

Primary-source claim: The three-stage template organizes Stage 1 around priority goals, enduring understandings, essential questions, and needed knowledge/skills; Stage 2 around evidence — especially authentic performances judged against criteria — that would demonstrate those results; and Stage 3 around learning experiences and instruction, sequenced using the WHERETO principles (clarify direction, hook interest, equip and engage, provide chances to rethink and revise, support self-evaluation, tailor instruction, and organize the sequence effectively). (Source location: Chapter 1, "Backward Design," the UbD template description.)

Responsible paraphrase: Each stage answers a different question and none can substitute for another. Stage 1 asks what matters most. Stage 2 asks what would count as proof. Stage 3 asks what experiences would get a learner there. Skipping straight to Stage 3 — as most planning does under time pressure — means the "proof" gets improvised after the fact from whatever the activities happened to produce, rather than designed on purpose.

Primary-source claim: The authors illustrate the template with a nutrition unit in which students analyze diets, interpret food labels, design menus, receive feedback, and build a personal action plan; conventional quizzes support these tasks without replacing them as the unit's central evidence. (Source location: Chapter 1, "Backward Design," the nutrition-unit example.)

Responsible paraphrase: The quizzes still exist in this design — they check whether students know the vocabulary and facts a menu-design task requires. What changes is their role: they are enabling knowledge checks feeding toward a larger authentic performance, not the performance itself. A grade built entirely from quizzes could look identical on a gradebook to a grade partly built from menu design, while representing a very different kind of learning.

A Concrete Example: Blueprint Before Lesson Plan

You are asked to build a 30-minute onboarding session about handling confidential client information.

An activity-first plan might include a policy slideshow, a short video, a discussion, and five multiple-choice questions. These may all be reasonable pieces, but the list does not yet say what a learner should be able to do afterward — it only lists what will happen during the 30 minutes.

A backward-design blueprint starts differently, in the template's own order:

  • Stage 1 — Desired result: Given an unfamiliar disclosure request, a new colleague can identify the competing obligations, decide what to disclose or withhold, and recognize when to escalate.
  • Stage 2 — Acceptable evidence: The colleague responds to a realistic case, explains the decision, and self-assesses the response against known criteria — not just a multiple-choice score on policy recall.
  • Stage 3 — Learning experiences: Compare a disclosure case against a similar-looking non-case, model expert reasoning aloud, practice on increasingly ambiguous requests, and give feedback before the evidence task.

The slideshow, video, and quiz can still appear here — but now as Stage 3 tools chosen to build toward a stated Stage 2 performance, rather than as the plan's entire content.

Synthesis

Backward design does not forbid activities, coverage, or quizzes. It asks that all three follow from an explicit answer to two prior questions: what should the learner be able to do, and what evidence would convince us they can do it? Skipping straight to "what will we do" is the twin-sins trap the chapter names directly — and it is easy to fall into precisely because activity-first and coverage-first plans can look just as busy and complete as a backward-designed one.

Friday's session takes this framework into the classroom and asks what it looks like in daily practice once the destination and evidence are set — specifically, how a classroom actually structures instruction and grading around demonstrated mastery of clear targets.

Reflection Questions

  1. Pick a class, training, or onboarding session you have experienced. Was its plan closer to activity-first, coverage-first, or backward-designed? What is the evidence for your answer?
  2. In the confidential-information example, why does a self-assessed response to a realistic case count as stronger evidence than a multiple-choice score, according to the chapter's own criteria (not just intuition)?
  3. Name one of the two "twin sins." What makes it hard to notice from inside a class that has fallen into it?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe, Understanding by Design, expanded 2nd edition (ASCD, 2005), Chapter 1, "Backward Design," as processed into books/summaries/book_summary_understanding_by_design.md and its underlying chapter summary at books/pipeline_runs/understanding_by_design/summaries/01_chapter_1_summary.md. Source locations cite the chapter and named subsection rather than PDF page numbers, since the compiled book-pipeline summary does not carry page citations.
  • This reading draws on Chapter 1 only, as a bounded entry point into backward design, not a summary of the book's later chapters on essential questions, evidence design, or rubrics (Chapters 3, 5, 7, and 8 develop those in more depth).
  • The confidential-information onboarding scenario is instructor-invented for illustration and is not one of Wiggins and McTighe's own examples; the nutrition-unit example above it is drawn directly from the chapter.

pages.title: Professional Minds Friday - Week 7 Reading: What a Mastery-Based Classroom Actually Does
pages.body:
Week 7 Reading: What a Mastery-Based Classroom Actually Does

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 7 — How do we design meaningful learning?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7–9 minutes
  • Primary source: Rethinking Grading: Meaningful Assessment for Standards-Based Learning by Cathy Vatterott (ASCD, 2015), Chapter 3, "What Grading Looks Like in the Standards-Based Classroom"

Why This Matters Professionally

Wednesday's reading argued that design should start from a desired result and its evidence, not from a list of activities. That is a framework. Friday's reading takes the framework into an actual classroom and asks what changes on the ground when a teacher commits to it: how targets get written, how tasks get assigned, how students take ownership of their own progress, and — the hardest part for most institutions — what happens to the grade while a learner is still practicing.

This is not only a K–12 question. Any professional training program, certification track, or workplace onboarding that grades along the way faces the same design choice Vatterott describes: does the recorded score represent completed practice, or demonstrated mastery?

Primary-Source Ideas: What Rethinking Grading Argues

Primary-source claim: Vatterott describes standards-based grading as reorganizing the entire classroom process: standards drive the curriculum, learning targets — stated as student-friendly "I can" or "We can" statements — drive instruction and assessment, and students take on more control over their own learning. (Source location: Chapter 3, "What Grading Looks Like in the Standards-Based Classroom," opening framework.)

Responsible paraphrase: The starting point is the same instinct as backward design: begin with what a student should be able to do, unpacked into plain language the student can actually use to judge their own work, rather than leaving the target implicit in an assignment's instructions.

Primary-source claim: Rather than teaching and assessing every target in isolation through mechanical exercises, teachers group related targets into a single meaningful task — Vatterott's example is designing a golf course to address measurement, area, and slope together — producing rubric-assessable evidence while preserving the connections between standards. (Source location: Chapter 3, the target-grouping discussion and golf-course example.)

Responsible paraphrase: This is the classroom-level version of an "authentic performance": several separate learning targets are folded into one task that requires using them together, the way they would actually be used outside a worksheet. A grade on the finished task reflects whether the student can coordinate the targets, not just recall each one individually.

Primary-source claim: Vatterott ties student ownership to how higher-level thinking is built: teachers share targets, rubrics, and examples of both mastery and nonmastery work, then explicitly teach students to evaluate evidence and assess their own work against those examples — illustrated by a language-arts class where students rated writing samples against a rubric and had to defend their judgments. (Source location: Chapter 3, the student-ownership and self-assessment section.)

Responsible paraphrase: Self-assessment is not simply "students grade themselves" — it is taught as a skill, using the same criteria the teacher uses, with worked examples of both strong and weak work as the training material. Defending a judgment against a rubric, not just assigning a number, is what makes the practice formative rather than a shortcut.

Primary-source claim: During learning, mistakes are treated as necessary and expected, so formative work is followed by repeated, nonpunitive feedback from teachers, peers, or the students themselves; formative tasks may be monitored or even recorded as temporary "no-count" scores, but they do not affect the final grade and can be replaced once mastery is demonstrated. (Source location: Chapter 3, the feedback-and-revision section.)

Responsible paraphrase: This is the chapter's sharpest departure from a conventional gradebook. A score earned while a student is still practicing is deliberately kept separate from the grade that will eventually represent the target. That separation is what lets mistakes function as information rather than as a permanent penalty — the same distinction Wednesday's reading drew between enabling knowledge checks and Stage 2 evidence.

Primary-source claim: Learning experiences in this classroom are described as student-focused — offering choice, relevance, personalization, and collaboration — with examples including using menus and coupons to calculate fractions, reviewing books, designing a future middle school, and creating a moon-phase calendar, each generating a product that serves as assessable evidence; direct instruction still occurs, mainly as brief minilessons ahead of a chance to demonstrate understanding. (Source location: Chapter 3, the student-focused-experiences section.)

Responsible paraphrase: None of these tasks eliminate direct teaching. What changes is sequencing and proportion: a short, targeted explanation precedes an opportunity to use it, rather than a long explanation standing in for the opportunity. The task, not the lecture, is what eventually gets scored.

A Concrete Example: The Same Onboarding Session, Graded Two Ways

Return to Wednesday's confidential-information onboarding session, now through Vatterott's classroom lens.

  • Conventional grading: The new colleague completes the slideshow, watches the video, and answers five multiple-choice questions on the first attempt. The score on that first attempt becomes the permanent record, whether or not the colleague later demonstrates real judgment on an actual disclosure request.
  • Standards-based grading, per Chapter 3: The multiple-choice questions become an ungraded formative check — the colleague gets the answers wrong, receives feedback, and tries an ambiguous case again. The recorded score is attached to the later, realistic case response and the colleague's own defense of it against known criteria, not to the first attempt at recalling policy terms.

Nothing about the training content changed. What changed is which piece of evidence the institution treats as the grade — and whether an early mistake made while still learning is allowed to count against a final judgment of mastery.

Synthesis

Backward design (Wednesday) says: decide the destination and the evidence before the activities. Standards-based grading (Friday) shows one concrete way an institution can honor that decision once students are actually in the room — targets stated in usable language, tasks that group targets meaningfully, students trained to judge their own work against real criteria, and a grade that waits for demonstrated mastery instead of averaging every attempt made along the way, including the earliest and roughest ones.

The two readings share a discipline: neither treats "we did the activity" as equivalent to "the learner can now do the thing." Wednesday names the destination and the evidence in the abstract; Friday shows a classroom where the grade itself is redesigned to only reflect that evidence.

Reflection Questions

  1. Vatterott's golf-course example groups several targets into one task. Choose a skill you are learning or teaching, and describe one task that would group two or three of its component skills the way the golf-course task groups measurement, area, and slope.
  2. Explain the difference between a "no-count" formative score and the final recorded grade in Vatterott's classroom. Why does that separation matter for how students treat mistakes made while practicing?
  3. Apply Chapter 3's framework to the two-version onboarding example above. Which version's recorded score would you trust more as evidence that the colleague can actually handle a real disclosure request, and why?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Cathy Vatterott, Rethinking Grading: Meaningful Assessment for Standards-Based Learning (ASCD, 2015), Chapter 3, "What Grading Looks Like in the Standards-Based Classroom," as processed into books/summaries/book_summary_rethinking_grading.md and its underlying chapter summary at books/pipeline_runs/rethinking_grading/summaries/03_chapter_3_what_grading_looks_like_summary.md. Source is the user's personal-copy OCR of the complete book (books/Rethinking Grading (personal-copy OCR).md, gitignored, not committed); source locations cite the chapter and named subsection rather than page numbers, since the OCR pipeline's compiled summary does not carry page citations.
  • This reading and its paired deck supersede readings/week_07_designing_meaningful_learning.md and presentations/week_07_designing_meaningful_learning.md, both marked superseded in place. Those files were built under an earlier, pre-book-pipeline prompt from a 37-page ASCD "Advance Uncorrected Copy" sample of Rethinking Grading — a bounded, publisher-provided excerpt, not the complete book. This reading instead draws on the complete book via the user's personal-copy OCR, per books/session_book_ledger.md's Week 7 Friday row.
  • The two-version onboarding scenario above is instructor-invented for illustration and is not one of Vatterott's own examples; the golf-course, writing-sample, menus-and-coupons, and moon-phase-calendar examples are drawn directly from the chapter.
  • This reading draws on Chapter 3 only (the appetizer-chapter method — see book_pipeline/PLAN.md's Phase 3 methodology update), not a summary of the book's other chapters on grading culture, the case for change, grading mechanics, or reform strategy (Chapters 1, 2, 4, and 5).
