pages.title: Week 08 Monday - Think / Frame
pages.body:
Week 8 Monday - Make It Fast Without Breaking It

Question

Why does overlap improve throughput, and why does it create new problems?

Correct is not fast

Week 7 explained how one instruction can execute correctly. Performance begins when many instructions/work items compete for time and resources.

Latency versus throughput

Latency asks how long one dependency path takes. Throughput asks how many independent units of work can complete per unit time. A design can improve one without proportionally improving the other.

CPU-time model

Use the bounded model:

CPU time ≈ instruction count × CPI × cycle time

Every term is conditional. The formula organizes reasoning; it is not a universal benchmark score.

Teaching pipeline

Use a five-stage teaching path, IF/ID/EX/MEM/WB, only to make overlap visible. Do not claim every real CPU literally has five stages.

Hazards

  • data dependency can force waiting;
  • forwarding can satisfy some dependencies sooner;
  • stalls preserve correctness when data/resources are not ready;
  • branches create uncertainty about which future instructions are useful;
  • structural conflicts occur when work competes for the same resource.

Native sensory experiment

The course compares a serial dependency chain with four more-independent chains while holding total update count fixed. The experiment is consistent with available instruction-level overlap, but does not expose exact physical pipeline depth.

AI Fluency

Have AI predict the result and state a mechanism before measurement. After the run, distinguish lucky prediction from an explanation that survives evidence.

Prediction

Commit to dependent versus independent behavior before seeing the canonical plot.

pages.title: Professional Minds Wednesday - Week 8 Reading: A Pragmatic Philosophy
pages.body:
Week 8 Reading: A Pragmatic Philosophy

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 8 — What does professional software craftsmanship look like?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7–9 minutes
  • Primary source: Andrew Hunt and David Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer: From Journeyman to Master, Chapter 1, "A Pragmatic Philosophy"

Why This Matters Professionally

Craftsmanship is easy to picture as a set of style rules: short functions, consistent formatting, a favorite naming convention. Hunt and Thomas open their book somewhere else — not with a rule about code, but with an attitude toward the work itself. Chapter 1 argues that what separates a "Pragmatic Programmer" from anyone who can write working code is how they handle responsibility, decay, change, scope, and learning. None of that is visible in a diff. All of it determines whether the diff can be trusted.

This matters beyond software. Any professional who ships work others depend on — a report, a lesson plan, a policy memo — faces the same pressures this chapter names: owning mistakes, resisting neglect, managing gradual change, and deciding how good is good enough. Week 8 asks what professional craftsmanship looks like; Chapter 1 answers first with a philosophy, before either book reaches a single line of code.

Primary-Source Ideas: What The Pragmatic Programmer Argues

Primary-source claim: Hunt and Thomas describe responsibility as something a person actively agrees to, not something assigned by title, and argue that pragmatic programmers do not blame vendors, tools, management, or coworkers when something goes wrong — they provide solutions instead of excuses. (Source location: Chapter 1, "The Cat Ate My Source Code," "Take Responsibility.")

Responsible paraphrase: Accepting responsibility does not mean accepting blame for everything, including causes genuinely outside your control. It means that when you do accept an outcome, you are expected to be accountable for it — and the professional move when something breaks is to say what happened and what can be done next, not to search for someone else to point at. "The cat ate my source code" is the chapter's own example of an excuse that ends a conversation instead of moving it forward.

Primary-source claim: The chapter uses the "broken window" theory of urban decay to argue that visible neglect — a bad design, a wrong decision, poor code left unrepaired — signals that no one is watching, which invites further decay; the same logic runs in reverse, since a system that is pristine tends to stay that way because people are reluctant to be the first to mess it up. (Source location: Chapter 1, "Software Entropy," including the "Putting Out Fires" contrast.)

Responsible paraphrase: Entropy is not primarily a technical force in this argument — it is social. A single unrepaired problem does not by itself sink a project; what sinks it is the message that unrepaired problem sends to everyone who sees it. Fixing or visibly containing a "broken window" as soon as it is found is presented as cheaper than letting the signal spread.

Primary-source claim: Using the "stone soup" story, the chapter argues that people are more willing to join an already-visible success than to approve an entire ambitious project up front, so a small working contribution can act as a catalyst for larger change; the companion "boiled frog" caution warns that gradual, barely noticed change can let a project drift out of control precisely because no single step looks alarming. (Source location: Chapter 1, "Stone Soup and Boiled Frogs," including "The Villagers' Side.")

Responsible paraphrase: These two stories describe the same mechanism — people responding to what is gradual rather than to what is announced in advance — used for opposite purposes. Showing an early, working piece builds momentum; the same insensitivity to small changes is also how a project drifts feature by feature until nothing of the original design remains. The chapter's own distinction: broken windows spread because people stop caring; the boiled frog problem happens because no one notices the change at all.

Primary-source claim: The chapter insists "good enough" does not mean sloppy — the scope and quality of a system should be an explicit requirement, decided with users rather than for them, because a solid version delivered earlier can generate feedback that a theoretically perfect version delivered too late cannot. (Source location: Chapter 1, "Good-Enough Software," "Involve Your Users in the Trade-Off" and "Know When to Stop.")

Responsible paraphrase: This is a caution in two directions. Programmers should not promise impossible schedules or cut basic engineering safeguards to hit a deadline — but they also should not over-polish a program past the point of usefulness, since over-refinement can damage a sound piece of work. Quality is a trade-off to be named and agreed to, not a default to be maximized or a corner to be silently cut.

Primary-source claim: The chapter treats a programmer's knowledge as an "expiring asset" that loses value unless actively maintained, and recommends managing a "Knowledge Portfolio" the way an investor manages a financial one: invest regularly, diversify, balance risk, and periodically review and rebalance. (Source location: Chapter 1, "Your Knowledge Portfolio," "Building Your Portfolio," "Goals," and "Critical Thinking.")

Responsible paraphrase: The chapter frames continuing education as a professional obligation with the same shape as financial planning, not an optional hobby for the unusually curious. It closes with a companion obligation: communication. Ideas, however good, only do work if a specific audience — with its own priorities and preferred style — actually receives them, which the chapter develops through knowing what you want to say, knowing your audience, and choosing your moment. (Source location: Chapter 1, "Communicate!")

A Concrete Example: The Missed Deadline

A developer promised a feature by Friday. On Thursday, a third-party API the feature depends on changes two response fields without warning, and three integration tests start failing.

An excuse-first response: "The vendor changed their API — it's not our fault the deadline slipped." True, perhaps, but it gives the team nothing to decide.

A responsibility-first response: "The provider changed two response fields yesterday. Our adapter now fails three contract tests. We can ship Friday using the previous integration and schedule the new one for Monday after testing it against their sandbox, or hold the whole release until Monday. I recommend the first option." This still names a real cause outside the developer's control — but it pairs that fact with impact and options, which is the distinction Hunt and Thomas draw between an excuse and an accepted responsibility.

Synthesis

None of Chapter 1's ideas is a coding technique. Responsibility, entropy, gradual change, and good-enough scope are all claims about professional posture — how a person handles what they cannot fully control and what they tolerate going unrepaired. Friday's session moves from this philosophy to a single, concrete craftsmanship practice: how meaningful names make the smallest unit of code legible to the next person who has to trust it.

Reflection Questions

  1. Describe a time you (or someone you observed) offered an excuse rather than a responsible escalation. Using the chapter's own distinction, what would the escalation version have needed to include?
  2. Explain, in the chapter's terms, why the broken-window problem and the boiled-frog problem are different failures even though both describe a project declining over time.
  3. Pick one habit from "Your Knowledge Portfolio" you do not currently practice. What is one small, specific way you could start this month?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Andrew Hunt and David Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer: From Journeyman to Master (Addison-Wesley, 1999), Chapter 1, "A Pragmatic Philosophy," as processed into books/summaries/book_summary_the_pragmatic_programmer.md and its underlying chapter summary at books/pipeline_runs/the_pragmatic_programmer/summaries/01_chapter_1_summary.md. Source locations cite the chapter and named subsection rather than page numbers, since the compiled book-pipeline summary does not carry page citations.
  • This reading draws on Chapter 1 only, as the book's own framing of what a pragmatic professional is, not a summary of the book's later chapters on design, testing, or project practice.
  • The missed-deadline API scenario is instructor-invented for illustration and is not one of Hunt and Thomas's own examples; the broken-window, stone-soup, boiled-frog, and knowledge-portfolio material above it is drawn directly from the chapter.
  • This reading and its paired Friday reading supersede readings/week_08_software_craftsmanship.md, marked superseded in place. That file blended material from across both books at the week level, citing PDF page numbers from the user's local PDFs rather than the book-pipeline's per-chapter summaries. This reading instead draws on a single bounded chapter (Chapter 1) via the pipeline's chapter summary, per book_pipeline/CHAPTER_SLATE.md's Week 8 Wednesday row.

pages.title: Professional Minds Friday - Week 8 Reading: What a Name Owes Its Reader
pages.body:
Week 8 Reading: What a Name Owes Its Reader

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 8 — What does professional software craftsmanship look like?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7–9 minutes
  • Primary source: Robert C. Martin and contributors, Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship, Chapter 2, "Meaningful Names"

Why This Matters Professionally

Wednesday's reading argued that professional craftsmanship is mostly a posture: taking responsibility, resisting neglect, managing change deliberately, and investing in a knowledge portfolio. None of that is visible in a single line of code. Friday's reading is the opposite kind of claim — the smallest, most concrete unit of craftsmanship there is: the name given to a variable, function, or class.

Names are the first and most frequent thing a reader of code encounters. A codebase is saturated with them, and unlike a comment or a design document, a name cannot be skipped — it is read every time the code it labels is read. Chapter 2 argues that this makes naming a genuine skill, not a cosmetic afterthought, and one with a direct line to Wednesday's theme: a badly named piece of code is a small broken window that makes the next change harder and riskier than it needs to be.

Primary-Source Ideas: What Clean Code Argues

Primary-source claim: Martin argues a good name should reveal why a thing exists, what it does, and how it is used — and that if a name needs a comment to explain it, the name has already failed. His Minesweeper example replaces vague names such as d, theList, x, and 4 with gameBoard, cell, FLAGGED, and getFlaggedCells, making the code explicit without making its underlying logic any more complicated. (Source location: Chapter 2, "Meaningful Names," Introduction and "Use Intention-Revealing Names.")

Responsible paraphrase: The Minesweeper rewrite is a useful test case precisely because nothing about the algorithm changes — only the names do. That isolates naming as a variable on its own: the same logic can be nearly opaque or immediately legible depending entirely on what its parts are called. A comment explaining an unclear name is treated as a patch over a naming failure, not a substitute for fixing it.

Primary-source claim: The chapter warns against disinformation in names — names that imply an incorrect type or concept, or that differ from a related name only subtly, or that use visually confusing characters like lowercase l and uppercase O — and separately against noise words and names distinguished only to satisfy a compiler (such as a1 and a2), which Martin calls "number-series naming." (Source location: Chapter 2, "Avoid Disinformation" and "Make Meaningful Distinctions.")

Responsible paraphrase: These are two related but distinct failures. Disinformation actively misleads — a name that looks like a list but is not, or two names close enough to be swapped by accident. Meaningless distinction does not mislead so much as fail to inform: ProductInfo and ProductData read as interchangeable to anyone who has not memorized which one means what, because the words themselves carry no distinguishing information.

Primary-source claim: Names should be pronounceable and searchable, since pronounceable names support discussion among programmers and searchable names make constants and widely used variables easier to locate in a codebase; single-letter names are reserved for short-lived local variables in small scopes. Type or scope encodings such as Hungarian notation and member-variable prefixes like m_ are described as obsolete burdens in modern, strongly typed languages and development environments. (Source location: Chapter 2, "Use Pronounceable Names," "Use Searchable Names," "Avoid Encodings," and "Hungarian Notation.")

Responsible paraphrase: Both rules point at the same underlying test: can another person work with this name without extra translation? A name you cannot say aloud in a discussion or cannot search for across a codebase creates friction every single time it is used. Type-encoding prefixes were originally a substitute for information a compiler or IDE now supplies automatically — carrying them forward adds visual noise without adding information a modern reader still needs.

Primary-source claim: Martin recommends noun or noun-phrase names for classes, verb or verb-phrase names for methods, and using one word consistently per concept rather than "punning" — reusing the same word for operations that are not actually equivalent (such as calling both a class method and an instance method add when one appends to a collection and the other sums two values). (Source location: Chapter 2, "Class Names," "Method Names," and "Pick One Word per Concept.")

Responsible paraphrase: Consistency here is not a style preference — it is a promise to the reader. If add always means "append to a collection" everywhere in a codebase, a reader can trust that meaning without re-checking every call site. A pun breaks that trust silently: the code still compiles and runs, but the word has quietly stopped meaning one thing.

Primary-source claim: The chapter argues that context can be added by well-named classes, functions, or namespaces — an Address class gives an ambiguous field like state a clear meaning without any prefix — but warns against gratuitous context, such as prefixing every class in an application with the application's own acronym, which makes names longer and less reusable without adding real information. (Source location: Chapter 2, "Add Meaningful Context" and "Final Words.")

Responsible paraphrase: Context should come from structure, not decoration. Putting a field inside a well-named class does real work — it changes what the reader assumes about the field for free. Prepending a prefix to every name in a codebase does not add that kind of structural information; it adds characters the reader has to read past every time, whether or not the name needed disambiguating in the first place.

A Concrete Example: Renaming a Function Under a Deadline

A function is named process(record). It parses a record's fields, validates them, calculates a value, and returns a status code. A teammate needs to add one more check to the calculation, but reading process gives no hint about which part of the function they are supposed to touch.

Applying Chapter 2's tests directly: process is a verb, correctly, but it names nothing specific — it could describe almost any function in almost any codebase, which fails the "reveal why it exists" test from the Introduction. A single rename to calculateShippingCharge(record) does not change the function's logic at all, but it immediately tells the next reader what the function is for and whether it is the right place to add a shipping-related check — without adding a single comment.

Synthesis

Chapter 2's claim is narrow by design: naming is one small craftsmanship practice, not the whole discipline. But it is a practice every single line of code passes through, which is exactly why Martin treats it as a professional skill rather than a matter of taste. A name that reveals intent, avoids disinformation, stays searchable, and is used consistently for one concept is a small, repeatable way of doing what Wednesday's reading described in the abstract — leaving change safer than you found it, one identifier at a time.

Reflection Questions

  1. Find a name in code you have written or read recently that would fail the "does it need a comment to explain it" test. What would a better name be, and why?
  2. Explain the difference between a disinformative name and a meaninglessly-distinguished name, using the chapter's own examples (or your own).
  3. Using the process/calculateShippingCharge example above, explain why renaming a function can reduce the risk of a future change even when it does not touch the function's logic at all.

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Robert C. Martin and contributors, Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship (Prentice Hall, 2009), Chapter 2, "Meaningful Names," as processed into books/summaries/book_summary_clean_code.md and its underlying chapter summary at books/pipeline_runs/clean_code/summaries/02_meaningful_names_summary.md. Source locations cite the chapter and named subsection rather than page numbers, since the compiled book-pipeline summary does not carry page citations.
  • This reading draws on Chapter 2 only, as a concrete, single-scale application of Wednesday's philosophy, not a summary of the book's later chapters on functions, comments, objects, or classes (Chapters 3, 4, 6, and 10 develop those in more depth).
  • The process(record)/calculateShippingCharge renaming scenario is instructor-invented for illustration and is not one of Martin's own examples; the Minesweeper, Address-class, and application-acronym-prefix examples above it are drawn directly from the chapter.
  • This reading and its paired Wednesday reading supersede readings/week_08_software_craftsmanship.md, marked superseded in place. That file blended material from across both books at the week level, citing PDF page numbers from the user's local PDFs rather than the book-pipeline's per-chapter summaries. This reading instead draws on a single bounded chapter (Chapter 2) via the pipeline's chapter summary, per book_pipeline/CHAPTER_SLATE.md's Week 8 Friday row.

pages.title: Week 09 Monday - Think / Frame
pages.body:
Week 9 Monday - Follow the Program Down

Question

Can I follow one small program through the stack without losing the evidence chain?

Integration is an evidence problem

A source statement, a disassembly line, a register-state receipt, a datapath trace, and a performance plot answer different questions. Integration means connecting them without claiming that one artifact proves all the others.

Persistent specimen

The same transform() function remains the object. Nothing new to decipher.

Layer map

  1. source meaning;
  2. fixed-width representation;
  3. compiler output / RV32I instruction;
  4. architectural register/memory state;
  5. bounded datapath/control meaning;
  6. dependency/performance implication;
  7. resulting program behavior.

For every arrow ask: what artifact lets another person verify this handoff?

Boundaries

  • You do not explain compiler optimization passes.
  • The Week 7 datapath is not suddenly cycle accurate.
  • The Week 8 native timing is not welded into a fake exact CPI for the RV32I interpreter.

AI Fluency

Have AI generate a candidate trace, diagram, or explanation. Mark unsupported handoffs and scope mismatches. Your job is to repair the chain with evidence.

Checkpoint strategy

Reuse evidence, repair gaps, and write one coherent narrative. Bigger is not better; connected is better.

pages.title: Professional Minds Wednesday - Week 9 Reading: Refactoring Is a Discipline, Not a Cleanup Pass
pages.body:
Week 9 Reading: Refactoring Is a Discipline, Not a Cleanup Pass

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 9 — How do systems stay healthy over time?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7–9 minutes
  • Primary source: Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code, 2nd edition, by Martin Fowler, Chapter 2, "Principles in Refactoring"

Why This Matters Professionally

Most working systems degrade gradually rather than all at once. Each individual change is reasonable in isolation — one more special case in a conditional, one more field bolted onto a record, one more copy-pasted block because the original function was already doing something close. No single change breaks anything. The accumulation does.

Fowler's Chapter 2 is not about a cleanup sprint scheduled for whenever things get bad enough. It argues that keeping a system healthy is an ongoing discipline folded into the same work that adds features and fixes bugs — not a separate project competing with them for calendar time. This matters in any domain where work product gets revisited: a codebase, a shared document template, an onboarding process, a set of lab protocols. The question Week 9 asks — how do systems stay healthy over time — starts here, at the level of a single change to a single artifact.

Primary-Source Ideas: What Refactoring Argues

Primary-source claim: Fowler defines refactoring as changing software's internal structure to make it easier to understand and cheaper to modify, without altering its observable behavior — and distinguishes it from performance optimization, which may deliberately make code harder to understand in exchange for speed. (Source location: Chapter 2, "Principles in Refactoring," the definition.)

Responsible paraphrase: The test for whether a change counts as refactoring is not whether the code "got better" in some general sense — it is whether the system still does exactly what it did before, from the outside, while being easier to work with on the inside. A change that alters behavior, even to fix a bug, is not a refactoring; it is a different kind of change that happens to touch the same code.

Primary-source claim: The chapter introduces Kent Beck's "two hats" metaphor: a developer wears the adding function hat while building new capability, measured by tests, and the refactoring hat while restructuring code without adding behavior — switching hats often as new work exposes awkward structure or finished work needs clarifying. (Source location: Chapter 2, "Principles in Refactoring," the two-hats discussion.)

Responsible paraphrase: These are two modes of work with two different success criteria, and conflating them is a common source of trouble. Under the "adding function" hat, success means new passing tests. Under the "refactoring" hat, success means all the old tests still pass — no new capability should appear. Naming the switch explicitly keeps a session from drifting into changing behavior while believing you are only cleaning up.

Primary-source claim: Fowler argues refactoring preserves design, removes duplication, improves readability, and exposes bugs, and that clearer code helps both future maintainers and the original developer understand code that has gone unfamiliar with time; he offers the "rule of three" — tolerate the first instance of duplication, wince at the second, refactor on the third — as a practical trigger for when to act. (Source location: Chapter 2, "Principles in Refactoring," the value-of-refactoring and rule-of-three discussion.)

Responsible paraphrase: Refactoring is not justified purely by aesthetics. Fowler ties it to concrete downstream effects: duplicated logic is a place where a future fix gets applied to one copy and forgotten in another, and hard-to-read code is code where a hidden bug is hard to see. The rule of three guards against refactoring too early (guessing at generalization before there is evidence it is needed) as much as against refactoring too late.

Primary-source claim: The chapter states that refactoring has limits: database schema changes and data migration require particular caution, published interfaces must retain compatibility (often by having old methods delegate to new ones rather than deleting them outright), and refactoring should generally be deferred near a deadline because its benefits will not arrive in time to matter for that deadline. (Source location: Chapter 2, "Principles in Refactoring," the limits-of-refactoring discussion.)

Responsible paraphrase: Refactoring is not a universal good applied without judgment. A published interface other teams already depend on cannot simply be renamed for clarity — someone else's code will break. Investing in structural cleanup two days before a hard deadline trades a real, immediate cost for a future benefit that deadline pressure will not allow anyone to collect.

Primary-source claim: On performance, Fowler recommends building well-factored code first, then profiling to find the actual hot spots, then optimizing incrementally — rather than speculating about performance problems in advance or letting constant micro-optimization slow down every other change. (Source location: Chapter 2, "Principles in Refactoring," the refactoring-and-performance discussion.)

Responsible paraphrase: Guessing where a system is slow is often wrong, and code restructured in advance to be "fast" is frequently harder to change later for no measured benefit. The recommended order is: make it clear, measure where it is actually slow, then fix the measured problem — not the imagined one.

A Concrete Example: The Same Change, Two Ways (Instructor-Invented)

A shared onboarding checklist template has grown a conditional block: "If the new hire is remote, skip step 4 and add steps 9 and 10; if they are in the Chicago office, also add step 11 for badge access." A third condition — a hybrid schedule — needs to be added this week.

Adding function, without refactoring: A developer nests another if inside the existing block, producing a four-way tangle of conditions referencing "remote," "Chicago," and now "hybrid" in inconsistent order across the branches. It works. It also took longer to write correctly than it should have, because the reviewer had to trace three interacting conditions to check the new one did not break the other two.

Refactoring first, then adding function: Before touching the logic, the same developer restructures the existing two-way conditional into a small table keyed by work arrangement, with no behavior change — remote and Chicago cases still produce exactly the same steps as before. Only after confirming the restructuring changed nothing does the developer add a "hybrid" row. The new case is one row, not a nested condition, and a reviewer can check it by reading one line instead of tracing three branches.

Both paths end with the hybrid case handled. The second is safer to review and cheaper to extend next time, because the restructuring step (refactoring) and the new-capability step (adding function) were kept separate and each was checked against its own success criterion.

Synthesis

Chapter 2's core claim is procedural, not stylistic: a system stays healthy not because someone occasionally schedules a big cleanup, but because every developer routinely separates "does this still do the same thing, more clearly" from "does this now do something new" — applying the first discipline in small, frequent doses, guided by evidence rather than guesswork or aesthetic preference.

Friday's session moves from a single change inside one file to the shape of an entire system: what happens to a codebase's health when many components, built by many people, accumulate dependencies on each other over time.

Reflection Questions

  1. Explain the "two hats" metaphor in your own words. Why does Fowler treat "adding function" and "refactoring" as needing different success criteria rather than being the same kind of work?
  2. In the onboarding-checklist example, what specifically made the second path's hybrid-case change cheaper to review than the first path's? Point to a specific claim from the chapter, not just intuition.
  3. Fowler says refactoring should generally be deferred near a deadline. Why does that follow from what refactoring is supposed to buy you, according to the chapter?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Martin Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code, 2nd edition, Chapter 2, "Principles in Refactoring," as processed into books/summaries/book_summary_refactoring.md and its underlying chapter summary at books/pipeline_runs/refactoring/summaries/03_chapter_2_principles_in_refactoring_summary.md. Source locations cite the chapter and named subsection rather than page numbers, since the compiled book-pipeline summary does not carry page citations.
  • This reading draws on Chapter 2 only, under the appetizer-chapter method — it is not a summary of the book's later chapters on specific refactoring catalogs, code smells, or testing infrastructure.
  • The onboarding-checklist example above is instructor-invented for illustration and is not one of Fowler's own examples; the "two hats" metaphor, the rule of three, and the performance-optimization guidance are drawn directly from the chapter.
  • This reading and its paired deck supersede readings/week_09_systems_stay_healthy.md and presentations/week_09_systems_stay_healthy.md, both marked superseded in place. Those week-level files blended both books into a single combined reading/deck rather than a day-specific concept/application pair; this reading instead draws on Chapter 2 of Refactoring alone, per book_pipeline/CHAPTER_SLATE.md's Week 9 Wednesday row.

Week 10 - Make the Memory Hierarchy Hurt

Central machine question: Why do we need layers of memory, and what does crossing a layer feel like?

Week at a Glance

Prior belief: cache is fast, RAM is slow, and one speed number describes memory well enough.

Prediction: as the working set grows from tiny to tens of MiB, predict the shape of dependent-access time and whether streaming bandwidth should show the same shape.

AI Fluency: Lens 10 - Critique.
Professional Minds: Wednesday - Software Engineering; Friday - Agile Software Development.

Monday attacks the Week 5 hierarchy ledger with locality, latency, bandwidth, working set, cache lines, misses, and a bounded AMAT model. Wednesday runs the memory sweep. Friday interprets regions and noise without claiming exact cache boundaries the evidence cannot support.

Machine Dossier

Action: ADD. Add the memory plot and revise the hierarchy ledger so capacity, latency, bandwidth, scarcity/cost, and workload sensitivity are separate dimensions.

Required path

./lab/bin/archlab run memory --out-dir dossier/evidence/week10-memory
./lab/bin/archlab plot memory dossier/evidence/week10-memory/memory.csv --out dossier/evidence/week10-memory/memory.png

Scope

This week cares about shape, not memorized nanosecond tables. Prefetching, TLB behavior, replacement, machine load, and real cache organization can make cliffs noisy or shifted.

pages.title: Week 10 Monday - Think / Frame
pages.body:
Week 10 Monday - Make the Memory Hierarchy Hurt

Question

Why do we need layers of memory, and what does crossing a layer feel like?

Attack the Week 5 ledger

Week 5 could inventory capacity and price. It could not yet say how a workload experiences the hierarchy. Now we add evidence.

Locality

Temporal locality reuses recently accessed data. Spatial locality accesses nearby data. Cache lines exploit nearby reuse; dependent pointer chasing intentionally limits easy streaming/prefetch behavior.

Latency versus bandwidth

Pointer chasing asks how quickly the next dependent address becomes available. Streaming asks how much contiguous data can move per unit time. These are different architecture questions.

Working set

As active data outgrows a level, service can come from farther away and behavior can change. Real transitions are not perfect stair steps.

Bounded cache mechanics

Use line/block, hit/miss, set/associativity, and replacement only far enough to explain why placement/reuse matter. Avoid hand-simulated cache-table marathons.

AMAT as a model

A small average-memory-access-time example can show why a small miss rate matters when miss cost is high. AMAT is a simplified reasoning model, not a prediction of the native sweep.

AI Fluency

Give AI a confident cache/memory claim or an exact boundary interpretation, then critique its precision with the measured curve and source evidence.

Prediction

Sketch pointer-chase latency and streaming-bandwidth shapes before running the experiment.

pages.title: Professional Minds Wednesday - Week 10 Reading: Quality Assurance Is a Coordinated Discipline, Not a Late Step
pages.body:
Week 10 Reading: Quality Assurance Is a Coordinated Discipline, Not a Late Step

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 10 — How do teams build quality software?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7–9 minutes
  • Primary source: Roger S. Pressman, Software Engineering: A Practitioner's Approach, seventh edition, Chapter 16, "Software Quality Assurance"

Why This Matters Professionally

Ask a new developer when quality gets checked, and a common answer is "at the end — testing." Pressman opens Chapter 16 by rejecting that picture: some developers believe software quality is something you begin to worry about after code has been generated, and he calls that belief mistaken. Quality assurance (often called quality management) is an umbrella activity applied throughout the whole software process, not a gate installed just before delivery.

This matters beyond software. Any professional process that produces something other people rely on — a lab result, a public report, an instructional plan — faces the same choice: build quality in through standards, review, and measurement across the whole process, or bolt a single inspection onto the end and hope it catches everything.

Primary-Source Ideas: What Software Engineering Argues

Primary-source claim: Pressman defines software quality assurance (SQA) as encompassing an SQA process, specific quality-control tasks (technical reviews and a multi-tiered testing strategy), effective engineering practice, control of work products and the changes made to them, compliance with development standards, and measurement and reporting mechanisms — with the goal of ensuring the organization does "the right things at the right time in the right way." (Source location: Chapter 16, introduction and "16.1 Background Issues.")

Responsible paraphrase: SQA is not one activity but a coordinated bundle of them, and responsibility for it is shared: software engineers, project managers, customers, salespeople, and a dedicated SQA group all carry some part of it. The SQA group's specific role is to act as the customer's in-house representative — checking the software from the customer's point of view and confirming that development actually followed the standards the team agreed to.

Primary-source claim: Section 16.2 lists the concerns SQA covers: standards adopted voluntarily or imposed by a customer; technical reviews (engineers checking engineers, aimed at finding errors) versus audits (SQA personnel confirming quality guidelines are being followed); testing; defect collection and analysis; change management; education; vendor management; security; safety; and risk management. (Source location: Chapter 16, "16.2 Elements of Software Quality Assurance.")

Responsible paraphrase: The review-versus-audit distinction is easy to blur but matters: a review checks the work for defects, while an audit checks whether the process itself — including whether reviews are happening as intended — is being followed. SQA is not redundant testing; it is oversight of whether the whole system of quality practices is operating.

Primary-source claim: The SQA group's tasks include preparing an SQA plan, participating in defining the project's process, reviewing engineering activities for compliance with that process, auditing designated work products, documenting and tracking deviations until corrected, and reporting noncompliance to senior management — all aimed at four goals: requirements quality, design quality, code quality, and quality-control effectiveness, each assessed through specific attributes and metrics (for example, ambiguity and traceability for requirements; architectural integrity and interface complexity for design; complexity and maintainability for code). (Source location: Chapter 16, "16.3 SQA Tasks, Goals, and Metrics," including "16.3.1 SQA Tasks" and "16.3.2 Goals, Attributes, and Metrics.")

Responsible paraphrase: These goals turn "quality" into something with measurable proxies at every stage, not only at the code. A defect traced to an ambiguous requirement is a different problem, with a different fix, than a defect traced to a coding-standard violation, and Pressman's framework is built to distinguish them.

Primary-source claim: Pressman describes two more quantitative approaches. Formal SQA treats a program as a mathematical object whose conformity to a rigorous specification can in principle be demonstrated through proofs of correctness. Statistical SQA instead collects and categorizes real defects, traces each to an underlying cause, and applies the Pareto principle — roughly 80 percent of defects trace to 20 percent of possible causes — to isolate and correct the "vital few" causes rather than chasing every individual defect. In Pressman's worked example, incomplete or erroneous specifications and misinterpreted customer communication are among the largest causes of defects overall, but the ranking shifts when only the most serious defects are counted. (Source location: Chapter 16, "16.4 Formal Approaches to SQA," "16.5 Statistical Software Quality Assurance," and "16.5.1 A Generic Example.")

Responsible paraphrase: The Pareto step is the practical payoff: an organization with limited time should not spread corrective effort evenly across every defect category, but find whichever few causes account for most of the damage. Because "most defects" and "most serious defects" can point at different causes, a team has to decide which ranking it is correcting for before it acts.

Primary-source claim: Six Sigma, "the most widely used strategy for statistical quality assurance in industry today" per Pressman, formalizes correction through the DMAIC cycle — define, measure, analyze, improve, control — for improving an existing process, or DMADV — define, measure, analyze, design, verify — when a process is built from scratch. Separately, Pressman distinguishes reliability (failure-free operation in a specified environment over a specified time) from safety, which evaluates how a failure interacts with the whole system and environment to create a hazard. (Source location: Chapter 16, "16.5.2 Six Sigma for Software Engineering" and "16.6 Software Reliability," including "16.6.2 Software Safety.")

Responsible paraphrase: Reliability and safety answer different questions. Reliability asks how often the program fails; safety asks what happens, to whom, when it does. A rare failure in a payroll report and a rare failure in a medical-device controller are not the same kind of risk even at identical failure rates, which is why Pressman treats safety as its own analysis, not a byproduct of a high reliability number.

A Concrete Example: Two Rankings of the Same Defect List

Picture a team that has collected a year of defect data, the way Pressman's generic example does. Sorted by raw count, "incomplete or erroneous specifications" and "misinterpretation of customer communication" dominate — most defects trace back to something that went wrong before a line of code was written. Sorted by severity instead, a different set rises: errors in data representation and errors in design logic, common but not the largest by count, cause a disproportionate share of the serious failures.

A team that looks only at the first ranking might invest in better requirements-gathering meetings — reasonable, but leaving the design-logic and data-representation problems untouched. Pressman's point is not that one list is correct and the other wrong; "the vital few" depends on which cost the team is trying to reduce, and that cost has to be named before the Pareto principle can be applied.

Synthesis

Chapter 16's throughline is that quality assurance is infrastructure, not inspection. Standards, reviews, audits, defect tracking, and metrics operate continuously, and SQA's job is to keep that system honest — checking not just the product but whether the process meant to produce a good product is actually being followed. Friday's reading turns to a related problem: what happens when the process itself, meant to prevent failure, becomes so heavy that it starts causing the failures it was built to stop.

Reflection Questions

  1. Explain, in the chapter's own terms, the difference between a technical review and an audit, and why Pressman treats them as distinct SQA activities.
  2. Using the two-rankings example above, explain why "the vital few causes" is not a single fixed list — what must a team decide before it can apply the Pareto principle?
  3. Pick a process you know that "checks quality" only at the very end. Which earlier-stage SQA element — standards, requirements-quality metrics, design review — could catch a problem sooner, and what would that require the team to do differently?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Roger S. Pressman, Software Engineering: A Practitioner's Approach, seventh edition (McGraw-Hill, copyright 2010), Chapter 16, "Software Quality Assurance," as processed into books/summaries/book_summary_software_engineering.md and its underlying chapter summary at books/pipeline_runs/software_engineering/summaries/17_chapter_16_software_quality_assurance_summary.md. Source locations cite the chapter and named subsection rather than page numbers, since the compiled summary does not carry page citations.
  • This reading draws on Chapter 16 only, as the book's own treatment of quality management, not a summary of the book's other chapters on requirements, design, testing techniques, or project management.
  • The two-rankings example is drawn directly from Pressman's own generic illustration in "16.5.1 A Generic Example," not instructor-invented; it is restated for classroom use but adds no claim beyond the chapter's Figure 16.2 data.
  • This reading supersedes readings/week_10_building_quality_software.md, marked superseded in place. pages.title: Professional Minds Friday - Week 10 Reading: When the Process Meant to Prevent Failure Starts Causing It
pages.body:
Week 10 Reading: When the Process Meant to Prevent Failure Starts Causing It

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 10 — How do teams build quality software?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7–9 minutes
  • Primary source: Robert C. Martin, Agile Software Development: Principles, Patterns, and Practices, Chapter 1, "Agile Practices"

Why This Matters Professionally

Wednesday's reading described SQA as a coordinated system of standards, reviews, audits, and metrics that keeps a process honest across its whole lifecycle. It is easy to read that and conclude the fix for any quality problem is more process: another standard, another review gate, another required artifact. Martin's Chapter 1 opens by describing exactly how that instinct backfires.

He calls it "runaway-process inflation." A team suffers a fiasco, adds constraints and artifacts to prevent it from happening again, suffers new errors, and adds still more constraints — until the cumbersome process itself starts producing the failures it was meant to prevent: slipping schedules, bloated budgets, and teams that build the wrong product because they are too slow to respond to what they are learning. This is not an argument against SQA's discipline. It is a caution about what happens when discipline stops being aimed at anything and simply keeps accumulating.

Primary-Source Ideas: What Agile Software Development Argues

Primary-source claim: Martin traces the cycle directly: fear of repeating a past failure motivates a team to create a process that constrains its activities and demands certain artifacts, drawn from what seemed to work before; but projects are rarely simple enough for a fixed set of constraints to reliably prevent error, so new errors prompt still more constraints, and "in a kind of runaway-process inflation," the process becomes ever larger — even as it can "create the very problems that it is designed to prevent." (Source location: Chapter 1, "Agile Practices," opening section.)

Responsible paraphrase: The mechanism Martin describes is not incompetence — it is a reasonable response to fear that stops working past a certain point. Each individual added constraint may have made sense given its own past incident. The failure mode is cumulative: no one step looks unreasonable, but the sum becomes a process too heavy to move quickly or respond to what the team actually learns.

Primary-source claim: In 2001, a group of industry experts calling themselves the Agile Alliance produced the Manifesto for Agile Software Development, valuing individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan — while explicitly stating that the items on the right still have value, just less than the items on the left. (Source location: Chapter 1, "The Agile Alliance," including "The Manifesto of the Agile Alliance.")

Responsible paraphrase: Each of Martin's four values comes with an explicit qualification, not a rejection of its counterpart. A strong process cannot save a project with a weak team, but tools still matter — Martin's own advice is to start small and grow tools only once a genuine need is demonstrated. Documentation is still necessary, especially a short, current record of a system's rationale and structure — his own rule is "produce no document unless its need is immediate and significant" — but code and direct interaction with the team, not paperwork, are what actually transfer knowledge to a new member.

Primary-source claim: Martin argues software cannot be commissioned like a fixed-price commodity: a contract that specifies requirements, schedule, and cost in advance is "fundamentally flawed" because its terms typically become meaningless before the project completes. He illustrates this with a project he personally negotiated, paid the team a low monthly rate plus large payouts for functionality blocks that passed the customer's acceptance test, delivered software to the customer almost every Friday, and reprioritized changes together week to week — a project that survived major requirement shifts because of that close collaboration. (Source location: Chapter 1, "Customer collaboration over contract negotiation.")

Responsible paraphrase: The contract's design is the actual lesson: it governed how the team and customer would work together rather than trying to pin down the scope and schedule in advance. That is a structural choice, not a personality trait of a particularly agreeable customer — a contract can be written to reward demonstrated, tested functionality instead of a specification that both sides know will drift.

Primary-source claim: Twelve principles operationalize the values, including: satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery; welcome changing requirements even late in development; deliver working software frequently, preferring the shorter end of weeks over months; keep business people and developers together daily; build projects around motivated individuals, trusted to get the job done; favor face-to-face conversation; measure progress by working functionality rather than documentation volume; sustain a constant pace instead of a burnout sprint; pursue continuous technical excellence; maximize the amount of work not done; let self-organizing teams shape architecture and design; and reflect regularly to tune the team's own behavior. (Source location: Chapter 1, "Principles.")

Responsible paraphrase: Several of these principles directly answer Wednesday's SQA concerns without adding process weight. "Working software is the primary measure of progress" is itself a metric, just a different one than a document-completion percentage. "Continuous attention to technical excellence" is Martin's own version of quality control: the chapter states plainly that agile teams do not defer cleanup — "if they make a mess, they clean it up before they finish for the day" — which functions like a review discipline embedded in daily work rather than a separate audit step.

A Concrete Example: The Same Defect, Two Responses

Recall Wednesday's Pareto example: a team traces many of its defects to incomplete or erroneous specifications and misinterpreted customer communication. An SQA-heavy response might add a formal sign-off step, requiring every requirement to be documented, reviewed, and approved before development starts — a reasonable fix to a real problem, but one that risks becoming Martin's runaway-process inflation if the sign-off keeps growing after each new misunderstanding.

Martin's chapter offers a different response to the same root cause: shorten the distance between a requirement and the evidence that tests it. The weekly-delivery contract in his own example did not eliminate misunderstood requirements — it made them visible and correctable within days instead of months, because the customer watched the software evolve and reprioritized changes as soon as a gap appeared. Neither response is "correct" in the abstract; they trade a heavier up-front check for a faster feedback loop, and the right choice depends on how expensive a late-discovered misunderstanding actually is for that project.

Synthesis

Martin's chapter complicates rather than contradicts Wednesday's picture of quality assurance. Both readings agree that a process oriented only toward avoiding blame for the last failure, without being checked against what it actually costs the team, can become the problem. Where Pressman built a system for making assumptions and deviations inspectable, Martin argues that inspection can happen through fast, frequent, face-to-face feedback instead of accumulating documents and gates — and that a team has to keep asking whether each piece of process still earns its keep.

Reflection Questions

  1. Explain, in the chapter's own terms, how "runaway-process inflation" can occur even when each individual added constraint was a reasonable response to a real past failure.
  2. Using the two-rankings example above, describe one situation where a heavier up-front requirements check would be worth its cost, and one where a faster feedback loop would serve better. What makes the difference?
  3. Martin states "produce no document unless its need is immediate and significant." Apply that rule to a document or process step you have encountered that seemed to exist mostly out of habit. What would change if the team applied his rule to it?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Robert C. Martin, Agile Software Development: Principles, Patterns, and Practices (Prentice Hall, copyright 2003), Chapter 1, "Agile Practices," as processed into books/summaries/book_summary_agile_software_development.md and its underlying chapter summary at books/pipeline_runs/agile_software_development/summaries/01_agile_practices_summary.md. Source locations cite the chapter and named subsection rather than page numbers, since the compiled summary does not carry page citations.
  • This reading draws on Chapter 1 only, as the book's own framing of agile values and principles, not a summary of the book's later chapters on design principles, patterns, or the payroll case study.
  • The SQA-heavy-response paragraph in "A Concrete Example" is instructor-invented for illustration and is not one of Martin's own examples; the weekly-delivery contract example above it is drawn directly from the chapter.
  • This reading supersedes readings/week_10_building_quality_software.md, marked superseded in place. That file blended material from both this week's books at the week level, citing PDF page numbers rather than the book-pipeline's per-chapter summaries. This reading instead draws on a single bounded chapter (Chapter 1) via the pipeline's chapter summary, per book_pipeline/CHAPTER_SLATE.md's Week 10 Friday row.

pages.title: Week 11 - Week at a Glance
pages.body:
Week 11 - The Useful Lie of Memory

Central machine question: What hardware mechanisms create the memory/process world software thinks it sees?

Week at a Glance

Prior belief: when my program uses an address, it is basically naming a place in physical RAM.

Prediction: if two processes show similar virtual address ranges, does that mean they must be using the same physical memory?

AI Fluency: Lens 11 - Verify.
Professional Minds: Wednesday - Software Project Management; Friday - Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests.

Week 10 made physical hierarchy behavior visible. Week 11 begins from one memory access and asks what the program's address actually means.

Required concepts

Virtual vs physical address, pages/page tables, TLB, protection/privilege, page faults, traps/exceptions/syscalls, interrupts, and a bounded device/I/O relationship. This is not an Operating Systems survey.

Machine Dossier

Action: REVISE. Add only the VM/protection/process evidence that improves the persistent memory model.

Required live path

On Linux/WSL where supported:

getconf PAGESIZE
cat /proc/self/maps

Use a short privacy-safe excerpt, not an environment dump. A curated trace is the equal-ceiling fallback on other surfaces.

Scope

/proc/<pid>/maps is direct evidence about virtual mappings/permissions. It is not a complete physical-memory map. Root-only physical-frame archaeology is not required.

pages.title: Week 11 Monday - Think / Frame
pages.body:
Week 11 Monday - The Useful Lie of Memory

Question

What hardware mechanisms create the memory/process world software thinks it sees?

An address is part of an abstraction

A process typically issues virtual addresses. Hardware translation plus OS-managed mappings create a private/protected view that need not correspond to an obvious physical address.

Pages and page tables

Virtual address space is divided into pages. Translation structures map virtual pages toward physical frames or other states. Work one small address split into virtual page number + page offset; do not perform a giant multi-level walk.

The TLB

Translation itself would be expensive if every access walked page tables. A TLB caches recent translations, adding another locality-sensitive structure to the memory story.

Protection and privilege

Mappings carry permissions. Processor privilege and translation/protection machinery let the system reject accesses that should not succeed.

Faults are transitions

A page fault means the current state cannot complete the memory reference normally. The OS may allocate, load, remap, reject, or otherwise handle the event.

Traps, syscalls, interrupts

At bounded depth:

  • a syscall intentionally requests privileged service;
  • exceptions/traps transfer control because of synchronous program/processor state;
  • interrupts represent asynchronous events.

Exact naming/taxonomy can vary by architecture; use the RISC-V/Linux sources for our bounded model.

Observable process evidence

Linux /proc/<pid>/maps exposes virtual mapping ranges, permissions, and file-backed paths where applicable. That is powerful evidence, but it does not tell you a simple physical frame number for every address.

Storage/I-O boundary

File-backed mappings and persistence connect memory to storage/I-O. Keep the story on translation/protection/cooperation rather than turning this into a storage benchmark week.

AI Fluency

Ask AI for a specific VM/process claim, then verify it with local evidence and primary documentation. Scope is part of the answer.

pages.title: Professional Minds Wednesday - Week 11 Reading: A Plan Only Helps If Someone Checks It Against Reality
pages.body:
Week 11 Reading: A Plan Only Helps If Someone Checks It Against Reality

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 11 — How do projects become reliable products?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7–9 minutes
  • Primary source: Bob Hughes, Mike Cotterell, and Rajib Mall, Software Project Management, fifth edition, Chapter 9, "Monitoring and Control"

Why This Matters Professionally

A schedule, a budget, and a task list are forecasts, not facts. The chapter argues that planning has value only if execution is continuously compared against those forecasts, deviations get identified, and someone decides whether to replan the work or revise the target. A plan that is never checked against reality is not managing anything — it is decoration.

This applies to any coordinated effort that produces something other people depend on, not only software: a renovation, a research study, a semester-long curriculum rollout. The professional skill this chapter teaches is not making a good initial plan — it is noticing, early and with real evidence, when the plan and reality have started to diverge.

Primary-Source Ideas: What Software Project Management Argues

Primary-source claim: Responsibility for monitoring typically runs through a reporting hierarchy — team members report to team leaders, the project manager consolidates progress across the team, and a steering committee or project board oversees the major decisions. Monitoring should use objective evidence wherever possible — completed deliverables, intermediate milestones, counted products — because percentage-complete estimates invite the "99% complete" syndrome, where a task reported as nearly finished stays nearly finished for weeks. (Source location: Chapter 9, opening discussion of monitoring responsibility and objective evidence.)

Responsible paraphrase: "I'm about 90% done" is a claim, not evidence. The chapter's fix is structural: build the plan around checkpoints that produce something countable or verifiable — a passed review, a deployed slice, a completed deliverable — so that "done" has a definition nobody can quietly renegotiate as the deadline approaches.

Primary-source claim: The chapter presents several ways to collect and visualize progress. Traffic-light reporting classifies each piece of work green, amber, or red according to the likelihood of meeting its target — not how much work has been completed — which keeps the report focused on risk rather than effort expended. Reviews are described as another major control mechanism: they detect defects in requirements, designs, plans, and code, often more cost-effectively than testing, because testing can only be applied to executable software while a review can catch a design-stage or requirements-stage problem long before there is code to test. (Source location: Chapter 9, sections on traffic-light reporting and reviews.)

Responsible paraphrase: Traffic-light color is a risk judgment, not a progress bar — a task can be 80% complete and still red if the remaining 20% is the part nobody has solved yet. Reviews extend monitoring earlier than testing can reach: by the time there is code to test, a bad requirement has already been built on top of.

Primary-source claim: Gantt charts, slip charts, and timeline charts make schedule status and changing completion forecasts visible over time, not just current status. Cost monitoring must be interpreted alongside actual project status rather than in isolation, and earned value analysis compares planned value, earned value, and actual cost through schedule and cost variances and performance indices — forecasts the chapter calls useful but approximate, particularly when parallel activities affect the critical path. (Source location: Chapter 9, sections on visualizing progress and earned value analysis.)

Responsible paraphrase: A project can be under budget and behind schedule at the same time, or on schedule and badly over budget — cost and schedule are two different signals, and reading only one hides the other kind of trouble. Earned value gives a number, but the chapter is explicit that the number is an approximation, not a guarantee, especially once several activities are running in parallel.

Primary-source claim: Monitoring effort should be prioritized around critical-path activities, activities with little or no float, high-risk work, and tasks dependent on scarce or expensive resources — not spread evenly across every task on the plan. When a project drifts, the chapter lists specific responses: shortening the critical path by adding or extending resources, reallocating staff, reducing scope, or — more cautiously — reducing quality; relaxing precedence constraints is also possible but can increase rework and risk. Any decision must preserve the project's business case, and changes to scope, cost, delivery date, or stakeholders may require a formal exception report and sponsor approval. (Source location: Chapter 9, sections on prioritizing monitoring effort and responding to drift.)

Responsible paraphrase: Not every late task is equally dangerous — a task with slack can slip without moving the finish date, but a critical-path task cannot. The chapter's menu of responses to drift is also a menu of tradeoffs: every option (more resources, reallocated staff, less scope, lower quality, relaxed sequencing) costs something else, and the chapter is explicit that "reduce quality" is the response to reach for last and carefully.

Primary-source claim: Requirements and other baselined products need formal change control — authorized requests, impact and cost assessment, prioritization, controlled modification, testing, and release — and software configuration management extends this same discipline across all work products by controlling versions, revisions, baselines, variants, access, and concurrent edits. Change-control boards and tools provide traceability, prevent unauthorized or conflicting changes, support rollback, and help managers determine the project's actual current state. (Source location: Chapter 9, sections on change control and configuration management.)

Responsible paraphrase: Once something is "baselined" — agreed and locked as a reference point — a change to it is not a quick edit, it is a tracked decision with an assessed cost and an approval step. Without that discipline, a manager cannot actually answer "what state is the project in right now," because the baseline itself keeps moving informally.

A Concrete Example: Two Weeks of the Same Yellow Task

Picture a team tracking a data-migration task. Week one's status report says "85% complete." Week two's status report also says "85% complete" — the same number, seven days later. Under the chapter's traffic-light logic, this task should have been flagged red the moment the percentage stopped moving, regardless of what number it was reporting, because the signal that matters is the likelihood of hitting the target, not the raw completion figure. A manager reading only the percentage sees stability. A manager reading the traffic-light color, tied to evidence like "test environment access still not granted," sees a task that cannot move until an external blocker clears — a genuinely different, more urgent, situation than a task that is merely slow.

Synthesis

Chapter 9's throughline is that a plan without monitoring is just an opening guess. Objective evidence, prioritized attention on the tasks that can actually sink the schedule, and formal control over changes to what has already been agreed are what let a manager compare intention against reality and act on the gap before it becomes unrecoverable. Friday's reading turns from the management side of this problem to the technical side: how a development team generates its own continuous evidence, at the level of code rather than the level of a status report, that the thing being built still does what it is supposed to.

Reflection Questions

  1. Explain, in the chapter's own terms, why traffic-light color is described as a measure of risk rather than a measure of completed effort.
  2. Using the two-weeks example above, explain what makes a status report like "85% complete, unchanged" more informative once it is reframed as a traffic-light signal instead of a raw percentage.
  3. Pick a task or project you know that reports progress only as a percentage. What objective evidence — a deliverable, a milestone, a passed check — could replace that percentage, and what would it take to define it?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Bob Hughes, Mike Cotterell, and Rajib Mall, Software Project Management, fifth edition (Tata McGraw-Hill India adaptation), Chapter 9, "Monitoring and Control," as processed into books/summaries/book_summary_software_project_management.md and its underlying chapter summary at books/pipeline_runs/software_project_management/summaries/09_monitoring_and_control_summary.md. Source locations cite the chapter and named section rather than page numbers, since the compiled summary does not carry page citations.
  • This reading draws on Chapter 9 only, as the book's own treatment of monitoring and control, not a summary of the book's other chapters on estimation, planning, risk, contracts, or people management.
  • The two-weeks data-migration example is instructor-invented to illustrate the traffic-light-versus-percentage distinction; it is not drawn from the chapter's own text and is labeled as such here.
  • This reading, together with Friday's readings/week_11_fri_point_of_tdd.md, supersedes readings/week_11_projects_become_products.md, marked superseded in place. That file blended material from both this week's books at the week level, citing PDF page numbers rather than the book-pipeline's per-chapter summaries. These two readings instead each draw on a single bounded chapter via the pipeline's chapter summaries, per book_pipeline/CHAPTER_SLATE.md's Week 11 rows.

pages.title: Professional Minds Friday - Week 11 Reading: Tests Are How a Team Learns Whether It Is Right
pages.body:
Week 11 Reading: Tests Are How a Team Learns Whether It Is Right

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 11 — How do projects become reliable products?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7–9 minutes
  • Primary source: Steve Freeman and Nat Pryce, Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests, Chapter 1, "What Is the Point of Test-Driven Development?"

Why This Matters Professionally

Wednesday's reading described monitoring and control at the level of a status report: is the plan still matching reality, and what objective evidence proves it? Freeman and Pryce open their book by arguing that the same question applies one level down, inside the code itself. Most software projects involve unfamiliar domains, technologies, or organizational processes — so developers, customers, and users discover what they actually need only as the system takes real shape. A team that assumes its requirements were settled correctly in advance is making the same mistake as a manager who trusts an unchanging "85% complete" report: both are substituting an old assumption for current evidence.

This matters beyond programming. Any professional producing something for people who will use it under conditions not fully known in advance — a curriculum, a policy, a piece of infrastructure — faces the same choice Chapter 1 poses: build in repeated, cheap ways to check the current assumption against reality, or wait until the end and discover the mismatch when it is expensive to fix.

Primary-Source Ideas: What Growing Object-Oriented Software Argues

Primary-source claim: The chapter frames software development as fundamentally a learning process, and argues that empirical feedback is the essential tool for managing the resulting uncertainty. It describes repeated, nested feedback loops — unit tests, pair programming, acceptance tests, meetings, iterations, and releases — that let a team compare its assumptions with reality and adapt. Inner loops focus on technical detail; outer loops evaluate the team and the system's usefulness to its actual users. (Source location: Chapter 1, opening argument on software development as learning and the nested-feedback-loops model.)

Responsible paraphrase: The loops are nested on purpose, not just numerous — a fast inner loop (does this one unit of code behave correctly?) catches a narrow class of mistake quickly and cheaply, while a slower outer loop (does the whole system deliver a real result the user wanted?) catches a broader, more expensive class of mistake that the inner loops cannot see by design. A team needs both, because passing every inner-loop check says nothing about whether the outer question has been answered.

Primary-source claim: Because manual regression testing becomes impractical as a system grows, automated tests are what make it possible to keep protecting existing behavior while adding new features. Refactoring — small, behavior-preserving improvements that remove duplication and clarify design — keeps code understandable and safe to modify, with the test suite providing the safety net after each step. Test-Driven Development reverses the usual order: write the test first. This makes testing a design activity, not just a verification one — tests clarify acceptance criteria, encourage loosely coupled components, document behavior, and build the regression suite as a byproduct. The chapter states TDD's governing rule directly: never write new functionality without a failing test first, and running the tests reveals when the intended work is actually complete, discouraging unnecessary "gold plating." (Source location: Chapter 1, sections on automated testing, refactoring, and the TDD cycle.)

Responsible paraphrase: Writing the test first changes what the test is for. A test written after the code tends to confirm what the code already does; a test written before the code has to state what the code is supposed to do, which forces the design question — what should this component's interface even look like — to happen before the implementation commits to an answer.

Primary-source claim: TDD must operate beyond isolated unit tests. A feature begins with an acceptance test that demonstrates the desired system behavior and defines when the feature is complete; unit tests then guide the implementation through the inner test/implement/refactor cycle. Acceptance testing should, wherever possible, exercise the system end-to-end through its real external interfaces and realistic build and deployment processes — a project that tests only its internal objects can appear successful while the actual running application does nothing useful. The chapter's testing hierarchy distinguishes acceptance tests (whole-system behavior), integration tests (interactions with unchangeable external code), and unit tests (individual objects), together addressing both external quality — meeting users' needs — and internal quality — being understandable and safely changeable. (Source location: Chapter 1, sections on acceptance testing and the testing hierarchy.)

Responsible paraphrase: A green unit-test suite is a claim about internal quality, not external quality — it can be entirely true and the finished system can still fail to do the one thing a user actually needed. The acceptance test is what stands in for the user; without one, "all tests pass" quietly stops meaning "the software works."

Primary-source claim: Difficult-to-write unit tests are treated as valuable design feedback in their own right: they may reveal implicit dependencies, excessive responsibilities, tight coupling, or low cohesion in the code being tested. "Listening to the tests" is the chapter's term for using this difficulty to produce code whose responsibilities form meaningful units and whose components can change independently of one another. (Source location: Chapter 1, closing section on tests as design feedback.)

Responsible paraphrase: When a test is awkward to write — too much setup, too many collaborators to fake, unclear what to assert — the chapter's claim is that the awkwardness is information about the design, not just an inconvenience to work around. The instinct to reach for a testing trick to force the test through is, in this framework, usually a signal to fix the design instead.

A Concrete Example: The Same "Green" Suite, Two Different Claims

Picture two teams, each reporting "all tests passing" at a Friday status meeting — echoing Wednesday's reading, where a status number alone said less than it appeared to. Team A has a large suite of fast unit tests covering every class in isolation, plus mocked-out dependencies for anything external, and no acceptance test that exercises the whole system through its real interface. Team B has fewer tests overall, but includes one acceptance test that starts the actual application, sends it a real request through its real entry point, and checks the real response.

Team A's green suite proves the internal pieces behave as their own tests expect. It says nothing about whether those pieces are wired together correctly, whether the real deployment configuration works, or whether the feature is reachable by an actual user. Team B's single acceptance test, even though it is slower and covers less ground per run, is the only evidence either team has that the system, as a whole, currently does the thing it is supposed to do. Freeman and Pryce's hierarchy explains why "tests are passing" is not one claim — it is several different claims, and a status report needs to say which kind of evidence it actually has.

Synthesis

Chapter 1's throughline connects directly to Wednesday: a plan (or a design) is only as trustworthy as the evidence checking it against reality, and that evidence has to be deliberately built, at multiple nested levels, rather than assumed. Wednesday's monitoring-and-control discipline generates that evidence at the level of a project's schedule, cost, and deliverables. Freeman and Pryce generate the equivalent evidence at the level of code, through a hierarchy of tests that separately answer "does this component work" and "does the system actually do what the user needs." Both readings reject the same shortcut: treating an unverified assumption — a stale percentage, a passing but narrow test suite — as if it were current proof.

Reflection Questions

  1. Explain, in the chapter's own terms, the difference between what a passing unit-test suite proves and what a passing acceptance test proves.
  2. Using the two-teams example above, explain why "all tests passing" is not, by itself, enough information for someone outside the team to know whether the system works.
  3. Pick a project or task you know where progress is reported only through an inner-loop signal (a narrow check, a partial demo, a completed step) with no outer-loop check on the real outcome. What would an acceptance-test-style check look like for that project?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Steve Freeman and Nat Pryce, Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests (Addison-Wesley, 2010), Chapter 1, "What Is the Point of Test-Driven Development?," as processed into books/summaries/book_summary_growing_object_oriented_software.md and its underlying chapter summary at books/pipeline_runs/growing_object_oriented_software/summaries/02_chapter_1_summary.md. Source locations cite the chapter and named section rather than page numbers, since the compiled summary does not carry page citations.
  • This reading draws on Chapter 1 only, as the book's own introductory argument for TDD and the nested-feedback-loop model, not a summary of the book's later chapters on specific testing techniques, mock objects, or sustaining a test suite over time.
  • The two-teams "green suite" example is instructor-invented to illustrate the acceptance-versus-unit-test distinction; it is not drawn from the chapter's own text and is labeled as such here.
