pages.body:
Week 16 - Farkle + Machine Learning: What Did the Compute Buy?

Central machine question: What does it cost a machine to make a better Farkle decision, and when is that extra cost actually worth paying?

Dead-days grading boundary

Fall 2026 Week 16 is the three-class-day dead-days window immediately before finals.

Therefore this week is a real learning/application experience but not a graded recurring-work week:

  • no Machine Dossier checkpoint;
  • no graded AI Fluency assignment;
  • no graded Professional Minds assignment;
  • no graded Architecture Investigation assignment;
  • no graded Explain / Defend assignment;
  • no premium tool/hardware path creates points.

You may still run the benchmark, write the judgment, discuss the evidence, and keep the receipt as portfolio/learning evidence. The work exists because it is useful and fun, not because Canvas is dangling points over it.

Week at a Glance

Prior belief we are testing/refining: a more computationally expensive strategy or a more powerful machine is automatically the better architecture.

Prediction before measurement: choose two fixed Farkle strategies and predict which will be more effective, which will consume more preparation or runtime work, and whether the extra work will be worth paying for under one objective you name.

AI Fluency lens: Lens 16 - Reflect and Improve. Use it as an ungraded reflection lens this week.

Professional Minds: Wednesday - Generative AI Design Patterns reflection; Friday - semester reflection: what kind of professional do I want to become? These remain enrichment/reflection surfaces rather than graded Week 16 assignments.

Day Mode What happens Evidence
Monday Think / Frame Separate effectiveness, preparation cost, operating cost, and machine context. Make a prediction. short prediction for yourself / discussion
Wednesday Investigate / Break / Measure Run two fixed strategies on one validated CPU lane and inspect repeated machine-readable evidence. JSON/CSV receipt + observed relationship
Friday Explain / Defend Decide whether the extra computation bought enough effectiveness for your declared objective. bounded ungraded architecture judgment

Continuity

What returns from an earlier week: latency/throughput, parallelism, locality, specialization, resource constraints, and the habit of choosing evidence that matches a workload.

What this week intentionally carries forward: the architect's job is not to maximize every metric. It is to choose a machine under a workload, objective, and constraint.

Machine Dossier handoff

Action: NO CHANGE.

The technical Machine Dossier froze in Week 14. Week 16 may consult earlier Architecture ideas to explain evidence, but it does not create a new dossier layer or Checkpoint 4.

The shared machine

The Farkle rules, learner, strategies, fair simulation, and common evidence semantics come from the canonical jeremy-evert/Farkle_and_Machine_Learning computational core vendored under:

weeks/week-16/code/farkle_ml/

Computer Architecture owns only the execution-context layer under:

weeks/week-16/code/architecture_farkle/

That layer records the host, repeats timings, preserves raw effectiveness evidence, and writes JSON/CSV receipts. It does not fork the game or silently rewrite the learning algorithms.

The required lane

The required learning path is:

  • native Python;
  • CPU;
  • ordinary supported computer;
  • no paid AI/API;
  • no GPU;
  • no cloud/NRP/Kubernetes;
  • no special family hardware.

A machine may physically contain a GPU. That does not make a native Python CPU run a GPU benchmark.

If your local machine cannot run the lane cleanly, use the course-provided real fallback receipt and do the same reasoning task. Hardware convenience does not create a grading ceiling because Week 16 itself is ungraded.

Student path

  1. Read monday.md and make the prediction before seeing benchmark results.
  2. Follow wednesday.md, choose two fixed strategies, and run repeated evidence on one CPU lane when practical.
  3. Complete the reasoning in friday.md using the receipt rather than a screenshot dump. Keep it as learning/portfolio evidence; it is not a graded Week 16 submission.
  4. Use references.md when you need to trace ownership or verify what the benchmark does.

Fixed strategy menu

Use the provided strategies rather than rewriting the workload:

  • bank_at_300 - cheap human threshold;
  • learner:500 - small preparation/training budget;
  • learner:2000 - larger preparation/training budget;
  • rollout:10 - modest decision-time simulation;
  • rollout:25 - larger decision-time simulation.

The usual comparison baseline is bank_at_425.

Cost currencies

Keep them separate.

Effectiveness

  • win rate against the same baseline;
  • raw wins/ties and starter balance;
  • stability under the same deterministic workload.

Preparation

  • training turns;
  • preparation wall time;
  • learned-table/model size when applicable.

Operation

  • evaluation wall time;
  • games per second;
  • timing variation across repeated runs.

Machine / environment

  • actual host and CPU;
  • logical CPU count;
  • execution mode;
  • declared hardware lane.

Do not collapse these into one magic score unless you have first declared exactly what that score is optimizing.

Scope

This week is about: making one Architecture-informed cost-versus-effectiveness judgment from a fixed shared workload.

This week is not trying to teach: new ML theory, GPU programming, deep profiling, Kubernetes, a production tournament platform, or another technical capstone.

Optional Stack Showcase

The instructor may later run the exact same benchmark contract on additional verified hardware lanes. Those runs are enrichment and shared evidence, not a student's grading ceiling.

pages.title: Week 16 Monday - Think / Frame
pages.body:
Monday - Think / Frame: More Compute Is Not a Verdict

Machine question

What does it cost a machine to make a better Farkle decision, and when is that extra cost actually worth paying?

Week 16 does not add a new Computer Architecture mechanism. Instead, it gives the ideas you already have one playful workload to argue about.

The shared program can make a Farkle decision in several ways. Some are cheap rules. Some spend time learning before play. Some spend computation while deciding whether to roll again.

The trap is to ask only:

Which strategy wins more?

An architect asks a harder question:

What did the additional effectiveness cost, and did that trade make sense for the objective I actually care about?

Keep two axes separate

There are two different knobs in this experiment.

Axis 1 - algorithmic effort

The software may spend more or less work making a decision.

  • bank_at_300: tiny rule, almost no preparation;
  • learner:500: modest preparation, cheap decisions after training;
  • learner:2000: more preparation, still cheap decisions after training;
  • rollout:10: little preparation, extra work at decision time;
  • rollout:25: still more decision-time work.

Axis 2 - execution substrate

The same fixed workload may later run on different machines or execution environments.

A faster CPU might run the exact same strategy faster. A future verified accelerator backend might change the shape again. But algorithm choice and machine choice are not the same variable.

If we change both at once and declare a winner, we no longer know what bought the improvement.

Four currencies

1. Effectiveness

How well did the strategy play under the fixed benchmark?

2. Preparation cost

What did we spend before gameplay? Training turns and training wall time belong here.

3. Operating cost

What did we spend during gameplay? Evaluation time and games per second belong here.

4. Machine / environment cost

What machine actually executed the workload? What execution path was used? A GPU sitting idle in the chassis does not count as accelerator work.

Amortization

Preparation and operation create an interesting architecture question.

Suppose one strategy takes longer to train but then plays cheaply. Another starts immediately but pays extra compute on every decision.

The correct choice may depend on how many games you expect to run.

That is an amortization question:

When does the up-front cost become small enough, per game, that the more expensive preparation was worth it?

You do not need a new formula unit here. You need to recognize the shape of the tradeoff.

Throughput is noisy

Wall-clock timing is not a law of nature. Background processes, CPU scheduling, temperature, and other machine activity can perturb one timing.

That is why the Architecture runner repeats each measurement and reports:

  • median games per second;
  • minimum observed games per second;
  • maximum observed games per second.

One fast stopwatch reading is a story. Repeated evidence is a better story.

Correctness comes first

A machine that completes more wrong games per second is not the champion.

The shared core preserves:

  • balanced starters;
  • raw wins and ties;
  • raw turns and Farkles;
  • deterministic seeds;
  • a fixed game contract.

Architecture performance only matters after that computational contract holds.

Your prediction

Before running Wednesday's experiment, choose two fixed strategies from the Week 16 menu.

Write four short predictions:

  1. Which strategy will have the higher effectiveness for the fixed workload?
  2. Which will cost more to prepare?
  3. Which will cost more while playing?
  4. Under one objective you name, do you expect the extra computation to be worth paying for?

Your objective might be:

  • highest win rate;
  • most valid games per second;
  • lowest preparation burden;
  • simplest adequate architecture;
  • cheapest path to a declared effectiveness floor.

There is no requirement that one strategy win all of those.

Scope

This model does not prove that one machine is universally better. It does not establish energy use, purchase price, GPU speedup, or cloud cost unless those things are actually measured later with a compatible receipt.

Wednesday's unresolved question is simple:

When the machine runs the fixed workload, what does the extra compute actually buy?

pages.title: Professional Minds Wednesday - Week 16 Reading: Why Production AI Needs Patterns, Not Just Prompts
pages.body:
Week 16 Reading: Why Production AI Needs Patterns, Not Just Prompts

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 16 — What kind of professional do I want to become?
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7-9 minutes
  • Primary source: Valliappa Lakshmanan and Sara Robinson, Generative AI Design Patterns, Chapter 1, "Introduction"

Why This Matters Professionally

Anyone can type a request into a chat window and get an impressive result back. Lakshmanan and Robinson's opening chapter names the exact gap between that experience and a professional one: "GenAI is so powerful and easy to use that even nontechnical users can easily prototype very compelling applications on top of GenAI. However, taking such GenAI prototypes to production is hard because GenAI models are unreliable." The chapter's whole premise is that closing that gap requires design patterns — proven, catalogued solutions to problems that recur across projects, not one-off tricks discovered under deadline pressure.

This is the closing week's real question: what kind of professional do I want to become? Not "how good am I at getting an AI tool to do something impressive once," but "do I have proven, communicable ways of handling the AI failures that recur every time." A hobbyist prototypes. A professional recognizes recurring problems and reaches for tested solutions with known tradeoffs.

Primary-Source Ideas: What Generative AI Design Patterns Argues

Primary-source claim: Design patterns are "proven solutions to common problems that occur during software design and development... standardized best practices that have evolved over time through the collective experience of software developers." The idea traces to architect Christopher Alexander's A Pattern Language (1977) and entered software engineering through the "Gang of Four" book, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software. Patterns matter because they "establish a common vocabulary developers can use to communicate efficiently" and improve quality, maintainability, and scalability. (Source location: "GenAI Design Patterns.")

Responsible paraphrase: A pattern is not a trick; it is a name for a problem-and-solution pair specific enough that two professionals who have never met can use the name and both know what is meant. That shared vocabulary is itself professional infrastructure — it is what lets a team review, critique, and improve a design instead of everyone reinventing an ad hoc fix from scratch.

Primary-source claim: Most AI applications today are built by prompting a foundational model (GPT-4, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek, and others) rather than training a custom model from scratch — an approach the book calls "AI engineering," following Chip Huyen's AI Engineering. But foundational-model applications hit recurring problems: "the generated content may not match the style you want, may be missing enterprise knowledge that the model doesn't know about, or may lack certain capabilities." The book catalogs 32 patterns addressing problems like these, organized by chapter around a specific recurring problem — for example, the whole of Chapter 3 addresses the problem that a foundational model cannot generate content grounded in confidential enterprise data it was never trained on. (Source location: "GenAI Design Patterns," paragraphs on AI engineering and the 32 patterns.)

Responsible paraphrase: The three specific problems named here — wrong style, missing enterprise knowledge, missing capability — are not edge cases. They are the default failure modes of "just prompt it," which is exactly why the book treats them as engineering problems with catalogued solutions rather than as bad luck to prompt around.

Primary-source claim: Complex tasks are commonly broken into smaller components handled by foundational models; software components that provide capability this way are called agents, and applications built by orchestrating multiple agents are agentic. Agents are expected to show goal orientation (working toward an objective, not just responding to one prompt), planning and reasoning (sequencing sub-steps without being explicitly programmed to), perception and action (gathering data and acting on an environment, often through tool calling), and adaptability (evaluating and correcting their own output). The book's own inventory-manager agent example plans a reorder quantity from sales history without being told the arithmetic steps to use. But the chapter is explicit that "agentic behavior remains an aspirational goal" because "nondeterminism, hallucinations, and various other failure modes pose challenges to building fully autonomous AI applications" — the same inventory prompt can return a different reorder quantity each time it runs. (Source location: "Agentic AI," "Characteristics of Agents.")

Responsible paraphrase: Autonomy is the headline feature of an agent and also its central risk: the same property that lets an agent plan without being told each step also means it can plan differently each time you ask, on the same input. The chapter's own worked example demonstrates both the promise and the caveat in the same three paragraphs — this is not the book hedging, it is the book stating agentic AI's actual current limitation.

Primary-source claim: The foundational-model landscape includes several distinct categories with real tradeoffs: frontier models (state-of-the-art capability, resource-intensive, cannot run locally), distilled models (reasonable capability at lower cost and faster response, e.g., Gemini Flash, Claude Sonnet), open-weight models (parameters public, customizable, but generally lag frontier capability and need hosting expertise), and locally hostable models (complete privacy, no ongoing API cost, but "significantly reduced capabilities compared to cloud models"). Model choice is presented as a budget-and-rating tradeoff read directly off a cost-vs-rating leaderboard, not a search for a single "best" model. (Source location: "The Landscape of Foundational Models.")

Responsible paraphrase: "Which model should I use" is a design decision with a stated tradeoff, the same way "which data structure" or "which loop" is — the chapter frames model selection as engineering judgment against constraints (cost, privacy, capability), not as picking whichever model is currently ranked first.

Primary-source claim: Foundational models also expose fine-grained generation controls — temperature (scales logits before the softmax step that converts them to probabilities, with temperature zero equivalent to always picking the single most likely next token), top-K sampling (restricts selection to the k most likely tokens), and nucleus/top-P sampling (dynamically selects the smallest token set whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold, adapting to the model's confidence at each step). The chapter's own worked example shows the same sentence stub completed at temperature 0.0, 0.5, and 0.8, with higher temperature producing more elaborated, more varied continuations. (Source location: "Fine-Grained Control," "Temperature," "Nucleus Sampling.")

Responsible paraphrase: These settings are not cosmetic knobs; they are the mechanism by which "the same prompt" can produce a deterministic, repeatable answer or a different answer every run, depending on a setting the developer chose. Knowing this distinguishes a professional who can explain why an application's output is (or is not) reproducible from one who just observes that it "seems random sometimes."

A Concrete Example: Two Ways to Call the Same Model

The chapter shows the same simple request — "write code to find the median value of a list of integers," directed at Claude Sonnet — implemented two ways: a direct call through the Anthropic Python SDK (client.messages.create(...)), and an equivalent call through the vendor-agnostic PydanticAI framework (Agent('anthropic:claude-3-7-sonnet-latest', ...)). The PydanticAI version's practical advantage is that switching providers means changing one model-name string — to openai:gpt-4o-mini, google-vertex:gemini-2.0-flash, or a locally hosted llama3.2 served through Ollama — rather than rewriting the integration code.

This single example carries the chapter's whole argument in miniature: the problem (how do I call a foundational model) has more than one proven solution (direct SDK vs. framework), and the right choice depends on a real tradeoff (simplicity now vs. portability later) — exactly the shape every pattern in the rest of the book will take.

Synthesis

Chapter 1's throughline is that GenAI's ease of prototyping is precisely what makes it easy to build something fragile: a system that looks finished after one good demo but has no answer for the recurring problems — wrong style, missing knowledge, missing capability, nondeterminism — that show up once real users and real stakes arrive. Design patterns exist because those problems are common enough, across enough projects, to be worth naming, cataloguing, and solving once rather than rediscovering under deadline pressure every time.

Reflection Questions

  1. The chapter states that agentic behavior "remains an aspirational goal" even though its own inventory-manager example demonstrates real planning and reasoning. Explain how both statements can be true at once, using the nondeterminism point from the reading.
  2. Using the frontier / distilled / open-weight / locally-hostable categories from the reading, explain why "which model should I use" does not have one universally correct answer.
  3. Pick one of the three recurring problems the chapter names (wrong style, missing enterprise knowledge, missing capability) and explain, in your own words, why it is a predictable engineering problem rather than bad luck.

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: Valliappa Lakshmanan and Sara Robinson, Generative AI Design Patterns (O'Reilly, 2025), Chapter 1, "Introduction," as processed into books/summaries/book_summary_generative_ai_design_patterns.md and its underlying chapter text at books/pipeline_runs/generative_ai_design_patterns/chapters/01_chapter_1_introduction.md.
  • This reading draws on Chapter 1 only — the book's introduction and orientation chapter — not the 32 individual patterns detailed in Chapters 2-10, which this book-pipeline run extracted but has not yet summarized or QC'd chapter-by-chapter.
  • Chapter 1's own worked examples (the median-value SDK/PydanticAI comparison, the inventory-manager agent, the temperature/top-K sampling text completions) are drawn directly from the chapter, not instructor-invented.
  • This is the Wednesday half of Week 16's paired session; Friday closes the semester with reflection on the course as a whole, not a second technical reading.

pages.title: Professional Minds Friday - Week 16 Friday Reading: From Studying to Learning
pages.body:
Week 16 Friday Reading: From Studying to Learning

[[DISCUSSION_SLIDES_LINK]]

  • Week and essential question: Week 16 — What kind of professional do I want to become?
  • Session role: Semester Reflection. This is the last Friday session of the semester, and the last time this course will ask you to sit with the question that has framed all sixteen weeks. It closes with the one book this course meant to open with.
  • Estimated reading time: approximately 7–9 minutes
  • Primary source: Teach Students How to Learn: Strategies You Can Incorporate Into Any Course to Improve Student Metacognition, Study Skills, and Motivation, 1st edition, Saundra Yancy McGuire with Stephanie McGuire — Chapter 4, "The Power of Teaching Bloom's Taxonomy and the Study Cycle to Students"
  • Perspective lens: none; single primary source, complete chapter.

Why You're Reading This Now, Not in Week 1

This book was supposed to be your Week 1 reading. It was meant to open this course by giving you a strategy for how to actually learn the sixteen weeks of material that followed, before you needed it. Week 1 became something else instead, and this reading sat unused — not because it stopped mattering, but because it lost its slot.

It belongs here instead, at the close. You have now spent a semester doing the thing this chapter describes: sometimes studying, sometimes actually learning. You have enough real experience behind you to test McGuire's distinction against your own habits rather than take it on faith. And the question this week asks — what kind of professional do I want to become? — is inseparable from a quieter question underneath it: what kind of learner do you intend to be, for the rest of your career, after this course stops assigning the readings for you?

The Strategy: Bloom's Taxonomy and the Study Cycle

Primary-source claim — Studying versus learning: McGuire presents studying as something students often associate with short-term memorization for an exam, while learning involves understanding information well enough to explain it, apply it, and reconstruct it. The chapter emphasizes focusing not only on the "whats," but also on the "hows," "whys," and "what ifs" of a subject (Chapter 4).

Primary-source claim — Teach it to understand it: The chapter asks learners to compare preparing to make an A on a test with preparing to teach the material to others. Teaching requires deeper knowledge because the learner must explain the material in more than one way, anticipate questions, and discover gaps in understanding before someone else exposes them. Learners do not need an actual class; they can explain the material to a colleague, family member, friend, or even an imagined audience (Chapter 4).

Responsible paraphrase — Bloom's revised taxonomy: The chapter presents Bloom's revised taxonomy as six levels of cognitive learning:

  1. Remembering: retrieving, recognizing, and recalling relevant knowledge.
  2. Understanding: putting information into one's own words and constructing meaning.
  3. Applying: using a procedure or concept to address a new problem or situation.
  4. Analyzing: breaking material into parts and examining how those parts relate.
  5. Evaluating: making judgments using criteria and standards.
  6. Creating: combining or reorganizing elements into a new pattern, product, or process.

The chapter presents these levels as a useful hierarchy: higher-level thinking generally depends on knowledge that has already been learned and understood. It also acknowledges that some educators view the levels as overlapping rather than strictly sequential. McGuire uses the hierarchy to remind students that they cannot reliably apply or critically evaluate information they have not learned and understood (Chapter 4).

Responsible paraphrase — Learning goals: Bloom's helps learners replace vague performance goals with specific learning goals. Instead of merely aiming for a certain grade or outcome, a learner can ask: Do I need to remember the information, explain it, apply it to an unfamiliar situation, analyze its parts, evaluate alternatives, or create something new? The chapter argues that identifying the required level makes study more purposeful (Chapter 4).

Primary-source claim — The five-step Study Cycle: McGuire introduces a Study Cycle consisting of five steps:

  1. Preview: Skim the material, notice headings and emphasized terms, review summaries and objectives, and develop questions to guide upcoming learning.
  2. Attend: Participate in the learning setting, ask and answer questions, and take meaningful notes.
  3. Review: Revisit notes as soon as possible, fill in gaps, and identify questions or areas requiring help.
  4. Study: Use focused, active study sessions. Ask questions such as "why," "how," and "what if," and work toward a specific goal.
  5. Assess: Check whether the learning method is working and whether the material can be explained to someone else. Adjust the strategy when necessary.

The chapter describes intense study sessions as a practical structure within the Study Cycle. A session includes setting a specific goal, working actively with the material, taking a restorative break, and briefly reviewing what was learned. The length can vary according to the learner's ability to maintain focus (Chapter 4).

A Concrete Example

Imagine that Maya, a new project coordinator, must learn how to use a project-management platform at work. Simply watching a demonstration and memorizing where buttons are located might help her remember basic functions. To learn the tool more fully, she previews the help materials, attends the onboarding session, and reviews her notes shortly afterward.

During a focused study session, Maya sets a goal: create and assign a small project with deadlines, dependencies, and a status report. She asks herself why each feature matters, how the features affect one another, and what she would do if a deadline changed. After practicing, she explains the workflow to a coworker. When the coworker asks how to handle a delayed task, Maya discovers a gap in her understanding. She then changes her next study session to focus on that problem.

Maya is moving beyond remembering menu locations. She is understanding the workflow, applying it to a task, analyzing relationships among project elements, evaluating possible responses, and eventually creating a process her team can use. Nobody assigned Maya this learning. She will keep doing it, in some form, for as long as she has a job — which is the same position you are about to be in.

Synthesis

McGuire's central lesson is that successful learning requires deliberate movement beyond short-term memorization. Bloom's Taxonomy helps professionals identify the level of thinking a task requires, while the Study Cycle turns that awareness into repeated practice: preview, participate, review, study actively, and assess honestly. Successful professionals learn by building knowledge they can use, explain, test, and adapt — a habit that has to survive the last day of a class, because no future employer is going to assign it a due date.

Reflection Questions

  1. Look back across this semester, not forward to a hypothetical task. Name one week or one skill where you were genuinely in "learn mode" — explaining, applying, reconstructing — and one where you were honestly in "make-an-A mode." What was different about how you approached each?

  2. Which level of Bloom's Taxonomy do you most need for the kind of professional you want to become — not the level that's easiest for you, but the one your intended work actually demands? Explain your reasoning.

  3. Design one Study Cycle for a real skill you intend to keep building after this course ends. What will you preview, when will you review, what will your focused study goal be, and how will you assess whether you can actually use the skill — with no instructor left to check your work?

Source and Limitation Note

  • Primary source: McGuire, Saundra Yancy, with Stephanie McGuire. Teach Students How to Learn: Strategies You Can Incorporate Into Any Course to Improve Student Metacognition, Study Skills, and Motivation. 1st edition. Chapter 4, "The Power of Teaching Bloom's Taxonomy and the Study Cycle to Students."
  • This reading draws on one chapter as an "appetizer" selection, not on the whole book. It was originally drafted for Week 1 ("Success Foundations") under the same title and chapter; the chapter's substance is unchanged here — only the framing (opening, closing, and Reflection Questions) has been adapted from an early-semester introduction to a semester-closing reflection, to fit this session's actual place in the course. See semester_kickoff_week/success_foundations_supplemental/fri_studying_vs_learning.md for the original early-semester framing of the same chapter.

pages.title: Week 16 - References / Verification
pages.body:
Week 16 reference map - Farkle cost versus effectiveness

1. Course-owned teaching surface

Start here:

  • README.md - Week at a Glance and scope;
  • monday.md - the cost/effectiveness model and prediction;
  • wednesday.md - required CPU experiment path;
  • friday.md - bounded Architecture judgment;
  • code/architecture_farkle/ - course-owned host/timing receipt layer.

2. Canonical computational truth

The generated package under:

code/farkle_ml/

comes from:

jeremy-evert/Farkle_and_Machine_Learning

The local file:

code/farkle_ml/_SHARED_PROVENANCE.json

records the shared repository, source path, source commit, synchronization-time repository head, and SHA-256 hashes for the generated package.

The canonical shared design documents that motivate the Architecture lens are:

  • planning/architecture-cost-effectiveness-lens.md in the shared repository;
  • planning/hardware-lane-and-receipt-map.md in the shared repository.

Those documents define the cross-course experiment doctrine. This course owns the student interpretation, not a second copy of that doctrine.

3. Primary truth inside the benchmark

For technical verification, inspect the generated shared modules directly:

  • code/farkle_ml/engine.py - classroom rules and turn engine;
  • code/farkle_ml/experiment.py - preparation/runtime/effectiveness receipt schema;
  • code/farkle_ml/simulate.py - fair repeated-game simulation and raw denominators;
  • code/farkle_ml/strategies.py - fixed strategy families.

Computer Architecture's execution evidence lives in:

  • code/architecture_farkle/host.py - host facts and explicit CPU execution claim;
  • code/architecture_farkle/runner.py - repeated timing receipts;
  • code/architecture_farkle/cli.py - student/instructor command path.

4. Optional reinforcement

Earlier course weeks remain the best source for the Architecture concepts students may use to explain their evidence:

  • latency / throughput;
  • memory and locality;
  • parallelism and scaling;
  • communication/data movement;
  • vectorization/specialization;
  • workload-driven design judgment.

Week 16 does not reopen those units or require new external reading.

Reuse note

No external textbook passage is copied into the Week 16 teaching surface. The Farkle computational package is generated from the course-family canonical repository with recorded provenance. Course-specific prose and judgment prompts remain owned here.

pages.title: Week 17 - Week at a Glance
pages.body:
Week 17 - Reflection and Closure

Central question: What can I see, measure, and explain about a computer now that I could not at the start of the semester?

Finals-week posture

No new technical material. No new Architecture lab. No Machine Dossier expansion.

Your evidence already exists. Week 17 is about reading that evidence as a record of changed understanding.

Required work

  1. Complete A7 - Final Reflection: What Can You See Now?
  2. Complete the university course evaluation through the institution's normal evaluation process. The Canvas course-evaluation object exists only to hold the accepted completion-credit category.

Evidence you may use

  • Week 2 verification receipt;
  • Week 3 reproducibility receipt;
  • Week 4 machine observations;
  • Weeks 5-14 labs, traces, plots, checkpoints, and frozen Machine Dossier;
  • Week 16 Farkle + ML cost/effectiveness evidence;
  • professional-pathway evidence where relevant to your next step.

Final boundary

Do not rebuild the course, add features to the frozen dossier, or manufacture new measurements merely to make the reflection look impressive. Use the evidence you genuinely made.
